questions.stem: At a section of a beam where the shear force is zero and changes sign, the bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**A maximum or minimum.**

**Because shear force is the DERIVATIVE of bending moment:**

> **V = dM/dx**

so where **V = 0**, **dM/dx = 0** — a stationary point of the bending moment diagram. If V also **changes sign** there, it is a genuine **maximum or minimum**.

**The full set of differential relations**, which govern every shear force and bending moment diagram:

> **w = −dV/dx**  (load intensity)
> **V = dM/dx**  (shear force)

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Slope of the SFD** at a point | **= −load intensity** there |
| **Slope of the BMD** at a point | **= shear force** there |
| **Change in V** between two points | **= −area of the load diagram** between them |
| **Change in M** between two points | **= AREA of the SHEAR diagram** between them |

**The area rule is the fastest way to draw a BMD by hand**, and it should be the default method: compute the shear diagram first, then accumulate its areas.

**The degree relationship** follows from the same integrations, and it is worth knowing because it tells you the shape of each diagram before you draw it:

| Loading | Load | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | — | **Constant** (jumps at the load) | **Linear** |
| **Uniformly distributed** | Constant | **Linear** | **Parabolic** |
| **Triangular (linearly varying)** | Linear | **Parabolic** | **Cubic** |
| Couple applied | — | No change | **Jumps** by the couple |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one.** A UDL gives a linear shear and a parabolic moment; that single fact resolves most diagram-shape questions.

**Discontinuities:**

| At a | Shear diagram | Moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Point LOAD** | **JUMPS** by the load | **Kink** (slope changes) — but continuous |
| **Applied COUPLE** | **No change** | **JUMPS** by the couple |
| Support reaction | Jumps by the reaction | Kink |

**The couple case catches people out**: an applied moment produces a **step in the BMD** and **no change at all in the SFD** — the opposite of a point load.

**Standard maximum moments** worth having by heart:

| Beam and loading | Maximum moment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported, central point load W** | **WL/4** |
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **wL²/8** |
| **Cantilever, end point load W** | **WL** (at the fixed end) |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **wL²/2** (at the fixed end) |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL w** | **wL²/12** at supports, **wL²/24** at midspan |
| Propped cantilever, UDL w | wL²/8 at the fixed end |

**Note the fixed-ended beam's advantage**: its maximum moment (wL²/12) is **two thirds** of the simply supported value (wL²/8), and it is distributed between support and span rather than concentrated at midspan. That redistribution is why continuity is structurally valuable — and why a continuous beam is lighter than a series of simply supported ones.

**A point of caution on the question's wording**: V = 0 is necessary but not sufficient for a maximum. Where the shear is zero over a **length** (an unloaded region with no shear), the moment is **constant** there — stationary but not a peak. The sign change is what makes it a true extremum.

examTip.trap: "Zero" is offered because the moment IS zero at a point of contraflexure — but that is where the moment **changes sign**, not where the shear does. Two different sections.
examTip.trick: **V = dM/dx**, so V = 0 is the stationary point of the moment diagram. Add a **sign change** and it is a genuine maximum or minimum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slope of the BMD is the shear; slope of the SFD is minus the load.** Each integration raises the degree by one: point load → constant shear → linear moment; UDL → linear shear → parabolic moment.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w per unit length. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**wL²/8**, occurring at **midspan**.

**Derivation.** By symmetry each reaction is **wL/2**. Taking moments at midspan:

> **M = (wL/2)(L/2) − (wL/2)(L/4) = wL²/4 − wL²/8 = wL²/8** ✓

**Or by the area rule**: the shear varies linearly from +wL/2 at the left support to zero at midspan, so the area of the shear diagram over that half-span is **½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8** ✓ — the change in moment from the support (where M = 0) to midspan.

**The two most-used standard results:**

| Loading on a simply supported span L | Maximum moment | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **UDL w** | **wL²/8** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/4** | **WL³/(48EI)** |

**A useful comparison.** For the **same total load** W = wL:

| | Moment | Deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **As a UDL** | **WL/8** | **5WL³/(384EI)** = WL³/76.8EI |
| **As a central point load** | **WL/4** | **WL³/(48EI)** |
| Ratio (point/UDL) | **2.0** | **1.6** |

> A central point load produces **twice the moment** and **1.6 times the deflection** of the same total load spread uniformly. Concentrating load is structurally expensive, which is why loads are distributed wherever the arrangement permits.

**Other standard maximum moments:**

| Beam | Loading | M_max |
|---|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | End load W | **WL** |
| **Cantilever** | UDL w | **wL²/2** |
| **Fixed both ends** | UDL w | **wL²/12** at supports, wL²/24 at midspan |
| **Fixed both ends** | Central load W | WL/8 at both supports and midspan |
| **Propped cantilever** | UDL w | **wL²/8** at the fixed end |
| Simply supported | Point load W at a from one end | **Wab/L** |

**The Wab/L result** is worth carrying because it generalises the WL/4 case: with a = b = L/2 it gives WL/4 ✓, and it handles any off-centre load directly.

**Note the L² dependence** in every distributed-load case:

> **Doubling the span QUADRUPLES the bending moment** for the same load intensity. That is the dominant fact of beam design, and it is why long spans require disproportionately deep sections — or a different structural system altogether (trusses, arches, cables), which carry load primarily by **axial** action rather than bending.

**And the L⁴ in deflection** is more severe still:

> Doubling the span increases the deflection **sixteenfold** at the same load intensity. For long spans **deflection, not strength, usually governs** — which is why span-to-depth ratio limits (IS 456 gives 20 for simply supported, 26 for continuous) exist as a deemed-to-satisfy check.

**A cross-check on the answer's plausibility**: wL²/8 for a 6 m span carrying 20 kN/m gives **90 kN·m** — a sensible design moment for a beam of that span, and consistent with a section around 300 × 500 mm in reinforced concrete.

examTip.trick: Get it from the **area of the shear diagram**: ½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8. Same answer, and it is a check on the formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **UDL wL²/8, central point load WL/4** — the point load gives **twice** the moment for the same total load. Note **M ∝ L²**: doubling the span quadruples the moment, which is why long spans need a different structural system rather than a deeper beam.

questions.stem: A point of contraflexure in a beam is a section where the:
questions.solution:
**Where the bending moment CHANGES SIGN, passing through zero.**

**Also called the point of inflexion.** At that section:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bending moment** | **ZERO** |
| **Curvature** | **Zero** — and it reverses |
| The beam changes from | **Sagging to hogging**, or the reverse |
| Tension moves from | One face to the other |

**Where they occur:**

| Structure | Points of contraflexure |
|---|---|
| **Overhanging beam** | Between the support and the point of maximum sagging moment |
| **Fixed-ended beam under UDL** | At **0.211L from each end** |
| **Propped cantilever under UDL** | At **0.25L from the propped end** |
| **Continuous beam** | Near each interior support |
| Portal frame column | Near mid-height under lateral load |

**Why they matter practically — three distinct reasons:**

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCEMENT CURTAILMENT** | The moment reverses, so **top steel is needed on one side and bottom steel on the other**. The contraflexure point locates where each can be curtailed |
| **HINGE PLACEMENT** in a hinged (Gerber) beam | A hinge carries no moment, so placing it at a natural contraflexure point makes the structure **determinate without changing its moments** |
| **Effective length** of columns | The distance between contraflexure points is the **effective buckling length** — it behaves as a pin-ended strut |

**The reinforcement point is the everyday one**, and getting it wrong is a real and recurring detailing failure:

> Near a continuous support the beam **HOGS** — tension is at the **TOP** — so the main steel must be in the **top face**. Away from the support it **SAGS** and the steel belongs at the **bottom**. Steel curtailed before the moment has actually reversed leaves a section with tension and no reinforcement to carry it.

IS 456 accordingly requires bars to extend a **development length beyond** the point where they are no longer required by calculation, and at least **d or 12φ** past the theoretical cut-off — a margin precisely because the true contraflexure position shifts with the loading pattern.

**That shifting is the subtlety worth stating:**

> The point of contraflexure **MOVES as the loading pattern changes**. A continuous beam loaded on alternate spans has its contraflexure points in quite different places from one loaded on all spans.

So curtailment must be based on the **envelope** of all load cases, not a single analysis — which is why detailing rules are conservative and why simple codified rules (curtail at 0.15L, 0.25L and so on) are provided for standard cases.

**The effective-length application** is worth a note because it links this topic to columns:

> Between two points of contraflexure a member is, in bending terms, **equivalent to a pin-ended strut** — zero moment at both ends. The distance between them is therefore the **effective length L_e** for buckling.

That is the physical reason behind the effective length factors: a fixed–fixed column has contraflexure points at the quarter points, so **L_e = 0.5L**; a fixed–free (cantilever) column has none within its length and its equivalent pin-ended strut is twice as long, so **L_e = 2L**.

**Distinguishing it from the distractors:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| Shear force maximum | Usually at a support |
| **Deflection maximum** | Where the **SLOPE is zero** — a quite different section |
| **Slope zero** | The point of maximum deflection |
| **Moment zero and reversing** | **Contraflexure** ✓ |

**Note that zero moment alone is not enough** — the moment is zero at the ends of every simply supported beam, and those are not points of contraflexure because the moment does not **reverse** there.

examTip.trap: "Deflection is maximum" describes where the **SLOPE is zero** — an entirely different section. And zero moment alone is not enough: the moment is zero at both ends of every simply supported beam, and those are not contraflexure points.
examTip.trick: The moment must **pass through zero AND reverse**. Sagging becomes hogging, so the tension face swaps.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tension moves from the bottom face to the top** — which is why the contraflexure point governs where **reinforcement can be curtailed**. It also **MOVES with the load pattern**, so curtail on the envelope, never on one analysis.

questions.stem: In the shear force diagram of a beam, an applied couple at a section produces:
options: A jump equal to the couple
No change in the shear force
questions.solution:
**No change in the shear force** — the couple produces a **jump in the BENDING MOMENT diagram** instead.

**The contrast with a point load** is the whole point, and it is a standard examination discriminator:

| Applied at a section | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **POINT LOAD W** | **JUMPS by W** | **Kink** — slope changes, but continuous |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change** | **JUMPS by M** |

**Why.** Consider a short element containing the couple:

> **Vertical equilibrium**: a couple applies **no net vertical force**, so the shear on either side is **unchanged**.
> **Moment equilibrium**: the couple must be balanced, so the bending moment **steps by exactly its magnitude**.

**A point load does the reverse**: it applies a vertical force (so V jumps) but contributes no moment at its own location (so M is continuous, though its slope changes because V has changed).

**The complete table of diagram behaviour:**

| Feature | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| Free end | V = 0 | M = 0 |
| **Simply supported end** | V = reaction | **M = 0** |
| **Fixed end** | V = reaction | **M = fixing moment** |
| Internal **hinge** | — | **M = 0** |
| Point load | **Jump** | Kink |
| **Couple** | **Nothing** | **Jump** |
| UDL | Linear | Parabolic |
| Free (unloaded) span | Constant | Linear |

**The internal hinge condition M = 0** is what makes hinged (Gerber) beams determinate: each hinge supplies one extra equation, so a beam with the right number of hinges can be solved by statics alone.

**Where applied couples actually arise in practice:**

| Situation | Source of the couple |
|---|---|
| A **bracket or cantilever** framing into a beam | The eccentric load is resolved into a force plus a **couple** |
| A column framing eccentrically into a beam | Eccentric axial load |
| **Torsion transferred** from a secondary beam | — |
| Fixed-end moments transferred at a joint | Frame analysis |
| A crane bracket on a column | The classic case |

**The bracket case is the everyday one**, and resolving it correctly is a routine skill:

> A load **P at eccentricity e** from a member's axis is statically equivalent to **P acting on the axis PLUS a couple Pe**. The force enters the shear diagram; the couple steps the moment diagram.

Failing to include the couple — analysing only the transferred force — understates the moment, and it is a genuine and common error in the design of brackets, corbels and eccentric column connections.

**Sign conventions**, which must be stated before any diagram is drawn:

| Convention | Positive |
|---|---|
| **Shear force** | Left portion tends to move **UP** relative to the right |
| **Bending moment** | **SAGGING** — compression on top, tension at the bottom |

> Any consistent convention gives correct answers, but **mixing conventions mid-problem** is a reliable source of sign errors. State it once and hold to it.

**A practical drawing check**: at the far end of any beam, the diagram must **close** — the shear must return to zero (or to the final reaction) and the moment must return to zero at a free or simply supported end. A diagram that does not close indicates an arithmetic error, and checking closure catches most slips before they propagate into a design.

examTip.trap: This is a deliberate discriminator and it catches people every sitting — a **point load** jumps the shear diagram, so candidates assume a couple must jump it too.
examTip.trick: A couple applies **no net vertical force**, so vertical equilibrium leaves the shear unchanged. Moment equilibrium forces the BMD to **step** by the couple.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load: jumps V, kinks M. Couple: nothing to V, jumps M.** Where does a couple come from in practice? A **bracket** — a load P at eccentricity e is P on the axis PLUS a couple Pe. Omitting the couple is a real design error.

questions.stem: A cantilever of length 3 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its whole length. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**54 kN·m**, at the fixed end.

> **M_max = wL²/2 = 12 × 3²/2 = 12 × 9/2 = 54 kN·m** ✓

**Option (a), 18 kN·m**, is **wL²/6**; option (c), 36 kN·m, is **WL/2** using the total load W = 36 kN with the wrong lever arm; option (d), 13.5 kN·m, is **wL²/8** — the simply supported value, applied to a cantilever.

**The physical route** confirms it: the total load is **W = 12 × 3 = 36 kN**, acting at its centroid **1.5 m** from the fixed end:

> **M = 36 × 1.5 = 54 kN·m** ✓

**Cantilever standard results:**

| Loading | M_max (at the fixed end) | δ_max (at the free end) |
|---|---|---|
| **End point load W** | **WL** | **WL³/(3EI)** |
| **UDL w** | **wL²/2** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** |
| Triangular, maximum at the fixed end | wL²/6 | 11wL⁴/(120EI) |
| Couple M at the free end | M (constant throughout) | ML²/(2EI) |

**Comparison with a simply supported beam** of the same span and loading:

| | Cantilever | Simply supported | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M_max under UDL** | **wL²/2** | **wL²/8** | **4×** |
| **δ_max under UDL** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** | **9.6×** |

> A cantilever carries **four times the moment** and **nearly ten times the deflection** of a simply supported beam of the same span and load. Cantilevers are structurally expensive, and their **deflection almost always governs**.

**That is why cantilever span-to-depth limits are so much tighter**: IS 456 gives a basic span/depth of **7 for a cantilever** against **20 for a simply supported** beam — a factor of nearly three in required depth.

**Practical points about cantilevers:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tension is at the TOP** | **Main reinforcement goes in the TOP face** — the single most important detailing fact, and a classic site error |
| **Deflection usually governs** | Not strength |
| The **fixed end must genuinely be fixed** | The backspan must provide the restraining moment, with enough dead load to prevent uplift |
| **No redundancy** | A cantilever is **determinate** — failure at the root is **total collapse**, with no alternative load path |
| Sensitive to **construction loading** | Propping removal sequence matters |

**The lack of redundancy deserves emphasis:**

> A cantilever has **no alternative load path**. A continuous beam that yields at one section redistributes moment to others and gives warning; a cantilever that fails at its root **falls**. Balconies and canopies have collapsed for exactly this reason, usually because the top steel was misplaced to the bottom during construction.

That combination — top steel, no redundancy, and an error that is invisible once the concrete is poured — makes cantilever reinforcement one of the details most worth checking personally before a pour.

**The backspan requirement** is the other common oversight: the fixing moment at the root must be equilibrated by the adjoining span. Where the backspan is short or lightly loaded, the cantilever can **lift the far support**, and the design must either provide sufficient dead load or physically tie the support down.

examTip.trap: 13.5 kN·m is **wL²/8** — the simply supported value applied to a cantilever. It is four times too small.
examTip.trick: Check physically: total load 12 × 3 = 36 kN acting at its centroid **1.5 m** from the support, so M = 36 × 1.5 = 54 kN·m ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Cantilever wL²/2 — FOUR times the simply supported wL²/8, and nearly TEN times the deflection.** And the detailing consequence that matters: **tension is at the TOP, so the main steel goes in the top face.** A cantilever is determinate, so an error at the root means collapse, not cracking.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load, the shear force diagram is:
options: Linear, varying from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other
questions.solution:
**Linear, varying from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other**, passing through zero at midspan.

**Because of the differential relation:**

> **dV/dx = −w**

With **w constant** (a UDL), the slope of the shear diagram is constant — so **V varies LINEARLY**.

**And integrating once more:**

> **dM/dx = V**, and V is linear, so **M is PARABOLIC** ✓ — with its maximum at midspan where V = 0.

**The degree ladder**, which predicts every diagram's shape before it is drawn:

| Loading | Load diagram | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | — | **Constant** | **Linear** |
| **UDL** | **Constant** | **Linear** | **Parabolic** |
| **Triangular** | Linear | **Parabolic** | **Cubic** |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one.** That single rule answers most diagram-shape questions without any calculation.

**Values for the simply supported UDL case:**

| Location | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Left support** | **+wL/2** | **0** |
| Quarter point | +wL/4 | 3wL²/32 |
| **Midspan** | **0** | **wL²/8 — maximum** |
| Three-quarter point | −wL/4 | 3wL²/32 |
| **Right support** | **−wL/2** | **0** |

**The sign change at midspan** is exactly the condition for the moment maximum, as required by V = dM/dx.

**Where each governs the design:**

| Quantity | Maximum at | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| **SHEAR** | **The SUPPORTS** | Shear reinforcement (stirrups), web thickness |
| **MOMENT** | **MIDSPAN** | Main flexural reinforcement, section depth |

> They are maximum at **different sections**, which is the basis of efficient detailing: **stirrups closely spaced near the supports** and widely spaced at midspan; **main bars fully provided at midspan** and curtailed toward the supports.

**A caution about the shear used in design**: IS 456 permits the **critical section for shear** to be taken at a distance **d from the face of the support** rather than at the support itself, where the reaction introduces compression that enhances the shear capacity. Using the support value is conservative but wasteful.

**The area rule as a check:**

> Change in moment = **area of the shear diagram**

From the left support to midspan: **½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8** ✓ — the moment at midspan, since M = 0 at the support. That agreement is a quick verification of any hand-drawn pair of diagrams.

**And the closure check**: over the whole span the shear diagram's area must be **zero** (two equal triangles of opposite sign), which correctly returns the moment to zero at the right support ✓.

**For a cantilever under UDL**, by contrast, the shear is **linear from 0 at the free end to wL at the fixed end** (all of one sign, no zero crossing within the span) and the moment is **parabolic from 0 to wL²/2**. The absence of a sign change is why the cantilever's maximum moment is at its **support** rather than within the span — a useful contrast to hold alongside this case.

examTip.trick: **dV/dx = −w**, and w is constant for a UDL, so the shear must vary **linearly** — from +wL/2 through zero at midspan to −wL/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear peaks at the SUPPORTS, moment at MIDSPAN.** Different sections, which is the whole basis of efficient detailing — stirrups close together near the supports, main bars fully provided at midspan. IS 456 also lets you take the critical shear section at **d from the support face**.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a point load of 40 kN at 3 m from the left support. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**75 kN·m**, under the load.

> **M_max = Wab/L**, with a = 3 m, b = 5 m, L = 8 m
> **= 40 × 3 × 5/8 = 600/8 = 75 kN·m** ✓

**Check by reactions:**

> **R_left = Wb/L = 40 × 5/8 = 25 kN**
> **R_right = Wa/L = 40 × 3/8 = 15 kN** (sum = 40 ✓)
> **M under the load = R_left × a = 25 × 3 = 75 kN·m** ✓

**Both routes agree.** Option (a), 80 kN·m, is **WL/4** — the value for a **central** load, which this is not.

**The Wab/L formula** generalises the familiar central-load case:

| Load position | a, b | M_max |
|---|---|---|
| **Centre** | L/2, L/2 | **WL²/4L = WL/4** ✓ |
| Quarter point | L/4, 3L/4 | 3WL/16 |
| **This case (3/8 span)** | 3, 5 | **15WL/64 = 75 kN·m** |
| Near a support | small a | Small |

> The maximum moment is **greatest when the load is at midspan** and falls as the load moves toward either support — which is why the central position is the critical one for a single moving load.

**The shear and moment diagrams** for this beam:

| Segment | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| Left support to the load | **+25 kN** (constant) | **Linear**, 0 → 75 kN·m |
| At the load | **JUMPS by 40 kN**, 25 → −15 | **Kink** — continuous at 75 |
| Load to right support | **−15 kN** (constant) | **Linear**, 75 → 0 |

**The maximum moment is at the load** because that is where the shear **changes sign** — from +25 to −15. The jump passes through zero, satisfying the condition for a moment extremum.

**Note that the peak moment occurs at a point where V is discontinuous**, not where it is smoothly zero. That is characteristic of point-load problems and is a small extension of the V = 0 rule: the moment peaks wherever the shear **passes through or jumps across zero**.

**MOVING LOADS** are the natural extension, and they matter for bridges and crane girders:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Where is the **absolute maximum moment** for a **single** moving load? | **At midspan**, value **WL/4** |
| Where is the **maximum moment at a GIVEN section**? | When the **load is at that section** |
| Maximum **shear** for a single moving load? | **At a support**, with the load **adjacent** to it, value **W** |

**For a train of loads**, the governing rule is less obvious and worth knowing:

> The **absolute maximum bending moment** occurs under the load nearest the resultant, when the **midspan bisects the distance between that load and the RESULTANT of all the loads on the span**.

**INFLUENCE LINES** are the systematic tool for moving loads:

> An **influence line** plots the value of one **response quantity at one fixed section** as a **unit load moves** across the structure.

| Influence line for | Shape (simply supported span) |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | Linear, 1 at A to 0 at B |
| **Moment at section x** | **Triangular**, peak **ab/L** at x |
| **Shear at section x** | Two parallel lines with a **unit step** at x |

**Do not confuse an influence line with a bending moment diagram:**

| | Bending moment diagram | Influence line |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | **Moment at EVERY section**, for a **FIXED** load | **One quantity at ONE section**, for a **MOVING** unit load |
| Varies with | Position along the beam | Position of the **load** |

They happen to have the same triangular shape for this case, which makes the confusion easy — but they answer entirely different questions.

examTip.trap: 80 kN·m is **WL/4**, the value for a **central** load. This load is not central.
examTip.trick: **M = Wab/L = 40 × 3 × 5/8 = 75 kN·m.** Check via reactions: R_left = Wb/L = 25 kN, and 25 × 3 = 75 ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Wab/L reduces to WL/4 when a = b = L/2** — one formula covers both. The peak sits under the load, because that is where the shear **jumps through** zero.

questions.stem: At an internal hinge in a beam, the condition that makes the structure statically determinate is that the:
questions.solution:
**The bending moment is zero.**

**A hinge transmits shear and axial force but NOT moment**, so it supplies **one additional equation of condition** — and each such equation reduces the degree of static indeterminacy by one.

**Static indeterminacy:**

> **D_s = (number of unknown reactions + internal forces) − (equations of equilibrium + equations of condition)**

For a plane beam: **3 equilibrium equations** (ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, ΣM = 0), plus **one condition equation per internal hinge**.

**Worked examples:**

| Beam | Reactions | Conditions | D_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simply supported | 3 | 0 | **0 — determinate** |
| Cantilever | 3 | 0 | **0 — determinate** |
| **Propped cantilever** | 4 | 0 | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | 6 | 0 | **3** |
| Continuous, 3 spans | 5 | 0 | **2** |
| **Fixed both ends with 2 internal hinges** | 6 | **2** | **1** |

**GERBER (hinged) beams** exploit this deliberately:

> Inserting the **right number of hinges in the right places** makes a continuous beam **determinate**, so it can be analysed by statics alone — and, more importantly, so that it is **insensitive to support settlement**.

**That insensitivity is the real engineering motive**, not the ease of analysis:

| Structure | Effect of a support settling |
|---|---|
| **Indeterminate** (continuous) | **Large secondary moments** are induced — potentially exceeding the design moments |
| **DETERMINATE** (Gerber) | **NO stresses induced at all** — the structure simply accommodates the movement |

> A **determinate** structure is **free of self-stress**: settlement, temperature change, shrinkage, creep and lack of fit produce **movement but no force**. An indeterminate one resists the movement and stresses itself doing so.

**Which gives the fundamental trade-off:**

| | **DETERMINATE** | **INDETERMINATE** |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis | **Statics alone** | Needs **compatibility** as well |
| Settlement, temperature, shrinkage | **No stress** | **Induces stress** |
| **Redundancy** | **NONE** — one failure means **collapse** | **Alternative load paths** — failure is contained |
| Material efficiency | Lower | **Higher** — moments are shared and peaks reduced |
| Deflections | Larger | Smaller |

**Redundancy is why most real structures ARE indeterminate**, despite the analytical inconvenience:

> A determinate structure has **exactly enough** members. Lose one and it becomes a **mechanism** — it collapses. An indeterminate structure can **redistribute** load around a failed element, which is the structural basis of **robustness** and the defence against **progressive collapse**.

**Where determinate structures are nevertheless preferred:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Poor or variable founding conditions** | Differential settlement is expected |
| **Long bridges** with large thermal movement | Avoids restraint forces |
| Structures on **mining or subsidence** ground | Movement is certain |
| Where a **simple, checkable analysis** is wanted | — |
| Precast construction with simple connections | Buildability |

**Locating the hinges in a Gerber beam** is not arbitrary: they are placed at the **natural points of contraflexure** of the equivalent continuous beam, so the moment distribution is essentially unchanged while the structure becomes determinate. That gives the efficiency of continuity with the settlement-tolerance of determinacy — an elegant compromise, and the reason the arrangement was used so widely for long bridge girders.

**Kinematic instability** is the trap to avoid: adding **too many** hinges, or placing them badly, turns the structure into a **mechanism**. A beam is unstable if D_s < 0, and it can also be unstable with D_s ≥ 0 if the restraints are badly arranged — for example, three parallel reactions, or three reactions whose lines of action meet at a point. **Counting alone does not prove stability**; the geometry must be checked too.

examTip.trick: A hinge transmits shear and axial force but **not moment**, so it supplies one **equation of condition** and reduces the indeterminacy by one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Determinate structures are FREE OF SELF-STRESS** — settlement, temperature and shrinkage produce movement but no force. That is the real reason for a Gerber beam, not the easier arithmetic. The price is **no redundancy**: one failure is collapse.

questions.stem: An overhanging beam is one which:
options: Has one or both ends projecting beyond the supports
Is supported at the centre only
questions.solution:
**One that has one or both ends projecting beyond its supports.**

**Types of beam by support arrangement:**

| Type | Description | D_s |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | A pin and a roller at the ends | **0** |
| **Cantilever** | **Fixed at one end**, free at the other | **0** |
| **OVERHANGING** | Supports **inboard** of one or both ends | **0** |
| **Propped cantilever** | Fixed one end, simply supported the other | **1** |
| **Fixed (built-in)** | Fixed at both ends | **3** |
| **Continuous** | More than two supports | **(n − 2)** for n supports |

**An overhanging beam is DETERMINATE** — it has only three reaction components, so statics suffices.

**Its characteristic behaviour, and the reason it is used:**

> The overhang produces a **HOGGING (negative) moment** at the support, which **REDUCES the SAGGING moment in the main span**.

**That reduction is a genuine structural benefit:**

| Beam, span L, UDL w | Maximum sagging moment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **wL²/8** |
| With overhangs of **0.207L** each side | **wL²/16** — **halved** |

**The optimum overhang** for a UDL, balancing the hogging and sagging peaks:

> **Overhang ≈ 0.207 L** (that is, L/(2 + 2√2)), giving **equal** hogging and sagging moments of **wL²/16** — **half** the simply supported value.

> Halving the design moment for the same span is a substantial saving, obtained purely by moving the supports inward. It is why cantilevered slab edges, overhanging bridge decks and balanced-cantilever construction are so common.

**Points of contraflexure** are the other characteristic feature: an overhanging beam has the moment **hogging over the support** and **sagging in the span**, so a contraflexure point lies between them — and it locates where the top and bottom reinforcement must each be carried to.

**The practical caution — UPLIFT:**

> If the **overhang is heavily loaded and the main span is not**, the far support can experience **UPLIFT** — a **negative reaction**.

| Consequence | Requirement |
|---|---|
| A **roller or simple bearing cannot resist uplift** | It lifts off |
| The beam may **tip** | Loss of support |
| Design response | **HOLDING-DOWN bolts** or **anchor** at that support, or sufficient dead load |

**Checking for uplift requires the ADVERSE load pattern**, not the full-load case:

> Take **maximum load on the overhang** and **minimum load (dead load only, with the load factor reduced to 0.9) on the main span**. That combination, not the fully loaded one, is what produces uplift.

Analysing only the uniformly loaded case conceals the problem entirely, which is why the pattern-loading check is a code requirement rather than a refinement.

**Where overhanging beams appear:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Balconies and canopies** | The overhang is the useful part |
| **Bridge decks** projecting beyond the outer girders | Reduces the deck's internal moments |
| **Cantilever (balanced) bridge construction** | Built out symmetrically from piers |
| **Crane runway girders** | — |
| Roof purlins over end walls | — |

**Balanced cantilever construction** is the large-scale expression of the principle: segments are built out **symmetrically** from each pier so the hogging moments balance and the pier carries little net moment during construction — then the tips are joined to form a continuous deck. It allows long spans to be built without falsework, which is decisive over deep valleys and rivers.

examTip.trick: The overhang produces a **hogging** moment at the support that partly cancels the sagging moment in the span. With overhangs of **0.207L** the maximum moment is **halved**, from wL²/8 to wL²/16.
examTip.mnemonic: **Move the supports inboard and halve the design moment** — for nothing but a change of position. The check that catches people is **UPLIFT**: load the overhang and leave the span light, and the far support can go into tension.

questions.stem: For a beam fixed at both ends carrying a uniformly distributed load w over span L, the bending moment at each support is:
questions.solution:
**wL²/12** (hogging), with **wL²/24** (sagging) at midspan.

**The complete picture for a fixed-ended beam under UDL:**

| Location | Moment | Sense |
|---|---|---|
| **Each support** | **wL²/12** | **Hogging** — tension at the **top** |
| **Midspan** | **wL²/24** | **Sagging** — tension at the **bottom** |
| **Contraflexure** | 0 | At **0.211L** from each end |

**Check the total**: the sum of the support moment and the midspan moment is **wL²/12 + wL²/24 = wL²/8** — exactly the **free bending moment** of a simply supported span. That is a general and very useful relation:

> **The FREE bending moment (wL²/8) is DISTRIBUTED between the supports and the span.** Fixing the ends does not reduce the total; it **redistributes** it.

**Comparison with the simply supported case:**

| | Simply supported | **Fixed both ends** |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum moment** | **wL²/8** | **wL²/12** — **33% less** |
| Maximum deflection | 5wL⁴/(384EI) | **wL⁴/(384EI)** — **80% less** |
| Degree of indeterminacy | 0 | **3** |

**Both improvements are substantial**, and the deflection reduction — to **one fifth** — is the more dramatic. It is why continuity is so structurally valuable and why a continuous beam is significantly lighter than a series of simply supported ones.

**But fixity has costs:**

| Cost | Note |
|---|---|
| **Settlement induces moments** | A differential settlement δ generates **6EIδ/L²** at each end — potentially large |
| **Temperature and shrinkage** induce stress | The restraint is the source of the stress |
| **True fixity is hard to achieve** | A real support is somewhere between pinned and fixed |
| Analysis is more involved | Compatibility as well as equilibrium |

**The settlement sensitivity is the practical one:**

> A fixed-ended beam is **indeterminate**, so **any imposed movement generates force**. A settlement of only a few millimetres at one support can produce moments comparable with the design moments — which is why fixed ends are avoided on compressible or variable ground.

**Fixed-end moments (FEM)** for standard cases, needed for moment distribution and slope-deflection:

| Loading | FEM at each end |
|---|---|
| **UDL w** | **wL²/12** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8** |
| **Point load W at a from left** | **Wab²/L²** (left), **Wa²b/L²** (right) |
| Couple M at midspan | M/4 |
| Triangular, zero at left to w at right | wL²/30 (left), wL²/20 (right) |

**Note the point-load FEM is unequal** for an off-centre load — the **larger fixed-end moment is at the NEARER support**, which is intuitive once seen but easy to reverse in application.

**A propped cantilever** for comparison, under the same UDL:

| Location | Moment |
|---|---|
| **Fixed end** | **wL²/8** (hogging) |
| Maximum sagging | **9wL²/128** at 0.375L from the prop |
| **Reactions** | **5wL/8** at the fixed end, **3wL/8** at the prop |

**The unequal reactions are worth noting**: the fixed end takes **5/8** of the load and the prop only **3/8**, because the fixed end is stiffer. That asymmetry is characteristic of indeterminate structures — **load flows toward stiffness**, which is one of the most useful qualitative principles in structural analysis.

examTip.trap: wL²/8 is the simply supported value and wL²/24 is the **midspan** value of this same beam. All three appear together.
examTip.trick: Useful check: **wL²/12 + wL²/24 = wL²/8** — the free moment is **redistributed** between supports and span, never reduced in total.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixing the ends cuts the peak moment by a third and the deflection to a FIFTH.** The price is indeterminacy: a settlement of a few millimetres induces 6EIδ/L² at each end, which is why fixed ends are avoided on compressible ground.

questions.stem: An influence line diagram shows the variation of a response quantity at a fixed section as:
options: The section moves along the beam
A unit load moves across the structure
questions.solution:
**As a UNIT LOAD moves across the structure.**

**The essential distinction** — and the source of most confusion in this topic:

| | **Bending moment diagram** | **INFLUENCE LINE** |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | The moment at **EVERY section** | **ONE quantity at ONE section** |
| For | A **FIXED** set of loads | A **MOVING unit load** |
| The horizontal axis is | Position along the **beam** | Position of the **LOAD** |
| Answers | "How is this loading resisted?" | "Where should the load go to make this worst?" |

> They can have the **same shape** for simple cases, which makes them easy to confuse — but they answer entirely different questions.

**Standard influence lines for a simply supported span L**, for a section at distance a from the left (b = L − a):

| Quantity | Shape | Peak |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | **Linear**, 1 at A → 0 at B | **1** at A |
| **Moment at the section** | **TRIANGULAR** | **ab/L** at the section |
| **Shear at the section** | Two parallel lines with a **UNIT STEP** at the section | **+b/L** and **−a/L** |

**Using an influence line** — the two rules that make it powerful:

| Load type | Response |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × (ordinate of the influence line at the load's position)** |
| **UDL w over a length** | **w × (AREA under the influence line over that length)** |
| Several point loads | **Σ W_i y_i** |

**And the placement rules follow immediately:**

| To maximise | Place the load |
|---|---|
| A response with a **point load** | At the **maximum ORDINATE** |
| A response with a **UDL** | Over the **whole length of the same SIGN** |
| A **shear** with a UDL | Over **one side only** — because the diagram changes sign at the section |

**The shear case is the instructive one**: because the shear influence line has **positive area on one side and negative on the other**, loading the whole span **partially cancels**. The maximum shear at a section comes from loading **only one side** — which is exactly the **pattern loading** principle.

**PATTERN LOADING** for continuous beams is the same idea applied to live load:

| To maximise | Load pattern |
|---|---|
| **Sagging moment in a span** | That span **plus alternate** spans |
| **Hogging moment at a support** | The **two spans adjacent** to it, plus alternate ones beyond |
| Reaction at a support | The adjacent spans |

> **Loading EVERY span is NOT the worst case for a continuous beam.** Alternate-span loading produces larger sagging moments, because the unloaded adjacent span provides less restraint. IS 456 requires the pattern cases to be considered, and analysing only the full-load case is unconservative.

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S PRINCIPLE** is the elegant general method for drawing influence lines:

> **The influence line for any response quantity has the same shape as the DEFLECTED FORM the structure takes when the corresponding restraint is REMOVED and a unit displacement imposed in the direction of that quantity.**

| To draw the influence line for | Remove | Impose |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction** at a support | The **support** | A **unit vertical displacement** |
| **Moment** at a section | The **moment restraint** — insert a **HINGE** | A **unit relative ROTATION** |
| **Shear** at a section | The **shear restraint** — insert a **shear release** | A **unit relative SLIP** |

**Its great value is for INDETERMINATE structures**, where influence lines are **curved** and cannot be obtained by simple statics. The deflected shape is easy to sketch qualitatively even when the ordinates require computation — which is enough to identify the critical load positions and patterns.

**Where influence lines matter:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **BRIDGE design** | The essential tool — vehicle loading must be positioned for the worst effect |
| **Crane runway girders** | Moving wheel loads |
| **Continuous beams** with pattern live load | — |
| Industrial floors with moving plant | — |

**For bridges specifically**, the design vehicle (IRC Class A, Class AA, 70R) is moved along the influence line until the response is maximised — a process now automated, but one whose logic is entirely contained in the two placement rules above.

examTip.trap: It is constantly confused with a bending moment diagram. A BMD shows the moment at **every section for a fixed load**; an influence line shows **one quantity at one section as the load moves**.
examTip.trick: The horizontal axis means different things: position along the **beam** for a BMD, position of the **load** for an influence line.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load → place it at the maximum ordinate. UDL → cover the whole region of ONE SIGN.** Because a shear influence line changes sign at the section, maximum shear comes from loading **one side only** — which is exactly the pattern-loading principle.

questions.stem: The degree of static indeterminacy of a plane frame with 3 members, 4 joints, and 6 reaction components is:
questions.solution:
**3.**

**For a rigid plane frame:**

> **D_s = 3m + r − 3j**

where **m** = members, **r** = reaction components, **j** = joints.

> **D_s = 3(3) + 6 − 3(4) = 9 + 6 − 12 = 3** ✓

**Why the formula takes that form:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **3m** | Each rigid plane member carries **3 internal forces** — axial, shear and moment |
| **r** | Unknown reaction components |
| **3j** | Each joint provides **3 equilibrium equations** (ΣH, ΣV, ΣM) |

**The formulae for each structure type**, which must be kept apart:

| Structure | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Plane TRUSS** (pin-jointed) | **D_s = m + r − 2j** |
| **Plane FRAME** (rigid-jointed) | **D_s = 3m + r − 3j** |
| **Space truss** | D_s = m + r − 3j |
| **Space frame** | D_s = 6m + r − 6j |
| **Beam** | D_s = r − 3 − (number of hinges) |

**The truss formula has 2 and the frame formula has 3** because a pin joint carries **no moment** — so each truss member has only **one** unknown (its axial force) and each joint gives only **two** equations.

**Interpreting the result:**

| D_s | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **< 0** | **UNSTABLE** — a mechanism |
| **= 0** | **Determinate** — solvable by statics alone |
| **> 0** | **Indeterminate** to that degree — needs compatibility equations |

**Internal hinges reduce D_s**: each hinge in a frame provides **(number of members meeting at it − 1)** additional equations. A hinge between two members supplies one; a hinge where three members meet supplies two.

**KINEMATIC indeterminacy** is the companion concept, needed for stiffness methods:

> **D_k = number of unknown JOINT DISPLACEMENTS** (degrees of freedom)

| | **Static indeterminacy D_s** | **Kinematic indeterminacy D_k** |
|---|---|---|
| Counts | Redundant **FORCES** | Unknown **DISPLACEMENTS** |
| Used by | **FORCE (flexibility)** methods | **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness)** methods |
| Methods | Consistent deformation, **column analogy**, three-moment | **Slope-deflection**, **moment distribution**, **matrix stiffness** |

**Choosing a method** used to depend on which was smaller:

> **If D_s < D_k**, a **force** method involves fewer unknowns. **If D_k < D_s**, a **displacement** method does.

**But modern practice uses stiffness methods almost universally**, and the reason is decisive:

> The **stiffness method is SYSTEMATIC and easily PROGRAMMED** — the structure's behaviour is assembled from standard member stiffness matrices with no case-by-case judgement. Force methods require **choosing** the redundants, and a poor choice makes the arithmetic far worse. Every commercial analysis package is a stiffness solver.

**A crucial caution on counting:**

> **The formulae check DEGREE, not STABILITY.** A structure can have D_s ≥ 0 and still be **unstable** if its restraints are badly arranged.

**The classic geometric instabilities:**

| Arrangement | Why unstable |
|---|---|
| **Three PARALLEL reactions** | Cannot resist a force perpendicular to them |
| **Three CONCURRENT reactions** | Cannot resist a moment about their common point |
| A truss panel without diagonal bracing | A **mechanism** — the panel racks |
| Members all meeting at a point | — |

**So the count must always be accompanied by a look at the geometry.** A frame with the right number of restraints, all vertical, will happily slide sideways — and no arithmetic reveals it.

**Internal versus external indeterminacy** is a useful further breakdown:

> **External D_s = r − 3** (for a plane structure) — redundant **reactions**
> **Internal D_s = total − external** — redundant **members**

For this frame: external = 6 − 3 = **3**, internal = 3 − 3 = **0**. So the frame is **externally indeterminate to degree 3** and internally determinate — which is exactly what one expects of a portal frame with two fixed bases.

examTip.trick: **D_s = 3m + r − 3j = 9 + 6 − 12 = 3.** The 3s appear because a rigid plane member carries three internal forces and each joint gives three equations.
examTip.mnemonic: **Frame 3m + r − 3j; TRUSS m + r − 2j** — the truss uses 2 because a pin carries no moment. Critical caveat: **the count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.** Three parallel or three concurrent reactions give a valid count and an unstable structure.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam with a UDL, if the span is doubled while the load intensity is unchanged, the maximum bending moment becomes:
questions.solution:
**Four times as large.**

> **M = wL²/8**, and **M ∝ L²** — so doubling L multiplies the moment by **2² = 4** ✓

**The scaling relations across the whole family**, which are worth holding together because they explain most of structural design's economics:

| Quantity | Varies as | Doubling the span |
|---|---|---|
| **Bending moment** (UDL) | **L²** | **× 4** |
| **Shear force** (UDL) | **L** | × 2 |
| **Deflection** (UDL) | **L⁴** | **× 16** |
| **Required section modulus Z** | L² | × 4 |
| **Required I for a deflection limit** | **L³** | × 8 |

**Deflection at L⁴ is the severe one**, and it drives the design of long spans:

> Doubling a span increases the deflection **SIXTEENFOLD** at the same load intensity. For long spans, **deflection rather than strength usually governs** — which is why span-to-depth limits exist as a design check in their own right.

**The required I for a deflection limit varies as L³, not L⁴**, because the limit itself is usually expressed as a **fraction of the span** (L/250, L/350). Setting **5wL⁴/(384EI) = L/250** gives **I ∝ L³**.

**Span-to-depth limits (IS 456 cl. 23.2.1)**, the deemed-to-satisfy check:

| Support condition | Basic span/effective depth |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **7** |
| **Simply supported** | **20** |
| **Continuous** | **26** |

modified by factors for the tension steel percentage, compression steel and flanged sections.

**Deflection limits (IS 456 cl. 23.2):**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total deflection** (including creep and shrinkage) | **span/250** |
| Deflection **after construction of partitions**, or **20 mm**, whichever is less | **span/350** |

**The second limit is the one that matters for serviceability**, because it protects **brittle finishes** — plaster, blockwork partitions, glazing — which crack under movement occurring **after** they are built. The first limit protects appearance and function; the second protects the things attached to the structure.

**Why long spans need a different STRUCTURAL SYSTEM, not merely a deeper beam:**

> Because the required depth grows with the span, a beam's **own weight** grows too — and that weight is itself part of w. Beyond a certain span, **the beam spends most of its capacity carrying itself**, and simply making it deeper stops helping.

**The alternatives all replace BENDING with AXIAL action:**

| System | Mechanism | Typical span range |
|---|---|---|
| **Solid beam** | Bending | up to ~15 m |
| **TRUSS** | **Axial** tension and compression in members | 15 – 60 m |
| **ARCH** | **Axial COMPRESSION** | 30 – 300 m |
| **CABLE / suspension** | **Axial TENSION** | 200 – 2000 m |
| Space frame, shell | Membrane and axial action | Large areas |

> **Bending is an INEFFICIENT way to carry load**, because only the extreme fibres are fully stressed — the material near the neutral axis does almost nothing. **Axial** action stresses the whole cross-section uniformly.

That single fact explains the progression above, and it is why the world's longest spans are all **cables** — the most efficient structural action there is, with every fibre working at full tension.

**A practical illustration of the L² penalty**: a 6 m beam carrying 20 kN/m needs a design moment of 90 kN·m; the same beam at 12 m needs **360 kN·m**, and to keep the same deflection ratio it needs **eight times** the second moment of area — which for a rectangular section means **twice the depth**, since I ∝ d³.

examTip.trick: **M ∝ L²**, so doubling L multiplies the moment by 4. But note the companion: **δ ∝ L⁴**, so deflection goes up **sixteenfold**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment ×4, deflection ×16.** That is why **deflection, not strength, governs long spans**, and why the answer to a long span is a different structural system — truss, arch or cable, all of which carry load **axially** rather than in bending. Bending is inefficient because only the extreme fibres work.

questions.stem: In a simply supported beam, the maximum shear force under a uniformly distributed load occurs:
questions.solution:
**At the supports**, with magnitude **wL/2**.

**Because the shear diagram is linear**, running from **+wL/2** at one support through **zero at midspan** to **−wL/2** at the other. The extreme values are therefore at the ends.

**Shear and moment peak at DIFFERENT sections**, which is the practically important point:

| Quantity | Maximum at | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| **SHEAR** | **The SUPPORTS** | **Stirrups**, web thickness, bearing |
| **MOMENT** | **MIDSPAN** | **Main flexural steel**, section depth |

> That separation is the basis of efficient detailing: **stirrups closely spaced near the supports** and widely spaced at midspan; **main bars fully provided at midspan** and curtailed toward the ends.

**The critical section for shear design** is not at the support face, however:

> **IS 456 cl. 22.6.2** permits the critical section to be taken at **a distance d from the face of the support**, where the support reaction introduces **vertical compression** that enhances the concrete's shear capacity.

Using the value at the support itself is conservative but wasteful, and the reduction is worth taking on a heavily loaded beam.

**Shear design in reinforced concrete:**

> **τ_v = V_u/(b d)** — the nominal shear stress

| Condition | Action |
|---|---|
| **τ_v ≤ τ_c** (concrete capacity) | **Minimum stirrups only** |
| **τ_c < τ_v ≤ τ_c,max** | **Design stirrups** for the excess: **V_us = V_u − τ_c b d** |
| **τ_v > τ_c,max** | **The SECTION IS INADEQUATE** — it must be enlarged or the concrete grade raised |

**The τ_c,max limit is absolute** and cannot be met by adding more stirrups:

> Beyond τ_c,max the failure mode changes to **CRUSHING of the concrete web strut** in the truss analogy — and no amount of transverse steel prevents the concrete from crushing. The section must be made bigger.

**τ_c depends on the tension steel percentage**, which surprises people until the mechanism is seen:

> More longitudinal tension steel means **smaller crack widths**, hence better **aggregate interlock** across the crack and greater **dowel action** — both of which carry shear. So the concrete's shear capacity rises with the flexural reinforcement.

**Minimum shear reinforcement** is required even where τ_v < τ_c:

> **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)**

because shear failure is **sudden and brittle** — diagonal tension cracking gives little warning — whereas flexural failure of an under-reinforced section is **ductile**. Minimum stirrups ensure that even an unexpected shear does not cause a sudden collapse, and they hold the longitudinal bars in position.

> **That contrast — brittle shear versus ductile flexure — is why shear is designed with a larger margin than bending**, and why the codes are prescriptive about minimum steel and maximum spacing.

**Maximum stirrup spacing** (IS 456 cl. 26.5.1.5): the least of **0.75d**, **300 mm**, or the spacing required by calculation — so that any potential diagonal crack, which forms at roughly 45°, is **certain to be crossed by at least one stirrup**.

**Other shear cases** worth distinguishing:

| Type | Where |
|---|---|
| **One-way (flexural) shear** | Beams, one-way slabs — critical at **d** from the support |
| **Two-way (PUNCHING) shear** | Flat slabs, footings — critical on a perimeter at **d/2** from the column |
| **Torsional shear** | Combined with flexural shear in the design |
| Interface shear | At a construction joint or between precast and in-situ concrete |

**Punching shear** is the one that governs footing and flat-slab thickness, precisely because it is resisted by the **concrete alone** and the only variable available is the **depth**.

examTip.trick: The shear diagram runs linearly from +wL/2 to −wL/2, so the extremes are at the ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear governs stirrups; moment governs main steel — and they peak at opposite ends of the beam.** Design consequence worth knowing: if **τ_v exceeds τ_c,max the SECTION is inadequate** and no amount of extra stirrups will do, because the failure mode becomes crushing of the web strut.

questions.stem: A propped cantilever of span L carries a UDL w. The reaction at the propped end is:
questions.solution:
**3wL/8** at the prop, with **5wL/8** at the fixed end.

**The reactions are UNEQUAL**, and the reason is a general principle worth stating:

> **LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS.** The fixed end is stiffer than the simple prop, so it attracts the larger share — **5/8 against 3/8**.

**Check**: 5wL/8 + 3wL/8 = **wL** ✓ — the total load.

**Derivation** by the compatibility (consistent deformation) method — the structure is indeterminate to degree 1:

1. **Release the prop**, leaving a cantilever. Its free-end deflection under the UDL is **wL⁴/(8EI)** downward.
2. **Apply the unknown prop reaction R** upward. Its deflection at the same point is **RL³/(3EI)** upward.
3. **Compatibility**: the prop is unyielding, so the net deflection is **zero**:

> **wL⁴/(8EI) = RL³/(3EI)**
> **R = 3wL/8** ✓

**The complete results:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at prop** | **3wL/8** |
| **Reaction at fixed end** | **5wL/8** |
| **Moment at fixed end** | **wL²/8** (hogging) |
| **Maximum sagging moment** | **9wL²/128** at **0.375L** from the prop |
| **Point of contraflexure** | **0.25L** from the prop |
| **Maximum deflection** | wL⁴/(185EI) at 0.4215L from the prop |

**Note that 9/128 = 0.0703 is less than 1/8 = 0.125**, so the **fixed-end hogging moment governs** the design — which is characteristic of propped cantilevers and continuous end spans.

**Comparison of the three UDL cases:**

| Beam | M_max | δ_max | D_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **wL²/8** | 5wL⁴/384EI | 0 |
| **Propped cantilever** | **wL²/8** (at the fixed end) | wL⁴/185EI | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | **wL²/12** | wL⁴/384EI | **3** |

**Interesting**: the propped cantilever's maximum moment is the **same** as the simply supported beam's — but its **deflection is 2.6 times smaller**, and the moment now occurs at the support (where a deeper section is often available) rather than at midspan.

**The methods available for a structure of D_s = 1:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Consistent deformation** (force method) | Release a redundant, restore compatibility — used above |
| **Slope-deflection** | Write member end moments in terms of joint rotations |
| **Moment distribution** (Hardy Cross) | Iterative balancing of joint moments — excellent by hand |
| **Three-moment theorem** | For continuous beams |
| **Matrix stiffness** | The general and programmable method |

**A practical caution about the prop:**

> The result **3wL/8** assumes the prop is **UNYIELDING**. If it settles by δ, the reaction **reduces** — and if it settles enough, the beam reverts toward cantilever behaviour with a fixed-end moment approaching **wL²/2**, four times the design value.

**That sensitivity to support movement is the defining characteristic of indeterminate structures**, and it must be checked wherever the prop's stiffness is uncertain:

> **R = 3wL/8 − 3EIδ/L³**

A settlement of δ = wL⁴/(8EI) removes the prop reaction entirely.

**Where propped cantilevers occur**: the **end span of a continuous beam** behaves very nearly as one (fixed at the interior support by continuity, simply supported at the end wall), and **temporary propping** during construction creates the condition explicitly — which is why the **sequence of prop removal** matters and is specified rather than left to site judgement.

examTip.trap: wL/2 is the symmetric answer and is wrong — the two ends of a propped cantilever are **not** equally stiff, so they do not share the load equally.
examTip.trick: Compatibility: cantilever deflection wL⁴/8EI must be cancelled by RL³/3EI, giving **R = 3wL/8**. Check: 3wL/8 + 5wL/8 = wL ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS** — the fixed end is stiffer, so it takes 5/8. That single principle explains most indeterminate results. Caution: the answer assumes an **unyielding** prop; if it settles, the reaction falls and the fixing moment rises.

questions.stem: In a continuous beam, loading alternate spans rather than all spans is considered because it:
options: Produces the maximum sagging moments in the loaded spans
questions.solution:
**Because it produces the MAXIMUM SAGGING moments in the loaded spans.**

**The principle** is not obvious and is worth stating carefully:

> **Loading EVERY span is NOT the worst case for a continuous beam.** An unloaded adjacent span provides **less restraint** to the loaded one — its end rotates more freely — so the loaded span behaves more like a simply supported beam and its **sagging moment increases**.

**The pattern loading rules (IS 456 cl. 22.4.1):**

| To maximise | Load pattern |
|---|---|
| **SAGGING moment in a span** | **That span + ALTERNATE spans** |
| **HOGGING moment at a support** | **The two spans ADJACENT to it**, plus alternate ones beyond |
| **Reaction at a support** | The adjacent spans |
| Shear at a section | One side of it |

**Dead load** is always applied to **all spans** — it is permanent and cannot be patterned. Only the **live (imposed) load** is varied, and that is what option (d) gets wrong.

**Why it works — the Müller-Breslau connection:**

> The influence line for a sagging moment in a continuous beam is **positive in that span and alternate spans**, and **negative in the adjacent ones**. Loading only the positive regions maximises the response; loading the negative regions would partially cancel it.

So the alternate-span pattern is not a rule of thumb but a direct reading of the influence line.

**A simplification IS 456 permits**: for beams of approximately equal span carrying substantially uniform load, **coefficients** may be used in place of full pattern analysis (cl. 22.5.1) — for example **wL²/12** at the first interior support and **wL²/16** in the end span for dead load. These coefficients already embody the pattern-loading envelope.

**The design ENVELOPE** is what pattern analysis produces:

> Each load case gives one moment diagram. The design must satisfy the **worst value at every section across ALL cases** — so the diagrams are superimposed and the **outer envelope** taken.

**Two consequences of the envelope worth knowing:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| A section may need **BOTH top and bottom steel** | Because the moment there is hogging in one case and sagging in another |
| The **points of contraflexure MOVE** between cases | So curtailment must be based on the envelope, not one analysis |

**That second point is the practical detailing implication**, and it is why IS 456's curtailment rules carry generous margins: bars must extend a **development length beyond** the theoretical cut-off, and at least **d or 12φ** past it, precisely because the true contraflexure position is not a single point but a range.

**MOMENT REDISTRIBUTION** is the related refinement that codes permit:

> A ductile reinforced concrete section, having reached its capacity, **rotates without losing strength** — so moment sheds to less-stressed parts of the structure. IS 456 allows the elastic moments to be **redistributed by up to 30%**, subject to conditions.

| Condition (IS 456 cl. 37.1.1) | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Equilibrium must be maintained** | The redistributed diagram must still be statically valid |
| Redistribution **≤ 30%** | Limits the rotation demanded |
| **x_u/d ≤ 0.6 − δM/100** | Ensures the section is **ductile enough** to rotate |
| Applies to **ultimate limit state** only | Serviceability uses elastic values |

**The x_u/d condition is the essential safeguard**: redistribution requires **plastic rotation** at the yielding section, and only an **under-reinforced** section (with the neutral axis high) can provide it. An over-reinforced section fails by concrete crushing without rotating, and redistribution assumed but not delivered is a real hazard.

**Why redistribution is useful**: it lets the designer **reduce the peak hogging moments at supports** — which are congested with reinforcement from two spans meeting — at the cost of slightly larger span moments, where there is room. It is a practical detailing tool as much as an economy.

examTip.trap: "Loading every span" feels like the worst case and is not. An **unloaded** adjacent span restrains the loaded one **less**, so its sagging moment is larger.
examTip.trick: Read it off the influence line: it is positive in that span and alternate spans, negative in the adjacent ones. Load only the positive regions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sagging in a span: that span plus ALTERNATE spans. Hogging at a support: the TWO ADJACENT spans.** Dead load always goes on every span — only the live load is patterned. The result is an **envelope**, and some sections then need both top and bottom steel.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a UDL of 15 kN/m. The maximum shear force is:
questions.solution:
**45 kN**, at each support.

> **V_max = wL/2 = 15 × 6/2 = 45 kN** ✓

**Check**: the total load is **15 × 6 = 90 kN**, shared equally between two supports by symmetry — **45 kN each** ✓. Option (b), 90 kN, is the **total load**, not the reaction.

**And the companion moment:**

> **M_max = wL²/8 = 15 × 36/8 = 67.5 kN·m** at midspan

(which is option (d) — the moment value offered as a shear distractor, a common style of trap.)

**The complete set for this beam:**

| Quantity | Value | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Reactions** | **45 kN** each | Supports |
| **Maximum shear** | **45 kN** | Supports |
| **Maximum moment** | **67.5 kN·m** | Midspan |
| Shear at midspan | **0** | — |
| Moment at supports | 0 | — |

**A design sanity check on the numbers.** For a reinforced concrete beam carrying 67.5 kN·m:

> A section of roughly **250 × 450 mm** with about **1000 mm²** of tension steel (three 20 mm bars) would suit — entirely conventional for a 6 m span. The numbers are realistic.

**The nominal shear stress**, to check the section for shear:

> **τ_v = V_u/(b d)**. With a factored shear of **1.5 × 45 = 67.5 kN**, b = 250 mm and d = 410 mm:
> **τ_v = 67 500/(250 × 410) = 0.66 N/mm²**

which for M20 concrete with about 1% tension steel is close to **τ_c ≈ 0.62 N/mm²** — so **light designed stirrups** are needed, a typical outcome.

**Where the load comes from** — a realistic 15 kN/m for a floor beam:

| Component | Load |
|---|---|
| Self weight, 250 × 450 beam | 0.25 × 0.45 × 25 = **2.8 kN/m** |
| Slab (125 mm) over a 3 m tributary width | 0.125 × 25 × 3 = **9.4 kN/m** |
| Finishes, say 1 kN/m² × 3 m | **3.0 kN/m** |
| **Dead total** | **~15 kN/m** |
| Live load 3 kN/m² × 3 m | 9 kN/m (additional) |

> Note that **self weight and slab dead load alone reach 15 kN/m** — which is a useful reminder that **dead load usually dominates** in concrete construction, and that a preliminary design must include the structure's own weight from the outset rather than adding it later.

**Load factors** at ultimate limit state (IS 456 Table 18):

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** |
| DL + WL | 1.5(DL + WL), or **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** |
| DL + LL + WL | 1.2(DL + LL + WL) |

**The 0.9 DL case is the one most often forgotten**, and it matters: where the **dead load is STABILISING** — resisting overturning, uplift or wind reversal — it is factored **DOWN to 0.9**, because relying on a load that might be less than estimated is unsafe. Applying 1.5 to a stabilising dead load is a genuine error, and it conceals overturning and uplift problems entirely.

**Serviceability combinations** use factors of **1.0**, since the check is against actual expected loads rather than an ultimate condition.

examTip.trap: 90 kN is the **total load**, not the reaction; 67.5 kN·m is the **moment** offered as a shear distractor. Read what is being asked.
examTip.trick: **V = wL/2 = 45 kN** by symmetry — half the total load at each support.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead load dominates in concrete** — self weight plus slab alone reaches this 15 kN/m before any live load. Also remember the **0.9 DL** case: where dead load is **stabilising** (overturning, uplift), it is factored **down**, not up. Applying 1.5 there hides the problem.

questions.stem: Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit:
options: Stress is proportional to the square of strain
questions.solution:
**Stress is proportional to strain.**

> **σ = E ε**, where **E** is **Young's modulus** (the modulus of elasticity)

**Note that E has the units of STRESS** (N/mm² or GPa), because strain is dimensionless.

**Typical values:**

| Material | E (GPa) |
|---|---|
| **Structural STEEL** | **200 – 210** |
| **CONCRETE (M25)** | **25** — from **E_c = 5000√f_ck** |
| Aluminium | 70 |
| **Timber** (along the grain) | **8 – 15** |
| Glass | 70 |
| Rubber | 0.01 – 0.1 |

> **Steel is about EIGHT times stiffer than concrete** — which is the whole basis of the **modular ratio m = E_s/E_c** used in working stress design and in transformed-section analysis.

**The concrete relation E_c = 5000√f_ck** (IS 456 cl. 6.2.3.1) is worth remembering: concrete's stiffness depends on its **strength**, unlike steel's, because both derive from the same paste and aggregate structure.

**Regions of the mild steel stress–strain curve**, in order:

| Region | Description |
|---|---|
| **Proportional limit** | **Hooke's law holds** — the curve is straight |
| **Elastic limit** | Slightly beyond; strain still fully recovers, but not linearly |
| **UPPER and LOWER YIELD points** | The stress **drops** and strain increases at nearly constant stress |
| **Yield plateau** | Large strain at constant stress — the source of **DUCTILITY** |
| **Strain hardening** | Stress rises again as the material reorganises |
| **ULTIMATE strength** | The maximum stress; **NECKING** begins |
| **Fracture** | At a nominal stress **below** the ultimate, because the area has reduced |

**Why the nominal stress falls after the ultimate**: engineering stress is computed on the **ORIGINAL** area, but the specimen is **necking** and its actual area is shrinking fast. On **true stress** (using the instantaneous area) the curve continues to rise to fracture.

**The yield plateau is the property that matters most in structural engineering:**

> **DUCTILITY** — the ability to undergo large plastic strain **without losing strength** — is what gives a steel structure **WARNING before collapse**, allows **moment redistribution**, and provides **energy absorption in an earthquake**.

**Brittle materials have no plateau**, and the consequences are severe:

| | **DUCTILE** (mild steel) | **BRITTLE** (cast iron, plain concrete, glass) |
|---|---|---|
| Warning before failure | **Yes — large visible deformation** | **NONE — sudden** |
| Energy absorbed | **Large** | Small |
| Moment redistribution | **Possible** | Not possible |
| Notch sensitivity | Low | **High** |
| Failure surface | Cup and cone, shear | Flat, perpendicular to the stress |

> **Ductility is the single most valuable property a structural material can have**, and virtually every seismic design provision exists to ensure the structure fails in a ductile manner if it fails at all.

**High-strength steels lack a defined yield point** — their curve rises smoothly with no plateau — so the yield is defined by the **0.2% PROOF STRESS**: the stress at which a line of slope E, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the curve. Fe415 and Fe500 reinforcement are specified this way.

**Note also that E is essentially the SAME for all structural steels** — mild steel and high-strength steel both have E ≈ 200 GPa. **Strength differs; stiffness does not.** So using a higher-grade steel reduces the **section required for strength** but does **nothing for deflection**, which is why deflection often governs in high-strength steel design.

examTip.trick: **σ = Eε.** E has the units of **stress** because strain is dimensionless — which kills any option that is dimensionally wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steel 200 GPa, concrete 25 GPa (E_c = 5000√f_ck) — a ratio of about 8, which IS the modular ratio.** Critical point: **E is the SAME for every structural steel grade.** A higher grade buys strength, not stiffness, so deflection is unimproved — which is why it often governs in high-strength design.

questions.stem: Poisson's ratio for most metals lies in the range:
questions.solution:
**0.25 to 0.35.**

> **μ (or ν) = lateral strain / longitudinal strain**, taken as a positive number

**Typical values:**

| Material | μ |
|---|---|
| Cork | **~0** |
| **CONCRETE** | **0.15 – 0.20** |
| Cast iron | 0.25 |
| **STEEL** | **0.30** |
| Aluminium | 0.33 |
| **Saturated CLAY (undrained)** | **0.5** |
| **Rubber** | **~0.5** |

**The theoretical LIMIT is 0.5**, and the reason is physical:

> **μ = 0.5 means the material is INCOMPRESSIBLE** — the volume does not change under load.

**Because the volumetric strain is:**

> **e_v = ε(1 − 2μ)**

> At **μ = 0.5**, **(1 − 2 × 0.5) = 0**, so **e_v = 0** — no volume change ✓

**That is exactly why saturated clay under UNDRAINED loading has μ = 0.5**: the water cannot escape in the short term, so the volume cannot change. It is not a coincidence but a direct statement of the undrained condition — and it links this topic to soil mechanics.

**The theoretical range** is **−1 < μ < 0.5** for an isotropic material. Negative-μ (**auxetic**) materials exist — they get **fatter** when stretched — but they are engineered metamaterials and foams, not structural materials.

**The elastic constants and their relations:**

| Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **E** | Young's modulus — direct stress / direct strain |
| **G** (or N, C) | **Modulus of RIGIDITY** — shear stress / shear strain |
| **K** | **BULK modulus** — volumetric stress / volumetric strain |
| **μ** | Poisson's ratio |

**The three relations**, of which any two constants determine the rest:

> **E = 2G(1 + μ)**
> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**
> **E = 9KG/(3K + G)**

**For steel with μ = 0.3:**

> **G = E/[2(1 + 0.3)] = E/2.6 ≈ 0.385 E ≈ 77 GPa**
> **K = E/[3(1 − 0.6)] = E/1.2 ≈ 0.833 E ≈ 167 GPa**

**A useful mental approximation**: **G ≈ 0.4E** and **K ≈ 0.8E** for steel.

**Note what happens to K as μ → 0.5:**

> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** means **K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)] → ∞** as μ → 0.5

> An **infinite bulk modulus** is precisely the statement that the material is **incompressible** — consistent with the volumetric strain result above, and a good check that the relations hang together.

**Practical consequences of Poisson's ratio:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lateral expansion** under axial compression | A concrete cylinder bulges as it is crushed |
| **Confinement increases strength** | Restraining the lateral expansion — the basis of **spiral/helical reinforcement** in columns and of the triaxial test |
| **Biaxial and triaxial** stress states | Strains in each direction depend on all three stresses |
| **Thick cylinder** analysis | Lamé's equations involve μ |
| Plane stress versus plane strain | The distinction turns on μ |

**The confinement effect is the structurally important one:**

> Concrete crushes by **splitting laterally**. Prevent that lateral expansion — with **closely spaced spirals or ties** — and the concrete's strength and, far more importantly, its **DUCTILITY** are greatly increased.

That is the mechanism behind **confined concrete** in seismic design: closely spaced transverse reinforcement in the potential plastic hinge zones of columns and beam ends, which does little for the elastic strength but transforms the member's ability to sustain large rotations without disintegrating. IS 13920 prescribes it in detail, and it is the single most important detailing provision for earthquake resistance.

examTip.trick: **e_v = ε(1 − 2μ)**, so μ = 0.5 gives zero volume change — the theoretical upper limit, meaning **incompressible**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steel 0.3, concrete 0.15–0.2, saturated clay undrained 0.5.** The clay value is not a coincidence: undrained means no volume change, which is exactly what μ = 0.5 states. Practical use: restraining lateral expansion (**confinement**) greatly increases concrete's strength and, far more importantly, its **ductility** — the basis of IS 13920 detailing.

questions.stem: On a plane carrying the maximum shear stress in a two-dimensional stress system, the normal stress is:
options: Equal to the average of the principal stresses
Equal to the maximum principal stress
Equal to the maximum shear stress
questions.solution:
**Equal to the AVERAGE of the principal stresses, (σ₁ + σ₂)/2.**

**This is immediately visible on MOHR'S CIRCLE:**

> The **maximum shear** points are at the **top and bottom** of the circle. Their **horizontal coordinate — the normal stress — is the CENTRE of the circle**, which is at **(σ₁ + σ₂)/2**.

**Mohr's circle in summary:**

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Centre** | **(σ_x + σ_y)/2 = (σ₁ + σ₂)/2** — on the σ axis |
| **Radius** | **√[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²] = τ_max** |
| **Principal stresses** | Where the circle **crosses the σ axis** (τ = 0) |
| **Maximum shear** | **Top and bottom** of the circle |
| Angle on the circle | **TWICE** the angle in the physical plane |

**The key results:**

> **σ₁,₂ = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]**
> **τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = the radius**
> **tan 2θ_p = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y)**

**Two facts about the planes:**

| Fact | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Principal planes carry NO SHEAR** | That is their definition — τ = 0 there |
| **Maximum shear planes are at 45° to the principal planes** | Because they are **90° apart on the circle**, and circle angles are doubled |

**The 45° relationship explains a great deal of observed failure behaviour:**

| Observation | Explanation |
|---|---|
| A **ductile** steel tensile specimen fails on a **45° cone** | It fails in **SHEAR**, and the maximum shear is at 45° to the axial tension |
| A **brittle** specimen fails on a plane **perpendicular** to the tension | It fails in **direct tension**, on the principal plane |
| **Concrete in shear** cracks at roughly **45°** | Diagonal **TENSION** — the principal tensile stress is at 45° to a pure shear |
| Torsion of a brittle shaft gives a **helical (45°) fracture** | Principal tension at 45° to the shaft axis |

> **The same stress state produces different failure planes in ductile and brittle materials**, because each fails on the plane where **its own weakest mode** is most severely stressed — shear for ductile, tension for brittle.

**PURE SHEAR** is the case worth working through, because it is the basis of concrete shear design:

> For pure shear **τ** with no direct stress: the circle is **centred at the ORIGIN** with radius τ.
> **σ₁ = +τ** (tension) and **σ₂ = −τ** (compression), at **45°** to the shear planes.

> So **a state of pure shear is equivalent to equal tension and compression at 45°**.
