**That is why concrete cracks diagonally in shear.** Concrete is strong in compression and **weak in tension**; the shear produces a **principal TENSION at 45°**, and the concrete cracks perpendicular to it — giving the characteristic diagonal crack running up toward the load.

**And it explains the direction of shear reinforcement:**

| Reinforcement | Effectiveness |
|---|---|
| **Bars at 45°, perpendicular to the crack** | **Theoretically ideal** — directly resists the principal tension |
| **Vertical stirrups** | **Practically universal** — easier to fix, and they cross the crack adequately |
| Bent-up bars at 45° | Used historically, in combination with stirrups |

Vertical stirrups are less efficient than 45° bars but are used because they are far easier to place accurately, and the loss is acceptable.

**In 3-D**, three circles are drawn from the three principal stresses, and the **absolute maximum shear** is the radius of the **largest** — **(σ_max − σ_min)/2**. That matters because a 2-D analysis of a plane-stress problem where σ₁ and σ₂ have the **same sign** understates the maximum shear: the true maximum involves σ₃ = 0 and is **σ₁/2**, not (σ₁ − σ₂)/2.

examTip.trick: Read it straight off **Mohr's circle**: the maximum-shear points are the top and bottom, and their horizontal coordinate is the **centre**, at (σ₁ + σ₂)/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Principal planes carry no shear; maximum-shear planes are at 45° to them** (90° apart on the circle, and circle angles are doubled). This is why a **ductile** tensile specimen fails on a 45° cone (shear) while a **brittle** one fails square across (direct tension) — same stress state, different weakest mode.

questions.stem: The relation between the modulus of elasticity E, modulus of rigidity G and Poisson's ratio μ is:
questions.solution:
**E = 2G(1 + μ).**

**The three elastic-constant relations:**

> **E = 2G(1 + μ)**
> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**
> **E = 9KG/(3K + G)**

**Any TWO independent constants determine all four** for an isotropic material — which is a strong statement: an isotropic elastic solid has only **two** independent elastic properties, however many symbols we give them.

**Option (b), E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**, is a real relation but for the **bulk** modulus, not the rigidity modulus — a well-designed distractor, since it is correct in form and wrong in substance.

**For steel (μ = 0.3):**

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| **E** | **200 GPa** |
| **G = E/[2(1.3)]** | **77 GPa** — about **0.4 E** |
| **K = E/[3(0.4)]** | **167 GPa** — about **0.83 E** |

**Useful checks on the relations:**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| μ = 0 | **E = 2G** and **E = 3K** |
| μ = 0.5 | **E = 3G** and **K → ∞** (incompressible) ✓ |
| μ = 0.25 | **E = 2.5G** and **E = 1.5K**, so **K = G × 5/3** |

> The **μ = 0.5 case giving K → ∞** is the useful sanity check: an incompressible material must have an infinite bulk modulus, and the relation delivers exactly that.

**What each constant physically measures:**

| Constant | Loading | Deformation |
|---|---|---|
| **E** | **Uniaxial** direct stress | Direct strain |
| **G** | **SHEAR** stress | **Angular** distortion (change of shape, no change of volume) |
| **K** | **Hydrostatic** pressure (equal in all directions) | **Volume** change, no change of shape |

> **G governs change of SHAPE; K governs change of VOLUME.** Any general deformation decomposes into those two parts — the **deviatoric** and **volumetric** components — which is the basis of plasticity theory and of critical state soil mechanics.

**Why G matters in structural design:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Torsion** | **θ = TL/(GJ)** — the angle of twist |
| **Shear deflection** of deep beams | Significant when the span/depth ratio is below about 10 |
| **Shear walls** | Shear deformation is a large part of the total |
| **Bolted and welded connections** | Shear transfer |
| Web buckling | — |

**Shear deflection** is the one most often neglected and occasionally important:

> For a **slender** beam, **bending deflection dominates** and shear deflection is negligible. For a **deep** beam (span/depth < 10), shear deflection becomes significant — and for a **shear wall** it dominates entirely.

The ratio of shear to bending deflection scales as **(d/L)²**, which is why it vanishes for slender members and matters for stubby ones.

**Torsional rigidity GJ** deserves a note because **J** differs radically between section types:

| Section | Torsional constant |
|---|---|
| **Solid circular** | **J = πD⁴/32** — the polar second moment |
| **CLOSED thin tube** | **J = 4A²t/s** (Bredt) — **very stiff** |
| **OPEN section (I, channel, angle)** | **J = Σ(bt³/3)** — **extremely FLEXIBLE in torsion** |

> A **closed** section is enormously stiffer in torsion than an **open** one of the same material and weight — often by a factor of **hundreds**. An I-beam is a poor torsion member; a box section is an excellent one.

That is why **box girders** are used for curved bridges and for any deck subject to eccentric loading: the torsion has to go somewhere, and only a closed section carries it efficiently.

**For an ANISOTROPIC material** — timber, laminates, layered rock — the two-constant simplification fails entirely: timber's properties along and across the grain differ by an order of magnitude, and it requires separate moduli in each direction.

examTip.trap: **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** is offered and is a genuine relation — but for the **BULK** modulus, not the rigidity modulus. Correct in form, wrong in substance.
examTip.trick: Sanity-check with μ = 0.5: E = 2G(1.5) = 3G, and K → ∞ ✓ (incompressible). The relations must behave correctly at the limits.
examTip.mnemonic: **G ≈ 0.4E and K ≈ 0.83E for steel.** G governs change of SHAPE, K change of VOLUME — a split that underlies all plasticity theory. Note also that a **closed** section is hundreds of times stiffer in torsion than an **open** one of the same weight.

questions.stem: A steel bar 2 m long is prevented from expanding when its temperature rises by 30 °C. Taking α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C and E = 200 GPa, the induced stress is:
questions.solution:
**72 MPa (compressive).**

> **σ = α ΔT E = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 × 200 000 N/mm²**
> **= 12 × 30 × 200 000 × 10⁻⁶ = 72 000 × 10⁻³ = 72 N/mm² = 72 MPa** ✓

**Note what does NOT appear in the formula:**

> **The LENGTH is irrelevant.** Thermal stress depends only on **α, ΔT and E** — not on the member's length.

**Why**: the free thermal strain is **ε = αΔT**, which is a strain, not an extension — it is the same for a 1 m bar and a 100 m bar. Restraining it produces **σ = Eε = EαΔT** regardless of size. The **force** depends on the area, and the **extension prevented** depends on the length, but the **stress** does not.

That is a genuinely useful result: a fully restrained steel rail 1 km long develops exactly the same thermal stress as a 1 m specimen.

**The two-step logic** worth stating explicitly:

| Step | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Free expansion** | **δ = α L ΔT** — occurs if unrestrained, with **NO STRESS** |
| **Full restraint** | **Zero movement**, so the strain αΔT is suppressed: **σ = E α ΔT** |
| **Partial restraint** | Somewhere between; if the support yields by δ_s, **σ = E(αLΔT − δ_s)/L** |

> **Free expansion produces NO stress. Restraint produces stress.** It is the **restraint**, not the temperature change, that causes the problem.

**Coefficients of thermal expansion:**

| Material | α (× 10⁻⁶ /°C) |
|---|---|
| **Steel** | **12** |
| **Concrete** | **10 – 12** |
| Aluminium | 23 |
| Timber (along grain) | 3 – 5 |
| Glass | 9 |

**That steel and concrete have nearly the SAME α is the fortunate accident on which reinforced concrete depends:**

> If their coefficients differed appreciably, temperature change would **break the bond** between them, and reinforced concrete as a composite material would not work. Their near-equality (12 against 10–12) means they expand together and the interface stresses stay small.

**Magnitudes worth a feel for**: **a 30 °C rise in fully restrained steel gives 72 MPa** — a substantial fraction of the 250 MPa yield of mild steel. A 100 °C rise would give **240 MPa**, essentially yielding the material. Thermal stress is not a minor effect.

**Accommodating thermal movement** in structures:

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **EXPANSION JOINTS** | IS 456 requires them at intervals of about **45 m** in a concrete building |
| **Sliding / roller bearings** | Bridge decks — one fixed bearing, the rest free |
| **Expansion loops** in pipework | — |
| **Rail expansion joints**, or **continuously welded rail** held by ballast | Two opposite strategies |
| Flexible connections | — |

**Continuously welded rail is the interesting case**: rather than providing joints, the rail is **deliberately fully restrained** by the ballast and sleepers, and is **pre-stressed to a neutral temperature** so that the stress at the extremes of the temperature range stays within limits. The rail carries large axial forces permanently, and the risk managed is **buckling in hot weather** rather than fracture in cold.

**Thermal stress in indeterminate structures** is the general case: a **determinate** structure expands freely and develops **no stress at all**, while an **indeterminate** one resists the movement and stresses itself. That is one of the standing arguments for determinate arrangements on structures with large thermal ranges — long bridges, exposed roofs, and structures in the Terai where the annual swing exceeds 30 °C.

examTip.trick: **σ = αΔT·E = 12e−6 × 30 × 200 000 = 72 MPa.** Note what is **absent**: the length. Thermal stress does not depend on it.
examTip.mnemonic: **FREE expansion causes no stress; RESTRAINT causes stress.** A fully restrained 1 km rail develops exactly the same stress as a 1 m bar. Fortunate accident worth knowing: **steel and concrete have nearly the same α** (12 against 10–12) — reinforced concrete would not work otherwise.

questions.stem: The strain energy stored per unit volume in a bar stressed within the elastic limit is:
questions.solution:
**σ²/(2E)** — the **resilience** per unit volume.

**Derivation.** The work done by a gradually applied load is the **area under the load–extension curve**, which for linear elastic behaviour is a triangle:

> **U = ½ P δ = ½ (σA)(εL) = ½ σ ε (AL) = ½ σ ε × volume**
> Per unit volume: **u = ½ σ ε = ½ σ (σ/E) = σ²/(2E)** ✓

**The ½ is because the load builds up GRADUALLY** from zero — the average force during the extension is half the final force.

**Related definitions:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Resilience** | **Total** strain energy stored |
| **Proof resilience** | Strain energy at the **elastic limit** — the maximum recoverable |
| **MODULUS of resilience** | **Proof resilience per unit VOLUME** = **σ_e²/(2E)** |
| **TOUGHNESS** | **TOTAL** area under the **whole** stress–strain curve, to fracture |

**Resilience and toughness are different properties**, and the distinction matters:

| | **RESILIENCE** | **TOUGHNESS** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | Energy stored **ELASTICALLY** — recoverable | **TOTAL** energy absorbed to fracture |
| Area under the curve | To the **elastic limit** | To **fracture** |
| High in | **Springs** — high strength, low E | **DUCTILE** materials |
| Wanted for | Energy storage, springs | **Impact and EARTHQUAKE** resistance |

> A **high-strength spring steel** has great **resilience** but may have modest toughness. **Mild steel** has modest resilience and **enormous toughness**, because of its long plastic plateau.

**Toughness is what matters in earthquake engineering**, because the demand is to **absorb energy**, not to store and return it. A structure that survives an earthquake does so largely by **dissipating** the input energy through controlled plastic deformation — which requires area under the curve beyond yield, that is, **ductility**.

**IMPACT (suddenly applied) loading** is the striking application of strain energy:

| Loading | Stress produced |
|---|---|
| **Gradually applied** load P | **σ = P/A** |
| **SUDDENLY applied** load P (from zero height) | **σ = 2P/A — DOUBLE** |
| Load falling through height h | **σ = (P/A)[1 + √(1 + 2hAE/(PL))]** |

**Why a suddenly applied load doubles the stress** is worth understanding, because it is counter-intuitive:

> With a **gradual** load the work done is **½Pδ** (the load builds up). With a **sudden** load, the **full P acts through the whole displacement δ**, so the work is **Pδ** — **twice** as much. Equating that to the strain energy ½σεV gives **double the stress**.

The bar then **oscillates** about the static position, momentarily reaching twice the static deflection before damping brings it to rest at the static value.

**Energy methods** built on strain energy are among the most powerful tools in structural analysis:

| Method | Statement |
|---|---|
| **CASTIGLIANO'S first theorem** | **δ = ∂U/∂P** — the **deflection** at a load point is the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to that load |
| **Unit load (virtual work) method** | **δ = Σ∫(Mm/EI)dx** — for beams and frames |
| **Principle of least work** | Redundant forces take values that **MINIMISE** the strain energy: **∂U/∂R = 0** |
| Maxwell's reciprocal theorem | The deflection at A due to a load at B equals that at B due to the same load at A |

**The unit load method** is the practical workhorse for deflections of trusses and frames:

> **δ = Σ (P k L)/(AE)** for a truss, where **k** are the member forces under a **unit load** applied at the point and in the direction of the required deflection.

**The principle of least work** solves indeterminate structures elegantly: express the strain energy in terms of the redundant, differentiate, set to zero. For the propped cantilever it yields **R = 3wL/8** directly, without any compatibility diagram.

examTip.trick: The **½** comes from the load building up **gradually** — the work is the triangular area under the load–extension curve.
examTip.mnemonic: **Resilience is energy stored ELASTICALLY (recoverable); TOUGHNESS is the total area to fracture.** Toughness is what earthquake engineering needs, because the demand is to **absorb** energy, not return it. Hence ductility, not strength, is the property that saves structures.

questions.stem: In a composite (compound) bar of steel and concrete carrying an axial load, the two materials share the load such that:
options: The stresses in both are equal
The strains in both are equal
The concrete carries all the load
questions.solution:
**The STRAINS in both are equal, and the load divides in proportion to AE.**

**The two governing conditions:**

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **COMPATIBILITY** | **ε_s = ε_c** — the materials are bonded, so they **must deform together** |
| **EQUILIBRIUM** | **P = P_s + P_c** — the loads sum to the total |

**From compatibility:**

> **σ_s/E_s = σ_c/E_c**, so **σ_s = (E_s/E_c) σ_c = m σ_c**

where **m = E_s/E_c** is the **MODULAR RATIO** — about **8 to 15** for steel and concrete.

**And the load division:**

> **P_s/P_c = (A_s E_s)/(A_c E_c)** — in proportion to **AE**, the **axial rigidity**

**The general principle**, which recurs throughout indeterminate analysis:

> **LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS.** The stiffer material takes the larger share — here in proportion to AE, in a frame in proportion to EI/L.

**Because m ≈ 8 to 15, the STEEL carries a stress that many times greater than the concrete's**, even though it occupies a small fraction of the area. In a typical RC column with 2% steel, the steel may carry **20–25%** of the load from **2%** of the area.

**Solving the standard problem:**

1. Write **σ_s = m σ_c** (compatibility).
2. Write **P = σ_s A_s + σ_c A_c** (equilibrium).
3. Substitute: **P = σ_c(m A_s + A_c)**.
4. **σ_c = P/(A_c + m A_s)** — where **(A_c + mA_s)** is the **EQUIVALENT (transformed) AREA**.

**The transformed-section idea** is the general technique and is worth stating clearly:

> **Replace the steel by an EQUIVALENT area of concrete, m times as large.** The composite section then behaves as a single homogeneous concrete section of area **A_c + mA_s**, and ordinary formulae apply.

The same device handles **bending** of composite sections: the steel is transformed to equivalent concrete, the neutral axis and second moment of area are computed for the transformed section, and the **steel stress is recovered by multiplying the concrete stress at that level by m**.

**Where the analysis is used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **RC columns** under axial load | The classic case |
| **Composite steel–concrete** beams and columns | Deck slab acting with a steel girder |
| **Flitched beams** — timber with steel plates | Timber transformed to equivalent steel or vice versa |
| Bolted joints with different materials | — |
| Working stress design of RC generally | The modular ratio method |

**A crucial caveat for concrete — CREEP:**

> Concrete **CREEPS** under sustained load — its strain grows over time at constant stress. Steel does **not**. Since the two must strain **together**, the concrete's creep **TRANSFERS load progressively to the STEEL**.

**So the long-term steel stress is considerably HIGHER than the short-term analysis predicts** — and the concrete's lower. IS 456 accounts for this by using a **long-term modular ratio**:

> **m = 280/(3 σ_cbc)** — which builds in a creep allowance and gives values around 13 for M20 and 9 for M30, rather than the elastic E_s/E_c of about 8.

**That the code's modular ratio is deliberately larger than the elastic ratio is worth knowing**, because it looks like an error until the creep reason is understood.

**Shrinkage** acts similarly: concrete shrinks, steel does not, so the bonded steel **restrains the shrinkage** — putting the **steel into compression and the concrete into TENSION**. That self-induced tension is a principal cause of shrinkage cracking in restrained members, and it is why minimum reinforcement for crack control is specified independently of any calculated load.

examTip.trap: "Equal stresses" is the intuitive wrong answer. The materials are **bonded**, so it is the **STRAINS** that must match — and equal strain with different E means very different stress.
examTip.trick: **σ_s = mσ_c** where m = E_s/E_c, and the load splits in proportion to **AE**. Solve using the **transformed area A_c + mA_s**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load flows toward stiffness.** With m ≈ 8–15, steel at 2% of the area carries 20–25% of the load. Long-term subtlety: **concrete CREEPS and steel does not**, so load transfers progressively to the steel — which is why IS 456's design m = 280/(3σ_cbc) is deliberately larger than the elastic ratio.

questions.stem: Complementary shear stresses on two mutually perpendicular planes are:
options: Equal in magnitude and both directed toward or away from the common edge
Equal in magnitude and opposite in sign
questions.solution:
**Equal in magnitude, and both directed either toward or away from the common edge.**

**Why they must exist.** Consider a small rectangular element with a shear stress τ on its top and bottom faces. Those two form a **COUPLE**, which would spin the element. For **moment equilibrium**, an equal and opposite couple must act on the vertical faces:

> **τ_xy = τ_yx** — always, and this is the **complementary shear stress**

**The directional rule**: the arrows on the four faces either **all point toward** two opposite corners or **all point away** from them. They never form a consistent circulation, which would violate moment equilibrium.

**The consequences are far-reaching:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **A shear stress NEVER acts alone** | It is always accompanied by its complement on the perpendicular plane |
| **HORIZONTAL shear in beams** | The vertical shear must be accompanied by an equal **horizontal** shear — which is why beams delaminate along their length |
| The stress tensor is **SYMMETRIC** | τ_xy = τ_yx, τ_yz = τ_zy, τ_zx = τ_xz |
| **Mohr's circle** is valid | The construction depends on this symmetry |

**Horizontal shear in beams is the most important practical consequence:**

> A beam carries **vertical** shear. By complementary action there must be an equal **HORIZONTAL** shear stress on longitudinal planes — and it is that horizontal shear which tends to make the layers of a beam **slide over one another**.

**The demonstration** is the classic one: a stack of loose planks bent as a beam **slips at every interface**, and the ends form a staircase. Glue them together and the assembly becomes vastly stiffer and stronger — because the glue resists the horizontal shear and forces the planks to act as one deep member.

**The horizontal shear stress distribution:**

> **τ = VAȳ/(I b)**

| Section | Maximum τ | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **1.5 V/A** | **Neutral axis** |
| **Circular** | **1.33 V/A** | Neutral axis |
| **I-section** | **≈ V/(web area)** | **Web at the neutral axis** |

**Note that τ is MAXIMUM at the NEUTRAL AXIS** — precisely where the **bending stress is ZERO**. Bending and shear stresses peak at opposite extremes of the section, which is what makes an **I-section** so efficient:

> **FLANGES** (far from the neutral axis) carry the **BENDING**; the **WEB** (at the neutral axis) carries the **SHEAR**. Each part is placed where it is most useful.

**The design applications of horizontal shear:**

| Application | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Composite beams** — steel girder with concrete slab | **SHEAR CONNECTORS** (studs) must transfer the horizontal shear at the interface |
| **Precast plus in-situ topping** | Interface shear must be checked; roughening or links provided |
| **Construction joints** in concrete | The joint plane must transfer shear — hence roughening and shear-friction reinforcement |
| **Glued laminated timber** | The glue lines carry the horizontal shear |
| **Bolted/riveted plate girders** | Bolt spacing determined by **q = VAȳ/I**, the shear flow |

**Shear connectors on a composite beam** are the clearest illustration:

> Without connectors, the slab and girder bend **independently** — each about its own axis, giving a small combined I. With connectors resisting the interface shear, they act as **one deep composite section** with a far larger I.

The gain is typically a **doubling or tripling** of stiffness and strength for a modest number of welded studs — one of the best returns available in structural engineering, and entirely a consequence of complementary shear.

**Shear flow q = VAȳ/I** (force per unit length) is the quantity used to space the connectors: **spacing = (capacity of one connector)/q**, so connectors are **closely spaced near the supports** where V is greatest, and more widely at midspan.

examTip.trick: Moment equilibrium of a small element forces **τ_xy = τ_yx** — a shear on one face cannot exist alone or the element would spin.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vertical shear in a beam REQUIRES an equal HORIZONTAL shear** — which is what makes a stack of loose planks slip at every interface, and what glue or **shear connectors** resist. Note τ is maximum at the **neutral axis**, where bending stress is zero: flanges take the moment, the web takes the shear.

questions.stem: A bar of 20 mm diameter carries an axial tensile load of 60 kN. The tensile stress is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 191 MPa.**

> **A = πd²/4 = π(20)²/4 = 314.16 mm²**
> **σ = P/A = 60 000/314.16 = 190.99 ≈ 191 N/mm² = 191 MPa** ✓

**Option (b), 95 MPa**, halves it — the classic slip of using **πd²/2** or forgetting the /4. Option (d), 150 MPa, uses d² = 400 without the π/4.

**A useful shortcut for circular bars:**

> **A ≈ 0.785 d²**, so for **d = 20**, A ≈ 0.785 × 400 = **314 mm²** ✓

**Standard bar areas** worth knowing, since they recur constantly in reinforcement calculations:

| Diameter (mm) | Area (mm²) |
|---|---|
| 8 | **50** |
| 10 | **78.5** |
| 12 | **113** |
| **16** | **201** |
| **20** | **314** |
| **25** | **491** |
| 32 | 804 |

**A quick check on the result's significance**: 191 MPa in a mild steel bar (f_y = 250 MPa) is about **76% of yield** — high for a working stress but reasonable for a factored load. In Fe415 reinforcement it is 46% of yield.

**Permissible and design stresses:**

| Material | Yield / characteristic | Design stress (limit state) |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild steel Fe250** | 250 MPa | **0.87 × 250 = 217 MPa** |
| **Fe415** | 415 MPa | **0.87 × 415 = 361 MPa** |
| **Fe500** | 500 MPa | **0.87 × 500 = 435 MPa** |
| Structural steel E250 | 250 MPa | 250/1.10 = 227 MPa |

**The 0.87 factor** is **1/1.15** — the partial safety factor for steel in IS 456. For **concrete** the corresponding factor is **1/1.5**, and the design compressive strength is **0.67 f_ck/1.5 = 0.446 f_ck**.

**Why steel and concrete have different partial factors** is worth understanding:

> **Steel is FACTORY-MADE to specification** — its strength is reliable and its variability low, so γ_m = 1.15 suffices. **Concrete is made on SITE** from variable materials by variable workmanship, so its variability is far greater and γ_m = 1.5 is needed.

**And the additional 0.67 on concrete** accounts for the difference between the **cube strength** measured in the laboratory and the **actual strength in a structural member** — which is lower because of the sustained loading, the size and shape of the member, and the different curing conditions on site.

**Extension of the bar in this problem**, for completeness:

> **δ = PL/(AE)** — so for a 3 m bar of E = 200 GPa:
> **δ = 60 000 × 3000/(314.16 × 200 000) = 180 × 10⁶/62.83 × 10⁶ = 2.86 mm**

**Note the strain**: **ε = σ/E = 191/200 000 = 0.00095**, or **0.095%** — under a tenth of one percent, which is characteristic of steel at working stress and a reminder of how small elastic strains are.

**The axial rigidity AE** is the governing quantity for extension, exactly as **EI** is for bending and **GJ** for torsion:

| Action | Rigidity | Deformation |
|---|---|---|
| **Axial** | **AE** | **δ = PL/AE** |
| **Bending** | **EI** | δ ∝ WL³/EI |
| **Torsion** | **GJ** | **θ = TL/GJ** |

Holding those three in parallel makes the structure of the whole subject clearer: each is a load × length divided by a rigidity, and each rigidity is a material property times a geometric property.

examTip.trap: 95 MPa is exactly half — the classic slip of dropping the /4 or using πd²/2.
examTip.trick: **A ≈ 0.785 d² = 314 mm²; σ = 60 000/314 = 191 MPa.** Sanity-check it: 191 MPa is 76% of mild steel's 250 MPa yield, which is high but credible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bar areas worth memorising: 8→50, 10→78.5, 12→113, 16→201, 20→314, 25→491 mm².** They recur in every reinforcement calculation.

questions.stem: The volumetric strain of a bar subjected to uniaxial tensile strain ε is:
questions.solution:
**e_v = ε(1 − 2μ).**

**Derivation.** Under a uniaxial stress in the x-direction:

> **ε_x = ε** (the axial strain)
> **ε_y = ε_z = −μ ε** (lateral contraction)

For small strains the volumetric strain is the **sum** of the three:

> **e_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z = ε − με − με = ε(1 − 2μ)** ✓

**The consequences:**

| μ | (1 − 2μ) | Volume change under tension |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | 1 | **Increases by the full ε** |
| **0.25** | 0.5 | Increases by half |
| **0.3 (steel)** | **0.4** | Increases by 0.4ε |
| **0.5** | **0** | **NO volume change — incompressible** |

> **A bar in tension GAINS volume** (for μ < 0.5), and one in compression **loses** volume. Only at μ = 0.5 is the volume preserved.

**The μ = 0.5 case connects directly to the bulk modulus relation:**

> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**, so **K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)] → ∞** as μ → 0.5 ✓

An infinite bulk modulus is exactly what "incompressible" means, and the two results agree — a good internal check.

**For a general three-dimensional stress state:**

> **e_v = (σ_x + σ_y + σ_z)(1 − 2μ)/E**

**Note that the volumetric strain depends only on the SUM of the three normal stresses** — the **first stress invariant**, or three times the mean (hydrostatic) stress. **Shear stresses do not change volume at all.**

**That separation is fundamental** and underlies plasticity theory:

| Component | Causes | Governed by |
|---|---|---|
| **HYDROSTATIC (mean) stress** | **Volume change** | **K** |
| **DEVIATORIC stress** | **SHAPE change (distortion)** | **G** |

> **Metals yield by DISTORTION, not by volume change.** Hydrostatic pressure alone, however large, does not cause a metal to yield — which is why the **von Mises** and **Tresca** criteria depend only on the deviatoric part.

**The theories of failure**, which follow directly:

| Theory | Criterion | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum principal STRESS (Rankine)** | σ₁ = σ_y | **BRITTLE** materials |
| **Maximum shear stress (TRESCA)** | (σ₁ − σ₃) = σ_y | **DUCTILE** — safe and simple |
| **Maximum DISTORTION ENERGY (VON MISES)** | The deviatoric energy criterion | **DUCTILE — the best fit to test data** |
| Maximum principal strain (St Venant) | — | Rarely used; poor agreement |
| Maximum strain energy (Haigh) | — | Superseded by von Mises |

**Tresca versus von Mises:**

| | Tresca | von Mises |
|---|---|---|
| Yield surface (2-D) | A **hexagon** | An **ellipse** circumscribing it |
| Conservatism | **More conservative** (up to 15%) | Closer to experiment |
| Use | Simple hand calculation, some codes | **Finite element analysis**, most modern work |

> **Tresca is always the safer of the two** — its hexagon lies inside von Mises' ellipse — which is why it survives in codes despite von Mises fitting the data better.

**For CONCRETE and SOIL, none of these apply**, because those materials **do** depend on the hydrostatic stress:

> Confining a concrete cylinder or a soil sample **greatly increases its strength**. Their failure criteria — **Mohr–Coulomb**, Drucker–Prager — therefore include the mean stress explicitly, unlike the metal criteria.

That is the same **confinement** effect met earlier: the reason spiral reinforcement strengthens a column, and the reason a triaxial test gives a higher strength at higher cell pressure.

examTip.trick: Add the three strains: **ε + (−με) + (−με) = ε(1 − 2μ)**. At μ = 0.5 it vanishes — incompressible, consistent with K → ∞.
examTip.mnemonic: **Volume change depends only on the SUM of the normal stresses; shear never changes volume.** That split is why **metals yield on the DEVIATORIC part alone** (von Mises, Tresca) while **soil and concrete depend on the mean stress too** (Mohr–Coulomb) — confinement strengthens them.

questions.stem: In a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure, the ratio of hoop stress to longitudinal stress is:
questions.solution:
**2 — the hoop stress is TWICE the longitudinal stress.**

> **σ_hoop = pD/(2t)**
> **σ_long = pD/(4t)**
> **Ratio = 2** ✓

**Derivations:**

| Stress | Force balance |
|---|---|
| **Hoop** | Pressure on the diametral projection **pD × L** resisted by **two** wall sections **2tL**: **σ = pD/(2t)** |
| **Longitudinal** | Pressure on the end area **pπD²/4** resisted by the annular wall **πDt**: **σ = pD/(4t)** |

**The consequence is directly observable:**

> **A pressurised cylinder SPLITS LENGTHWISE**, along a longitudinal line — because the **hoop** stress reaches the limit first, and it acts to tear the cylinder apart circumferentially.

The same is true of a sausage bursting in a pan, and of a garden hose failing — always a longitudinal split, never a circumferential one.

**Comparison with a SPHERE:**

| Vessel | Stress | Relative to a cylinder |
|---|---|---|
| **Cylinder** | **pD/(2t)** hoop, pD/(4t) longitudinal | — |
| **SPHERE** | **pD/(4t)** in **ALL** directions | **HALF** the cylinder's maximum |

> A **sphere needs only HALF the wall thickness** of a cylinder for the same pressure and diameter — which is why **gas storage spheres are spherical**, and why the ends of a pressure vessel are **domed** rather than flat.

**Flat ends are the worst option**, because they carry the pressure in **bending** rather than membrane action — requiring far greater thickness. The progression is: flat (worst), conical, torispherical, hemispherical (best).

**Strains in a thin cylinder**, needed for volume change and for strain-gauge work:

> **Hoop strain: ε_h = (pD/2tE)(1 − μ/2)**
> **Longitudinal strain: ε_l = (pD/2tE)(1/2 − μ)**
> **Volumetric strain: e_v = 2ε_h + ε_l = (pD/2tE)(5/2 − 2μ)**

**Note that for μ > 0.5 the longitudinal strain would be negative** — the cylinder would shorten as it is pressurised. Since μ ≤ 0.5 for real materials, it always lengthens, but only slightly.

**Design of a pressure pipe or penstock:**

> **t = pD/(2σ_allowable) + corrosion allowance**

with **p** taken as the **maximum credible pressure**, including:

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Static head** | γH from the reservoir |
| **WATER HAMMER surge** | **Often doubles or triples** the static pressure |
| Test pressure | Usually 1.5 × working |

**The water hammer allowance is essential and not a refinement**: a penstock designed for the static head alone fails on the first emergency shutdown. **Δp = ρcΔV** for water at 3 m/s in a steel pipe is about **3.6 MPa ≈ 360 m** of extra head — frequently exceeding the static head itself.

**The thin-cylinder assumption** is **D/t > 20**, so the stress may be taken as uniform through the wall. For a **thick** cylinder the stress varies radially and **Lamé's equations** are required:

> **σ_r = A − B/r²**, **σ_θ = A + B/r²**

with the **hoop stress MAXIMUM at the INNER surface** — which is why thick cylinders fail from the bore outward, and why they are sometimes **autofrettaged** (deliberately overstrained to leave a favourable residual compression at the bore).

**For a TANK rather than a pipe**, the hoop force varies with depth because the pressure does:

> **T = γ h D/2** — **maximum at the base**, zero at the top

which is why a steel tank's shell plates are **thickest at the bottom** and step thinner up the height, following the pressure diagram.

examTip.trick: Hoop from a diametral cut (**pD/2t**, two wall thicknesses resisting), longitudinal from an end cut (**pD/4t**, the full annulus resisting). Ratio exactly 2.
examTip.mnemonic: **A pressurised cylinder SPLITS LENGTHWISE** — hoop reaches the limit first. A **sphere is pD/4t in every direction**, so it needs half the thickness, which is why gas storage vessels are spherical. For a penstock, always add the **water hammer** surge, which often exceeds the static head.

questions.stem: The principal planes in a stressed body are those on which:
questions.solution:
**Those on which the SHEAR stress is zero.**

**That is the definition**, and the normal stresses acting on those planes are the **PRINCIPAL STRESSES** — the maximum and minimum normal stresses at the point.

**The key results:**

> **σ₁,₂ = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]**
> **tan 2θ_p = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y)**

**Properties:**

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Principal planes carry NO shear** | By definition |
| They are **mutually PERPENDICULAR** | 90° apart in the physical plane (180° on Mohr's circle) |
| σ₁ is the **maximum** normal stress at the point | σ₂ the minimum |
| **Maximum shear planes** are at **45°** to them | 90° apart on the circle |
| **τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2** | The radius of Mohr's circle |
| On the maximum shear planes, **σ = (σ₁ + σ₂)/2** | The circle's centre |

**The invariants** — quantities unchanged by the choice of axes:

> **σ_x + σ_y = σ₁ + σ₂** (the first invariant)
> **σ_x σ_y − τ_xy² = σ₁ σ₂** (the second invariant)

**The first invariant is the most useful check on any calculation**: whatever axes you use, the **sum of the normal stresses is the same**. If your principal stresses do not sum to σ_x + σ_y, there is an arithmetic error.

**Why principal stresses matter:**

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **FAILURE criteria** are written in terms of them | Rankine, Tresca, von Mises all use σ₁, σ₂, σ₃ |
| **Brittle materials fail on the principal TENSION plane** | Perpendicular to σ₁ |
| **Crack directions** are predicted by them | Cracks run **perpendicular to the principal tension** |
| **Reinforcement direction** in concrete | Ideally aligned with the principal tension |
| Strain gauge rosettes | Measure three strains to find the principal directions |

**Crack direction is the practically visible consequence:**

| Loading | Principal tension | Crack direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure bending** | **Horizontal**, at the tension face | **VERTICAL** cracks |
| **Shear** near a support | At **45°** | **DIAGONAL** cracks running up toward the load |
| **Torsion** | **Helical at 45°** | **Spiral** cracks |
| Combined | Curved crack paths | — |

> **Reading the crack pattern tells you the stress state** — which makes crack mapping one of the most informative and cheapest structural investigations available. Vertical cracks at midspan mean flexure; diagonal cracks near supports mean shear; spiral cracks mean torsion.

**In concrete design, the 45° diagonal tension is what stirrups resist**, and the reason vertical stirrups work despite not being perpendicular to the crack is simply that they still cross it — with some loss of efficiency, accepted for the great gain in buildability.

**STRAIN ROSETTES** are the experimental application:

> A single strain gauge measures strain in **one direction** only. Three gauges at known angles — a **rosette** (45° or 60°) — allow the full 2-D strain state, and hence the **principal strains and their directions**, to be computed.

The principal **stresses** then follow from the principal strains through Hooke's law in two dimensions:

> **σ₁ = E(ε₁ + με₂)/(1 − μ²)**, **σ₂ = E(ε₂ + με₁)/(1 − μ²)**

**Note that principal STRESS and principal STRAIN directions coincide** for an **isotropic** material — but **not** for an anisotropic one such as timber or a fibre composite, where the material's own axes intervene. That is a real trap in experimental work on non-isotropic materials.

examTip.trap: "Maximum shear stress" is the near-miss — those planes are at **45°** to the principal planes, not on them.
examTip.trick: Zero shear is the **definition**. The normal stresses on those planes are then the maximum and minimum at the point.
examTip.mnemonic: **Invariant check: σ_x + σ_y = σ₁ + σ₂ always.** If your principal stresses do not sum to the originals, the arithmetic is wrong. Practical value: **cracks run perpendicular to the principal tension** — vertical at midspan (flexure), diagonal near supports (shear), spiral in torsion. Reading a crack pattern tells you the stress state.

questions.stem: A load applied suddenly (from zero height) to an elastic bar produces a stress compared with the same load applied gradually of:
questions.solution:
**Twice.**

**The energy argument:**

| Application | Work done by the load | Strain energy stored |
|---|---|---|
| **GRADUAL** | **½ P δ** (the load builds from zero) | ½ P δ |
| **SUDDEN** | **P δ** (the full load acts through the whole displacement) | ½ P δ_sudden |

Equating work to strain energy for the sudden case:

> **P δ_s = ½ P_equivalent δ_s**, giving an effective load of **2P**
> so **σ_sudden = 2P/A = 2 σ_gradual** ✓

**And the deflection doubles too**: **δ_sudden = 2 δ_static**.

**The physical picture** makes it clearer than the algebra:

> The bar **OVERSHOOTS**. It accelerates downward past the static equilibrium position, reaching **twice** the static deflection where the kinetic energy is again zero, then **oscillates** about the static position until damping brings it to rest **at the static value**.

So the doubled stress is a **transient peak**, not a permanent state — but it is the peak that must be designed for.

**The general IMPACT formula**, for a load P falling through a height h onto the bar:

> **σ = (P/A)[1 + √(1 + 2hAE/(PL))]**

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| **h = 0** (suddenly applied) | **σ = 2P/A** ✓ — the formula reduces correctly |
| **h large** | **σ ≈ (P/A)√(2hAE/(PL))** — grows as **√h** |
| Gradual | σ = P/A |

**The h = 0 check** is worth doing because it confirms the formula and the factor of two together.

**What reduces impact stress**, reading from the formula:

| Change | Effect | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Increase the LENGTH L** | **Reduces** the stress | More material to absorb the energy |
| **Reduce E** (a more flexible material) | **Reduces** the stress | Greater deflection absorbs the energy at lower stress |
| Increase the area A | Reduces the stress, but **less than proportionally** | A appears inside the root as well |
| Add a **spring or resilient pad** | **Greatly reduces** it | Increases the deflection over which the energy is absorbed |

**The counter-intuitive result is worth stating plainly:**

> Under **impact**, a **MORE FLEXIBLE** member is **BETTER** — it absorbs the same energy at a lower stress by deflecting further. Under **static** load, a stiffer member is better.

**Stiffness and impact resistance pull in opposite directions**, which is why crash structures, vehicle bumpers, rock-fall barriers and seismic isolators are all deliberately **flexible** and **energy-absorbing** rather than rigid.

**Where impact matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pile driving** | The hammer's energy governs the stresses in the pile |
| **Crane and hoist** loads | Codes apply an **impact factor** |
| **Bridge live load** | An **impact allowance** is added to vehicle loads — IRC gives factors up to 0.545/(6 + L) |
| **Rock-fall barriers** | Designed to absorb kinetic energy |
| **Vehicle barriers and crash cushions** | Deliberately deformable |
| Machine foundations | Dynamic amplification |

**Bridge impact factors** are the codified expression of this: a vehicle crossing a bridge is not a static load, and IRC and IS codes add a percentage — **larger for short spans** (where a single axle dominates and the dynamic effect is sharpest) and smaller for long ones.

**A caution on the factor of two**: it applies to a **linear elastic** member with the load applied to a stationary structure. Real impacts involve local plasticity, damping and contact effects, so the theoretical doubling is an upper bound for the idealised case — but a sound and standard basis for design.

examTip.trick: With a **gradual** load the work is ½Pδ; with a **sudden** load the full P acts through the whole δ, so the work is Pδ — twice as much, hence twice the stress.
examTip.mnemonic: **The bar OVERSHOOTS to twice the static deflection, then oscillates back.** Counter-intuitive corollary: under impact a **more FLEXIBLE member is better**, because it absorbs the same energy at lower stress. Stiffness and impact resistance pull in opposite directions — which is why crash barriers and seismic isolators are deliberately soft.

questions.stem: Stress concentration at a hole or notch in a member is most damaging under:
options: Static loading of a ductile material
Fatigue loading, or static loading of a brittle material
No loading condition — it is always negligible
questions.solution:
**Under FATIGUE loading, or static loading of a BRITTLE material.**

**Stress concentration** is the local elevation of stress at a geometric discontinuity:

> **σ_max = K_t σ_nominal**, where **K_t** is the **stress concentration factor**

| Discontinuity | Approximate K_t |
|---|---|
| **Small circular hole** in a wide plate (tension) | **3.0** |
| Elliptical hole | 1 + 2a/b — **large for a sharp ellipse** |
| **Sharp re-entrant corner** | **Very high**, theoretically infinite |
| **Generous fillet radius** | **1.5 – 2.0** |
| Shoulder with a small fillet | 2 – 3 |

**The circular hole's K_t = 3** is worth remembering as a benchmark: a hole triples the local stress, however small the hole is relative to the plate.

**Why the effect depends on the material and the loading:**

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **DUCTILE material, STATIC load** | The peak stress **YIELDS LOCALLY and REDISTRIBUTES**. The concentration is **largely relieved**, and the member's static strength is barely affected |
| **BRITTLE material, static load** | **NO redistribution is possible** — the peak stress **initiates FRACTURE** |
| **FATIGUE (cyclic) loading, any material** | The peak stress **initiates a CRACK**, which then **propagates**. **Critical** |

> **A ductile material under static load is forgiving of stress concentration; nothing else is.**

**That is why bolt holes in a steel tension member barely reduce its static strength** (beyond the loss of area) but are the **usual initiation sites for fatigue cracks** in a bridge or crane girder.

**FATIGUE** is the dominant application:

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Failure at stresses well BELOW the static strength** | Often below yield |
| Caused by **repeated cycles** | Millions in service |
| **Progressive crack growth** from an initiation site | Beach marks on the fracture surface |
| **SUDDEN final fracture** when the crack reaches critical size | **No warning** |
| **ENDURANCE LIMIT** for steel | Below about **0.5 × ultimate strength**, infinite life |
| Aluminium | **NO endurance limit** — fails eventually at any stress range |

**The absence of an endurance limit in aluminium** is an important practical difference: a steel component below its endurance limit lasts indefinitely, while an aluminium one accumulates damage at any stress range and must be designed for a **finite life**.

**Reducing stress concentration:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **GENEROUS FILLET RADII** — never a sharp re-entrant corner | The single most effective measure |
| **Gradual** changes of section | Avoid abrupt steps |
| **Smooth surface finish** | Machining marks are miniature notches |
| **Grinding weld toes** smooth | Weld toes are severe notches |
| Relief holes beside a notch | Redistributes the flow of stress |
| **Compressive residual stress** — shot peening, cold expansion of holes | Delays crack initiation |

**The fillet radius is worth emphasising** because it is a design detail that costs nothing:

> A **sharp internal corner** has a theoretically **infinite** stress concentration. A **radius** — even a modest one — brings K_t down to 2 or less. Specifying a radius on a drawing is free; omitting it can halve a component's fatigue life.

**In welded structures the weld itself is the concentration**, which is why fatigue codes classify **weld details** rather than materials:

| Detail | Fatigue class |
|---|---|
| **Plain rolled plate** | Best |
| **Butt weld, ground flush** | Good |
| Butt weld, as welded | Moderate |
| **Fillet weld, transverse attachment** | Poor |
| **Weld ending on the plate surface** | **Worst** |

> The **material grade is almost irrelevant to fatigue strength** in welded steel — a high-strength steel and a mild steel with the same weld detail have essentially the **same fatigue life**. Fatigue is governed by the **detail geometry**, not the material strength.

That is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and a common source of error: specifying a stronger steel to fix a fatigue problem achieves nothing, while improving the weld detail achieves a great deal.

**Where fatigue matters in civil engineering**: **bridges** (traffic cycles), **crane runway girders**, **machine foundations**, **offshore structures** (wave loading), and **wind-sensitive structures** such as masts and chimneys subject to vortex shedding.

examTip.trap: "Static loading of a ductile material" is the tempting answer because the concentration factor is the same — but a ductile material **yields locally and redistributes**, so its static strength is barely affected.
examTip.trick: Ask whether redistribution is possible. Ductile + static → yes, harmless. Brittle, or any material under **cyclic** load → no, and a crack starts.
examTip.mnemonic: **A circular hole gives K_t = 3.** Fatigue is governed by the **DETAIL GEOMETRY, not the material strength** — a high-strength steel and a mild steel with the same weld detail have essentially the same fatigue life. So specifying stronger steel to fix a fatigue problem achieves nothing; improving the detail achieves a great deal.

questions.stem: A steel rod 25 mm in diameter and 4 m long carries 100 kN. Taking E = 200 GPa, the extension is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 4.07 mm.**

> **A = πd²/4 = π(25)²/4 = 490.87 mm²**
> **δ = PL/(AE) = 100 000 × 4000/(490.87 × 200 000)**
> **= 4 × 10⁸/(9.817 × 10⁷) = 4.074 mm** ✓

**Check the stress**, which should always be done:

> **σ = P/A = 100 000/490.87 = 203.7 N/mm²**
> **ε = σ/E = 203.7/200 000 = 1.019 × 10⁻³**
> **δ = εL = 1.019 × 10⁻³ × 4000 = 4.07 mm** ✓

**Both routes agree.** The second is often the safer way to work, because the intermediate stress and strain values can each be sanity-checked: **203.7 MPa** is about **81% of the 250 MPa yield** of mild steel — high but elastic — and a strain of **0.1%** is entirely typical.

**The axial deformation formula:**

> **δ = PL/(AE)**

| Symbol | Increases δ? |
|---|---|
| **P** load | Yes, proportionally |
| **L** length | Yes, proportionally |
| **A** area | **No** — inversely |
| **E** modulus | **No** — inversely |

> **AE is the AXIAL RIGIDITY** — the exact analogue of **EI** in bending and **GJ** in torsion.

**For a stepped or varying bar**, the extensions **add**:

> **δ_total = Σ P_i L_i/(A_i E_i)**

and for a **continuously varying** section, **δ = ∫P dx/(A(x)E)**.

**Two special cases worth knowing:**

| Case | Extension |
|---|---|
| **Bar of TAPERING circular section**, diameters d₁ to d₂ | **δ = 4PL/(π d₁ d₂ E)** |
| **Bar under its OWN WEIGHT** (hanging) | **δ = WL/(2AE)** — **half** what the same total weight would give as an end load |

**The self-weight result** has a neat physical reading: the weight is distributed, so on average each element carries only **half** the total — hence half the extension. It matters for long hanging members such as **deep shaft linings, mine hoisting ropes and long piles being lifted**.

**A design perspective on the answer**: 4 mm over 4 m is a strain of **0.1%** — imperceptible, and typical of steel at working stress. That smallness is why **elastic deformation rarely governs** in an axially loaded member, and why **buckling** (for compression) or **connection design** usually decides the section instead.

**For a COMPRESSION member the same formula gives the shortening**, but only if the member does not **buckle** first — and for anything slender it will:

> **Euler: P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**

A 25 mm rod 4 m long has a slenderness ratio of **L/r = 4000/6.25 = 640** — enormously slender. Its Euler load is

> **I = πd⁴/64 = π(25)⁴/64 = 19 175 mm⁴**
> **P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 19 175/4000² = 3.79 × 10¹⁰/1.6 × 10⁷ = 2367 N ≈ 2.4 kN**

**So in compression the same rod would buckle at about 2.4 kN — against 100 kN in tension.** A factor of more than forty.

> **That asymmetry is the central fact of compression member design**: a member that is entirely adequate in tension may be useless in compression, and the governing quantity is **slenderness**, not strength. It is why bracing members are often designed as **tension-only**, and why a cable can carry enormous tension in a section that would buckle under trivial compression.

examTip.trick: Work it in two steps so each can be checked: **σ = 100 000/490.9 = 203.7 MPa**, then **δ = σL/E = 203.7 × 4000/200 000 = 4.07 mm** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Three rigidities in parallel: AE for axial (δ = PL/AE), EI for bending, GJ for torsion.** Striking comparison: this rod carries 100 kN in tension but would **buckle at about 2.4 kN in compression** (Euler, L/r = 640) — a factor of forty. Slenderness, not strength, governs compression members.

questions.stem: The maximum shear stress theory of failure (Tresca) compared with the maximum distortion energy theory (von Mises) is:
options: More conservative, giving a safe but slightly uneconomical design
questions.solution:
**More conservative — safe, but slightly uneconomical.**

**The two ductile-failure theories:**

| Theory | Criterion | Yield surface (2-D) |
|---|---|---|
| **TRESCA** (maximum shear stress) | **σ₁ − σ₃ = σ_y** | A **HEXAGON** |
| **VON MISES** (distortion energy) | **√[½((σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)²)] = σ_y** | An **ELLIPSE** circumscribing the hexagon |

**Because the Tresca hexagon lies INSIDE the von Mises ellipse**, Tresca predicts yielding at lower loads — hence it is **always the more conservative** of the two.

**The maximum divergence is 15.5%**, occurring in **pure shear**:

| Theory | Predicted shear yield strength |
|---|---|
| **Tresca** | **τ_y = 0.500 σ_y** |
| **von Mises** | **τ_y = 0.577 σ_y** |
| Experiment | **≈ 0.577** — von Mises is closer |

**They AGREE exactly in uniaxial tension and in balanced biaxial states** — the hexagon and ellipse touch at those points — so the choice only matters for genuinely multiaxial stress states.

**Why both survive in practice:**

| Theory | Argument for it |
|---|---|
| **Tresca** | **Simpler** to apply by hand; **always safe**; used in several pressure vessel codes |
| **von Mises** | **Better agreement with experiment**; **smooth** surface (no corners) makes it far easier to handle numerically — which is why **every finite element package uses it** |

**The smoothness point is the practical reason von Mises dominates modern work**: the Tresca hexagon has **corners** where the gradient is undefined, which causes numerical difficulty in a plasticity algorithm. The ellipse has none.

**The full set of failure theories:**

| Theory | Criterion | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum principal STRESS (Rankine)** | σ₁ = σ_ut | **BRITTLE** materials — cast iron, concrete, glass |
| **Maximum principal STRAIN (St Venant)** | ε₁ = ε_y | Rarely used — poor agreement |
| **Maximum SHEAR (Tresca)** | σ₁ − σ₃ = σ_y | **DUCTILE**; conservative |
| **Total strain energy (Haigh)** | — | Superseded |
| **DISTORTION energy (von Mises)** | As above | **DUCTILE — the best fit** |
| **MOHR–COULOMB** | τ = c + σ tan φ | **SOIL, ROCK, CONCRETE** |

**The essential division:**

| Material type | Fails by | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **DUCTILE** (steel) | **SHEAR / distortion** | **Tresca or von Mises** |
| **BRITTLE** (cast iron, glass) | **Direct TENSION** | **Rankine** |
| **FRICTIONAL** (soil, rock, concrete) | Shear, but **dependent on confining stress** | **MOHR–COULOMB** |

**Why metals need no hydrostatic term:**

> **Metals yield by DISTORTION, not by volume change.** Hydrostatic pressure alone, however large, does not cause a metal to yield — so Tresca and von Mises depend only on the **differences** between principal stresses, never on their sum.

**Why soil and concrete DO need one:**

> **Confinement greatly increases their strength.** A concrete cylinder under lateral pressure crushes at a far higher axial stress; a soil sample in a triaxial test is stronger at higher cell pressure. Their criteria must therefore include the **mean (normal) stress**, which is exactly what **Mohr–Coulomb's σ tan φ** term provides.

**That difference is not a detail but a statement about the failure mechanism**: metals fail by dislocations sliding, which is insensitive to pressure; granular and cementitious materials fail by particles sliding past one another, which pressure directly resists.

**A practical note on using them**: for ordinary structural steel design, neither theory is applied explicitly — the **codes have already embedded them** in the interaction formulae for combined bending, shear and axial force. Explicit use arises in **pressure vessels, machine components, and finite element post-processing**, where the von Mises stress is the standard output plotted as a contour map.

examTip.trick: The Tresca **hexagon** lies inside the von Mises **ellipse**, so Tresca always predicts yielding first. They agree exactly in uniaxial tension and diverge most — by **15.5%** — in pure shear.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tresca τ_y = 0.5σ_y; von Mises τ_y = 0.577σ_y**, and experiment favours von Mises. Von Mises dominates modern work because its **smooth** surface has no corners to trouble a numerical algorithm. Neither applies to soil or concrete, which need **Mohr–Coulomb** because their strength depends on confinement.

questions.stem: The bulk modulus K of a material is the ratio of:
questions.solution:
**Hydrostatic (volumetric) stress to volumetric strain.**

> **K = σ_hydrostatic / e_v**

**The four constants, each pairing a stress with its corresponding strain:**

| Constant | Stress | Strain | Deformation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **E** (Young's) | **Direct** | **Direct** | Change of **length** |
| **G** (rigidity) | **SHEAR** | Shear (angular) | Change of **SHAPE** |
| **K** (bulk) | **HYDROSTATIC** | **Volumetric** | Change of **VOLUME** |
| **μ** (Poisson) | — | Lateral/longitudinal | — |

> Each of the wrong options names a **different** one of these — (a) is G, (b) is E, (c) is μ — which makes this a definition question rather than a calculation.

**Hydrostatic stress** means equal normal stress in all three directions, with no shear — the state a body experiences under uniform pressure, as in deep water or a triaxial cell with equal all-round pressure.

**The relations:**

> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**, so **K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)]**

| μ | K/E |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.33 |
| 0.25 | 0.67 |
| **0.3 (steel)** | **0.83** |
| 0.4 | 1.67 |
| **0.5** | **∞ — incompressible** |

**The K → ∞ limit at μ = 0.5** is the check that ties the constants together: an incompressible material cannot change volume under any pressure, which is an infinite bulk modulus, and it agrees with **e_v = ε(1 − 2μ) = 0** at the same value.

**Values:**

| Material | K (GPa) |
|---|---|
| **Steel** | **167** |
| Concrete | ~15 |
| **WATER** | **2.1** |
| Air (isothermal) | **0.0001** |
| Rubber | High — nearly incompressible |

**Water's bulk modulus** connects this topic directly to fluid mechanics:

> **K_water = 2.1 GPa** is high enough that water is treated as **incompressible** for almost all purposes — a pressure of 1 MPa compresses it by only 0.05%.

> But it is **finite**, and that matters for **WATER HAMMER**: the pressure wave travels at **c = √(K/ρ) = √(2.1 × 10⁹/1000) = 1449 m/s**. Treating water as truly incompressible would make the wave speed **infinite** and the pressure rise **unbounded** — the analysis fails completely.

**The decomposition of any stress state** into its two parts is the deeper significance of K and G:

| Component | Definition | Causes | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HYDROSTATIC (mean)** | **(σ₁ + σ₂ + σ₃)/3** in all directions | **Volume** change | **K** |
| **DEVIATORIC** | The remainder | **SHAPE** change (distortion) | **G** |

> **Every stress state splits uniquely into these two parts**, and they act independently: the mean stress changes the volume without distorting, the deviatoric part distorts without changing volume.

**Why that decomposition matters:**

| Material | Yields on |
|---|---|
| **METALS** | The **DEVIATORIC** part only — hydrostatic pressure does not cause yielding |
| **SOILS and CONCRETE** | **BOTH** — confinement (mean stress) increases the strength |

**That single distinction explains the different families of failure criteria**: von Mises and Tresca use only the deviatoric part; Mohr–Coulomb and Drucker–Prager include the mean stress explicitly.

**In soil mechanics** the same decomposition appears as **p′ (mean effective stress)** and **q (deviator stress)**, which are the axes of the **critical state** plot — so the volumetric/deviatoric split learned here in elasticity is the same one that organises modern soil mechanics.

examTip.trap: Each wrong option names a **different** elastic constant — shear/shear is G, direct/direct is E, lateral/longitudinal is μ. It is a definition question, not a calculation.
examTip.trick: Hydrostatic means equal normal stress in all three directions with no shear — the state under uniform pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **E length, G shape, K volume.** Water's K = 2.1 GPa is high enough to treat as incompressible — **except for water hammer**, where the finite value gives c = √(K/ρ) = 1440 m/s. Assume true incompressibility there and the wave speed is infinite and the whole analysis collapses.

questions.stem: The bending equation for a beam in pure bending is:
questions.solution:
**M/I = σ/y = E/R.**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **M** | Bending moment at the section |
| **I** | Second moment of area about the neutral axis |
| **σ** | Bending stress at distance y from the neutral axis |
| **y** | Distance from the **neutral axis** |
| **E** | Young's modulus |
| **R** | Radius of curvature of the bent beam |

**The equation is really three statements in one:**

> **σ = My/I** — the **stress** at any fibre
> **1/R = M/(EI)** — the **curvature**, which is what gets integrated to find deflections
> **M = EI/R** — the **moment–curvature** relation

**Assumptions behind it**, all of which matter:

| Assumption | Consequence if violated |
|---|---|
| **Plane sections remain plane** | The strain would not vary linearly with y |
| Material is **homogeneous and isotropic** | A composite section needs the transformed-section method |
| **E is the same in tension and compression** | Cast iron and concrete violate this |
| Stresses are **within the elastic limit** | Beyond yield, plastic analysis is needed |
| The beam is **initially straight**, of constant section | A curved beam has a different (Winkler) theory |
| Loads act in a **plane of symmetry** | Otherwise there is unsymmetrical bending and twist |

**"Plane sections remain plane" is the load-bearing assumption**, because everything else follows from it: if plane sections stay plane, the **strain varies linearly** with distance from the neutral axis, and with Hooke's law the **stress does too**.

**The stress distribution:**

| Location | Bending stress |
|---|---|
| **Neutral axis** | **ZERO** |
| Extreme top fibre | Maximum compression (sagging) |
| Extreme bottom fibre | Maximum tension (sagging) |

> **σ_max = M/Z**, where **Z = I/y_max** is the **section modulus**.

**Note the contrast with shear stress**, which is exactly the reverse:

| | **Bending stress** | **Shear stress** |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution | **Linear** | **Parabolic** |
| Maximum at | **Extreme fibres** | **Neutral axis** |
| Zero at | **Neutral axis** | Extreme fibres |

> That complementarity is precisely why an **I-section** is efficient: the **flanges** sit where the bending stress is greatest, and the **web** sits where the shear is greatest. Each part of the section is placed where it is most useful.

**Where the neutral axis lies** is the companion result: for a homogeneous section in pure bending it passes through the **centroid**, because the net axial force on the section must be zero and only the centroidal axis satisfies ∫y dA = 0.

examTip.trap: **R/E instead of E/R** is the deliberate near-miss, and it is easy to write the wrong way round under pressure.
examTip.trick: Check by units. **M/I is N·m/m⁴ = N/m³**, and **σ/y is (N/m²)/m = N/m³** ✓. Then **E/R is (N/m²)/m = N/m³** ✓ — but R/E would be m³/N, which does not match.
examTip.mnemonic: **"M over I equals sigma over y equals E over R"** — read it aloud in that order and the arrangement sticks. The most-used rearrangements are **σ = My/I** and **1/R = M/EI**.

questions.stem: In a beam subjected to pure bending, the neutral axis:
options: Passes through the centroid of the cross-section
Passes through the mid-depth regardless of shape
Lies at the extreme compression fibre
questions.solution:
**It passes through the CENTROID of the cross-section.**

**Why.** In **pure bending** there is no net axial force on the section, so the compressive force above the neutral axis must exactly balance the tensile force below it:

> **∫σ dA = 0**, and since **σ = (E/R)y**, this becomes **∫y dA = 0**

> **∫y dA = 0 is the definition of the centroidal axis.** So the neutral axis and the centroidal axis are the same line.

**The trap in option (b)** is that mid-depth and centroid **coincide only for a section symmetrical about the horizontal axis**. For an unsymmetrical section they are different:

| Section | Neutral axis at mid-depth? |
|---|---|
| Rectangle, circle, symmetrical I | **Yes** — the centroid is at mid-depth |
| **T-section** | **NO** — the centroid sits well up toward the flange |
| **Channel, angle, unequal I** | **NO** |

**The consequence for a T-section** is important and often missed:

> Because the neutral axis is **not** at mid-depth, **y_top ≠ y_bottom**, so there are **TWO section moduli**: **Z_top = I/y_top** and **Z_bottom = I/y_bottom**.

> **Design on the SMALLER Z**, which corresponds to the **larger y** — that is the fibre that reaches the limiting stress first.

**For a material with unequal strengths**, the choice becomes deliberate rather than automatic:

> **Cast iron** is strong in compression and weak in tension. So a cast iron beam is made with an **unsymmetrical section that puts the neutral axis closer to the TENSION face**, keeping the tensile stress low while allowing a high compressive stress. That is why old cast-iron beams have a large bottom flange and a small top one.

**Locating the centroid** of a composite shape:

> **ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i)/ΣA_i**

then the second moment of area follows by the **parallel axis theorem**:

> **I = Σ(I_Gi + A_i h_i²)**

**A useful check**: the neutral axis must always lie **within** the section's depth, and for a T or channel it must lie **on the side of the bulk of the material**. If your calculation puts it outside the section, the arithmetic is wrong.

**Note the qualification "pure bending"**: if there is also an **axial force**, the neutral axis **shifts away from the centroid** — and if the axial force is large enough, it moves outside the section entirely and the whole section is in compression (or tension). That is exactly the **middle third** situation met in columns and masonry.

examTip.trap: "Mid-depth regardless of shape" is true only for a **symmetrical** section. For a **T-section or channel** the centroid is nowhere near mid-depth, and assuming it is gives a badly wrong stress.
examTip.trick: For an unsymmetrical section there are **two section moduli** — always design on the **smaller Z** (the larger y), because that fibre reaches the limit first.
examTip.mnemonic: **No axial force → neutral axis at the CENTROID.** Add an axial force and it shifts; add enough and it leaves the section altogether, which is the middle-third condition.

questions.stem: The flexural rigidity of a beam is represented by:
questions.solution:
**EI** — the product of Young's modulus and the second moment of area.

**It appears wherever curvature or deflection is computed:**

> **1/R = M/(EI)** — the moment–curvature relation
> **d²y/dx² = M/(EI)** — the differential equation of the elastic curve
> **δ ∝ WL³/(EI)** — every standard deflection formula

**The three rigidities, in parallel:**

| Action | Rigidity | Deformation |
|---|---|---|
| **Axial** | **AE** | **δ = PL/(AE)** |
| **Bending** | **EI** | δ ∝ WL³/(EI) |
| **Torsion** | **GJ** | **θ = TL/(GJ)** |

> Each is a **material property × a geometric property**, and each deformation is a **load × length divided by the rigidity**. Holding the three together makes the structure of the whole subject clearer than learning them separately.

**Every option offered is a real rigidity** — which is what makes this a definition question rather than a calculation:

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **EA** | **Axial** rigidity |
| **GJ** | **Torsional** rigidity |
| **E/I** | Not a rigidity at all — dimensionally meaningless here |
| **EI** | **Flexural** rigidity ✓ |

**Why EI matters so much in design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Deflection ∝ 1/EI** | Doubling EI halves the deflection |
| **I ∝ d³** for a rectangle | So **DEPTH is the powerful variable** |
| E is essentially **fixed** for a given material | You cannot buy a stiffer steel |
| Load distributes in proportion to **EI/L** | In indeterminate structures, **load flows toward stiffness** |

**The depth point deserves emphasis:**

> For a rectangular section **I = bd³/12**. **Doubling the WIDTH doubles I; doubling the DEPTH multiplies it by EIGHT.** So when a beam deflects too much, increasing the depth is always the more effective remedy.

**And E is not a design variable in steel:**

> **E ≈ 200 GPa for EVERY structural steel grade** — mild steel and high-strength steel alike. A higher grade buys **strength**, not **stiffness**. So specifying stronger steel reduces the section needed for strength but does **nothing** for deflection, which is why deflection so often governs in high-strength design.

**For concrete E does vary with strength**: **E_c = 5000√f_ck** (IS 456), so M25 gives 25 GPa and M40 gives 31.6 GPa — a modest gain for a large increase in strength. And concrete's effective EI is further complicated by **cracking** (which reduces I) and **creep** (which effectively reduces E over time, roughly halving the long-term stiffness).

examTip.trap: **GJ (torsional)** and **EA (axial)** are both genuine rigidities offered as distractors. Read which **action** the question is about.
examTip.trick: Match the letter to the action: **A** for area (axial), **I** for second moment (bending), **J** for polar (torsion) — and **G** goes with torsion because torsion is a shear problem.
examTip.mnemonic: **AE axial, EI bending, GJ torsion** — three rigidities, and every deformation is load × length ÷ rigidity. Note **I ∝ d³, so DEPTH is the powerful variable** when deflection governs.

questions.stem: The maximum deflection of a simply supported beam of span L carrying a central point load W is:
questions.solution:
**WL³/(48EI)**, at midspan.

**The standard deflection cases**, which should be known without derivation:

| Beam and loading | Maximum deflection | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported, central load W** | **WL³/(48EI)** | Midspan |
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** | Midspan |
| **Cantilever, end load W** | **WL³/(3EI)** | Free end |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** | Free end |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL w** | **wL⁴/(384EI)** | Midspan |
| **Fixed both ends, central load W** | WL³/(192EI) | Midspan |
| **Propped cantilever, UDL w** | wL⁴/(185EI) | 0.4215L from prop |

**Every wrong option here is a genuine standard case**, which is what makes the set instructive:

| Option | Which case it is |
|---|---|
| **WL³/(3EI)** | **Cantilever** with an end load |
| **5WL³/(384EI)** | Simply supported under **UDL** (with W = wL) |
| **WL³/(8EI)** | Cantilever under **UDL** (with W = wL) |

**Comparing the cases for the same TOTAL load W:**

| Beam | Deflection | Relative |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed both ends, UDL** | WL³/(384EI) | **1.0** |
| **Simply supported, UDL** | 5WL³/(384EI) | **5.0** |
| **Simply supported, central load** | WL³/(48EI) = 8WL³/(384EI) | **8.0** |
| **Cantilever, UDL** | WL³/(8EI) = 48WL³/(384EI) | **48** |
| **Cantilever, end load** | WL³/(3EI) = 128WL³/(384EI) | **128** |

> Two lessons fall out. **Fixing the ends cuts the deflection to one fifth.** And a **cantilever deflects enormously** — 128 times a fixed-ended beam under the same total load — which is why cantilever span/depth limits are so much tighter (7 against 26).

**The scaling relations** that govern long spans:

> **δ ∝ L³** for a point load, **δ ∝ L⁴** for a UDL, and **δ ∝ 1/I ∝ 1/d³**.

> So **doubling the span multiplies a UDL deflection by SIXTEEN**, while **doubling the depth divides it by eight**.

**Why deflection often governs rather than strength:**

| Limit (IS 456) | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total deflection** | **span/250** |
| Deflection **after partitions are built**, or 20 mm, whichever is less | **span/350** |

> The **second limit** is the one that bites, because it protects **brittle finishes** — plaster, blockwork, glazing — which crack under movement occurring **after** they are installed. A structure can be perfectly strong and still fail this check.

**Methods of finding deflections** when the case is not standard: **double integration**, **Macaulay's method** (a bookkeeping device for discontinuous loading), **moment-area theorems**, **conjugate beam**, and the **unit load (virtual work)** method — the last being the most general and the one that handles frames and trusses.

examTip.trap: **Every distractor is a real standard case** — cantilever end load (3), simply supported UDL (384), cantilever UDL (8). The trap is picking the right formula for the wrong beam, so read the support condition and the loading before the options.
examTip.trick: Memorise the denominators as a ladder for a **simply supported** beam: **48 for a central point load, 384/5 for a UDL**. Then a **cantilever** is far more flexible: **3 and 8**.
examTip.mnemonic: **"48 for a point, 384 over 5 for a UDL."** And hold the comparison: for the same total load a cantilever deflects about **16 times** a simply supported beam — which is why its span/depth limit is 7 and not 20.

questions.stem: Macaulay's method is used in beam analysis to:
options: Find the reactions of an indeterminate beam
Handle discontinuous loading in a single integration for slope and deflection
Compute the shear centre of a section
questions.solution:
**To handle discontinuous loading in a single integration** when finding slopes and deflections.

**The problem it solves.** Double integration of **EI d²y/dx² = M** works well when M has a single expression along the whole beam. But a beam with several point loads has a **different M expression in each segment**, so plain double integration would need a separate integration per segment — and **two constants of integration for each**, matched by continuity conditions at every junction. For a beam with four loads that is ten constants.

**Macaulay's device** is a bookkeeping notation using **angular brackets**:

> **⟨x − a⟩ⁿ = 0** when **x < a**
> **⟨x − a⟩ⁿ = (x − a)ⁿ** when **x ≥ a**

**So one expression covers the whole beam**, and the bracketed terms simply switch themselves on as you pass each load.

**The rules that make it work:**

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Integrate the bracket **as a whole** | **∫⟨x−a⟩ dx = ⟨x−a⟩²/2**, never expanded |
| **Never expand** the bracket | Expanding destroys the switching behaviour |
| Take moments from **one end only**, consistently | Usually the left |
| A **UDL that stops** must be **extended and cancelled** | Add an equal upward UDL from where it stops |
| Only **two constants** for the whole beam | Found from the two support conditions |

**The UDL cancellation trick** is the part most often got wrong:

> A UDL acting from **a to b** cannot be written directly. Instead, apply it **from a to the end of the beam**, then apply an **equal and opposite upward UDL from b to the end**. The two cancel beyond b, leaving exactly the loading required.

**The methods for deflection, compared:**

| Method | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Double integration** | Simple continuous loading |
| **MACAULAY** | **Several point loads and partial UDLs** — the workhorse |
| **Moment-area theorems** | When only the slope or deflection **at one point** is wanted |
| **Conjugate beam** | Cantilevers and beams with varying EI |
| **Unit load (virtual work)** | **The most general** — handles trusses and frames too |
| Castigliano | Where the strain energy is easy to write |

**What Macaulay's method is NOT for**, which is what the distractors test:

> It finds **slopes and deflections**. It does not find reactions (statics does, for a determinate beam), it has nothing to do with **plastic** analysis, and the **shear centre** is a quite separate problem in unsymmetrical bending and torsion.

**A worked outline.** For a simply supported beam with a point load W at distance a:

> **EI d²y/dx² = R_A x − W⟨x − a⟩**
> **EI dy/dx = R_A x²/2 − W⟨x − a⟩²/2 + C₁**
> **EI y = R_A x³/6 − W⟨x − a⟩³/6 + C₁x + C₂**

with **y = 0 at x = 0** giving C₂ = 0, and **y = 0 at x = L** giving C₁. Two conditions, two constants — for a beam of any number of loads.

examTip.trick: **Never expand the ⟨ ⟩ bracket** — integrate it as a single unit. Expanding it destroys the switching behaviour and the method collapses into ordinary integration.
examTip.trap: A **UDL that stops partway** must be extended to the end of the beam and **cancelled by an equal upward UDL** from the point where it stops. Writing it directly is the classic error and gives a wrong deflection beyond that point.
examTip.mnemonic: **Angular brackets switch ON as you pass the load and stay off before it.** The reward is only **TWO constants of integration for the whole beam**, found from the two support conditions — instead of two per segment.

questions.stem: Euler's crippling load for a column with both ends hinged is:
questions.solution:
**P_cr = π²EI/L²** for a column hinged at both ends.

**The general form is written with the EFFECTIVE length:**

> **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**

| End conditions | Effective length L_e | P_cr relative to hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **Both hinged (pinned)** | **L** | **1** |
| **Both fixed** | **0.5L** | **4** |
| **One fixed, one hinged** | **0.7L** | **2** |
| **One fixed, one FREE (cantilever)** | **2L** | **0.25** |

**Because P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², the end conditions matter enormously:**

> A **fixed–fixed** column carries **FOUR times** the load of a hinged one of the same length. A **cantilever** column carries only a **QUARTER**. That is a factor of **sixteen** between the best and worst end conditions.

**The physical meaning of effective length:**

> **L_e is the distance between POINTS OF CONTRAFLEXURE** — the length of the equivalent pin-ended strut. A fixed–fixed column has contraflexure points at its quarter points, so L_e = 0.5L. A cantilever has none within its length, and its equivalent pin-ended strut is twice as long.

**Two things are strikingly absent from Euler's formula:**

| Absent | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The material's STRENGTH** | Only **E** appears, not f_y. So a high-strength steel column of the same section buckles at exactly the same load as a mild steel one |
| Any measure of imperfection | Real columns, being imperfect, always fail below the Euler load |

> **That strength does not appear is the most important thing about the formula.** It means that for a slender column, **specifying stronger steel achieves nothing** — the answer is a stiffer section or a shorter effective length.

**In terms of slenderness:**

> **σ_cr = P_cr/A = π²E/(L_e/k)²**, where **k = √(I/A)** is the radius of gyration and **L_e/k** the **slenderness ratio**.

**Euler's formula is only valid for SLENDER columns:**

> It is valid while **σ_cr ≤ f_y**. Setting them equal gives the **critical slenderness ratio**: for mild steel with f_y = 250 and E = 200 000, **L_e/k ≈ 89**.

| Slenderness | Behaviour | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **Below ~80** | **CRUSHING** dominates | Euler gives absurdly high loads — do not use it |
| Around 80–120 | Both matter | Rankine, or a code curve |
| **Above ~120** | **BUCKLING** dominates | Euler applies |

**Rankine's formula** bridges the whole range and is why it survives despite being empirical:

> **P = f_c A/(1 + a(L_e/k)²)**

> At **small** slenderness it tends to the crushing load **f_c A**; at **large** slenderness it approaches the Euler load. One expression, both limits.

**Real design uses neither directly**: IS 800 uses **multiple buckling curves** that account for residual stresses, initial crookedness and the shape of the section — all effects Euler's idealisation ignores.
