examTip.trap: **4π²EI/L²** is the **fixed–fixed** value and **π²EI/4L²** is the **cantilever** value. All three appear together, so read the end conditions first, before looking at the options.
examTip.trick: Work from **L_e**, not from a memorised list of four formulas: **hinged L, fixed 0.5L, fixed–hinged 0.7L, cantilever 2L** — then square it.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Half, point-seven, one, two"** for fixed, fixed-hinged, hinged, cantilever. And note what is **missing** from Euler: the material's **strength**. A stronger steel does not help a slender column at all.

questions.stem: The slenderness ratio of a column is the ratio of its:
options: Effective length to its least radius of gyration
questions.solution:
**Effective length to the LEAST radius of gyration: λ = L_e/k_min.**

**Both qualifiers matter:**

| Qualifier | Why |
|---|---|
| **EFFECTIVE** length, not actual | The end conditions change the buckling length by up to a factor of four |
| **LEAST** radius of gyration | A column buckles about its **WEAKEST** axis, so k_min governs |

> **k = √(I/A)**, so **k_min = √(I_min/A)** — computed with the **smaller** of the two principal second moments of area.

**Why the least axis governs** is the point most often missed:

> A column will buckle about whichever axis gives the **largest slenderness**, and that is the axis with the **smallest k**. Checking only the major axis is a genuine and dangerous error — a deep narrow section is very strong about one axis and very weak about the other.

**Which is why beam sections and column sections look different:**

| Member | Shape | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **BEAM** | **Deep and narrow** | Bends about **ONE** axis only, so all the material goes where it helps |
| **COLUMN** | **Square-ish, or tubular** | Can buckle about **BOTH** axes, so k must be large in both directions |

> A deep I-beam makes a poor column, because its minor-axis k is small. That is why column sections (H-sections, box sections, circular hollow sections) are proportioned much more evenly.

**Classification by slenderness:**

| λ = L_e/k | Type | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| **< 32** (or L/d < 12 for concrete) | **SHORT** | **Crushing** |
| 32 – 120 | Intermediate | Combined |
| **> 120** | **LONG / slender** | **BUCKLING** |

**Code limits on slenderness** (IS 800):

| Member | Maximum λ |
|---|---|
| Carrying **compression** under dead and live load | **180** |
| Compression under **wind or seismic** load only | 250 |
| **Tension** member (to limit sag and vibration) | **400** |

> Note that even a **tension** member has a slenderness limit — not for strength (a tension member cannot buckle) but to prevent **excessive sag under its own weight** and **vibration or flutter** in the wind.

**How to reduce slenderness**, in order of effectiveness:

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Add intermediate BRACING** | Halving the unbraced length halves λ and **quadruples** the capacity |
| **Improve the end fixity** | L_e from L to 0.5L doubles the capacity... quadruples it |
| Use a section with a **larger k_min** | A tube or box, rather than a deep I |
| Increase the area | Least effective, since k grows only slowly with A |

**Bracing is by far the cheapest of these**, which is why it is the standard answer to a slender compression member: a small strut at mid-height costs almost nothing and can quadruple the column's capacity.

**For a rectangular section**, **k = d/√12 ≈ 0.289d** about the axis of depth d — and note that the **width cancels entirely**, so k depends only on the dimension in the plane of buckling.

examTip.trap: "Length to depth" is a real ratio used for concrete columns and for span/depth checks — but the **slenderness ratio** proper is **L_e/k**, and it uses the **effective** length and the **LEAST** radius of gyration.
examTip.trick: Ask which axis is weakest. A column buckles about the axis with the **smallest k**, so checking only the major axis is a genuine and dangerous omission.
examTip.mnemonic: **Beams are deep and narrow (one axis); columns are square-ish (both axes).** The cheapest fix for a slender column is **intermediate bracing** — halving the unbraced length quadruples the capacity.

questions.stem: A steel rod 3 m long, hinged at both ends, has a diameter of 40 mm. Taking E = 200 GPa, its Euler buckling load is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 27.6 kN.**

> **I = πd⁴/64 = π(40)⁴/64 = π × 2 560 000/64 = 125 664 mm⁴**
> **L_e = L = 3000 mm** (both ends hinged)
> **P_cr = π²EI/L_e² = π² × 200 000 × 125 664/(3000)²**
> **= 9.8696 × 200 000 × 125 664/9 000 000**
> **= 2.4805 × 10¹¹/9 × 10⁶ = 27 561 N ≈ 27.6 kN** ✓

**Check the slenderness**, which should always be done before applying Euler:

> **k = √(I/A)**, with **A = πd²/4 = 1257 mm²**
> **k = √(125 664/1257) = √100 = 10 mm** (which is **d/4** — a standard result for a solid circle)
> **λ = L_e/k = 3000/10 = 300**

> **λ = 300 is very slender**, far above the critical value of about 89 for mild steel — so **Euler is valid** here.

**Confirm by the critical stress:**

> **σ_cr = P_cr/A = 27 561/1257 = 21.9 N/mm²**

> That is **well below the 250 N/mm² yield**, which confirms the rod buckles long before it yields ✓

**The comparison that matters:**

| Loading | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Tension** | **A × f_y = 1257 × 250 = 314 kN** |
| **Compression (buckling)** | **27.6 kN** |
| Ratio | **More than 11 times** |

> The **same rod** carries eleven times more in tension than in compression. That asymmetry is the central fact of compression member design, and it is why **bracing members are often designed as tension-only** — a slender rod is an excellent tie and a useless strut.

**Useful standard results for a solid circular section:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **A** | πd²/4 |
| **I** (diametral) | **πd⁴/64** |
| **J** (polar) | πd⁴/32 |
| **Z** | πd³/32 |
| **k** | **d/4** |

> **k = d/4 for a circle** is worth remembering — it makes the slenderness of any circular member a one-line calculation: **λ = 4L_e/d**.

**How to improve this rod's compression capacity**, in order of effectiveness:

| Measure | New P_cr |
|---|---|
| **Brace at mid-height** (L_e = 1.5 m) | **× 4 = 110 kN** |
| **Fix both ends** (L_e = 1.5 m) | × 4 = 110 kN |
| Use a **50 mm** rod instead | × (50/40)⁴ = **× 2.44 = 67 kN** |
| Use **high-strength steel** | **NO CHANGE — E is the same** |

> The last row is the instructive one: **stronger steel does nothing for a slender column**, because Euler's formula contains **E but not f_y**.

examTip.trick: For a **solid circle, k = d/4** — so slenderness is simply **λ = 4L_e/d**, here 4 × 3000/40 = **300**. That one shortcut turns the validity check into a mental calculation.
examTip.trap: **Always verify Euler is valid before using it.** Below a slenderness of about 80 it gives absurdly high loads, because the column crushes before it can buckle. Here λ = 300, so it is safely in the Euler range.
examTip.mnemonic: **I = πd⁴/64 — the fourth power.** And hold the comparison: this rod takes **314 kN in tension but only 27.6 kN in compression**. Slenderness, not strength, governs compression members.

questions.stem: The section modulus of a rectangular section of width b and depth d about its centroidal axis is:
questions.solution:
**Z = bd²/6.**

**Derive it rather than memorise it:**

> **Z = I/y_max = (bd³/12)/(d/2) = bd³/12 × 2/d = bd²/6** ✓

**Check the dimensions**, which eliminates two options instantly:

> **Z must be a VOLUME (mm³)**, because **σ = M/Z** needs (N·mm)/(mm³) = N/mm² ✓

> So **bd²** (mm³) is right and **bd³** (mm⁴) is wrong — the latter is the second moment of area **I**, not the section modulus.

**Z and I compared:**

| | **I** | **Z** |
|---|---|---|
| Units | **mm⁴** | **mm³** |
| Rectangle | **bd³/12** | **bd²/6** |
| Circle | **πd⁴/64** | **πd³/32** |
| Governs | **STIFFNESS** (deflection) | **STRENGTH** (stress) |
| Appears in | δ ∝ WL³/EI | **σ = M/Z** |

> **Z governs strength; I governs stiffness.** Keeping the two apart is worth more than memorising either formula.

**Note the powers of depth:**

> **Z ∝ d²** — doubling the depth **quadruples** the moment capacity.
> **I ∝ d³** — doubling the depth multiplies the stiffness by **eight**.

> Both favour depth over width, but **stiffness benefits more**. That is why a deflection problem is best solved by increasing depth, and why the span/depth rules are written as they are.

**The strongest rectangular beam cut from a circular log** is a classic application:

> Maximising **Z = bd²/6** subject to **b² + d² = D²** gives **d = D√(2/3)** and **b = D/√3**, so **d/b = √2**.

> **The strongest rectangular section from a round log has a depth-to-width ratio of √2 ≈ 1.414.**

(The **stiffest** section is a different optimisation — maximising I gives d/b = √3 ≈ 1.732. Strength and stiffness do not give the same answer.)

**For an unsymmetrical section there are TWO section moduli:**

> **Z_top = I/y_top** and **Z_bottom = I/y_bottom**

> **Design on the SMALLER Z** — which corresponds to the **larger y** — because that fibre reaches the limiting stress first.

**Plastic section modulus** is the companion quantity in steel design:

> **Z_p = bd²/4** for a rectangle, against the elastic **bd²/6**.

> Their ratio is the **SHAPE FACTOR**: **(bd²/4)/(bd²/6) = 1.5** for a rectangle.

| Section | Shape factor |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **1.7** |
| Diamond | 2.0 |
| **I-section** | **1.10 – 1.20** |

> The **I-section has the lowest shape factor** precisely because its material is already concentrated in the flanges, so there is little under-worked material left to yield after the extreme fibre goes. A rectangle has plenty near the neutral axis, hence 1.5.

examTip.trap: **bd³/12 is I, not Z** — and it is the most tempting wrong answer because it is the formula everyone knows best.
examTip.trick: Settle it by **units**: σ = M/Z needs Z in **mm³**, so it must be **bd²** something. That kills both bd³ options in one step, leaving only the 6 versus 12 choice — and Z = I/(d/2) doubles the 12 into a 6.
examTip.mnemonic: **Z = bd²/6 (strength, mm³); I = bd³/12 (stiffness, mm⁴).** Plastic modulus is **bd²/4**, so the rectangle's shape factor is **1.5** — while an I-section's is only 1.10–1.20.

questions.stem: In the moment-area method, the first theorem states that the change in slope between two points on a beam equals the:
options: Area of the M/EI diagram between those points
Moment of the M/EI diagram about one of the points
Product of the moment and the distance
questions.solution:
**The AREA of the M/EI diagram between those two points.**

**The two moment-area theorems:**

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **First (slope)** | The **change in SLOPE** between A and B = the **AREA** of the M/EI diagram between them |
| **Second (deflection)** | The **deviation** of B from the tangent drawn at A = the **MOMENT of the AREA** of the M/EI diagram between them, taken **about B** |

> **First theorem: area. Second theorem: moment of area.** That single distinction is the whole method.

**Where they come from.** Since **d²y/dx² = M/(EI)**, one integration gives the slope:

> **θ_B − θ_A = ∫(M/EI) dx** — the **area** ✓

and a second integration, taking moments, gives the deviation:

> **t_{B/A} = ∫(M/EI) x dx** — the **first moment of the area** ✓

**The critical subtlety in the second theorem** is what it actually measures:

> It gives the **DEVIATION of B from the TANGENT at A** — not the deflection of B. Those are the same thing **only when the tangent at A is horizontal**, which happens at a **fixed support** or at a **point of maximum deflection** (where the slope is zero).

> For a **simply supported** beam the tangent at a support is **not** horizontal, so an extra geometric step is needed: compute the deviations of both ends from a convenient tangent and use similar triangles.

**When to use it:**

| Situation | Suitability |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **Excellent** — the tangent at the fixed end is horizontal, so deviation = deflection directly |
| **Slope or deflection at ONE point only** | **Excellent** — no need for the whole elastic curve |
| **Varying EI** (stepped or tapered beams) | **Excellent** — EI simply goes inside the diagram |
| Whole deflected shape wanted | Poor — use double integration or Macaulay |
| Many point loads | Awkward — Macaulay is cleaner |

**The M/EI diagram, not the M diagram** — the EI must be divided out **before** taking areas. For a prismatic beam this is a constant that can be factored out, but for a **stepped** beam it cannot, and that is exactly where the method shines.

**Sign convention**: a **sagging** (positive) M/EI area gives a positive change of slope, and the deviation is measured **from the tangent toward the beam**. Working the signs consistently matters more here than in most methods, because the geometry is easy to get backwards.

**The CONJUGATE BEAM method** is a repackaging of the same two theorems, and many find it easier:

> Load an imaginary **conjugate beam** with the **M/EI diagram** as its loading. Then:
> **Shear in the conjugate beam = SLOPE in the real beam**
> **Moment in the conjugate beam = DEFLECTION in the real beam**

> Its advantage is that the awkward geometry disappears — you simply compute a shear force and a bending moment, which is familiar work. Its price is that the **supports must be transformed**: a real fixed end becomes a conjugate free end, and a real free end becomes a conjugate fixed end.

**The full set of deflection methods:**

| Method | Best for |
|---|---|
| Double integration | Simple continuous loading |
| **Macaulay** | Several point loads, partial UDLs |
| **Moment-area** | One point, cantilevers, varying EI |
| **Conjugate beam** | The same, with easier bookkeeping |
| **Unit load / virtual work** | **The most general** — trusses and frames too |
| Castigliano | Where strain energy is easy to write |

examTip.trap: The second theorem gives the **deviation of B from the TANGENT at A**, not the deflection of B. Those coincide only where the tangent is **horizontal** — at a fixed end or at the point of maximum deflection.
examTip.trick: **First theorem: AREA. Second theorem: MOMENT of area.** One integration gives slope, two give deflection — exactly as with double integration, which is where both theorems come from.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use moment-area for CANTILEVERS and for VARYING EI** — the horizontal tangent at a fixed end makes deviation equal deflection directly, and a stepped EI simply goes inside the diagram.

questions.stem: In a flitched beam consisting of timber reinforced with steel plates, the two materials are analysed by:
options: Assuming each carries half the moment
Transforming one material into an equivalent area of the other using the modular ratio
Assuming equal stress in both materials
questions.solution:
**By transforming one material into an equivalent area of the other, using the MODULAR RATIO.**

**The two governing conditions**, exactly as for any composite member:

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **COMPATIBILITY** | The materials are **bonded**, so at any given distance from the neutral axis the **STRAIN is the same** in both |
| **EQUILIBRIUM** | The two moments of resistance sum to the applied moment |

**From equal strain:**

> **σ_s/E_s = σ_t/E_t**, so **σ_s = (E_s/E_t)σ_t = m σ_t**

where **m = E_s/E_t** is the **modular ratio** — about **20** for steel and timber.

**Option (d) is exactly wrong**, and it is the natural misconception:

> The **STRAINS** are equal, not the stresses. With m ≈ 20, the **steel carries about twenty times the stress** of the timber at the same distance from the neutral axis. That is precisely why a small area of steel is worth adding.

**The transformed section method:**

> **Replace the steel by an equivalent area of TIMBER, m times as wide**, at the same distance from the neutral axis. The section then behaves as one homogeneous timber beam.

**The critical detail** — which dimension is multiplied:

| Multiply | Correct? |
|---|---|
| The **WIDTH** by m | ✓ **Correct** |
| The **depth** by m | ✗ **Wrong** — it would move the material to a different distance from the neutral axis and change I entirely |

> The transformation must **preserve the distance from the neutral axis**, because that is what determines the strain. Only the **width** may be scaled.

**The procedure:**

1. Choose one material as the reference (usually the weaker — timber).
2. **Multiply the width** of the other material by **m**.
3. Find the **centroid and I** of the transformed section.
4. Compute **σ = My/I** in the reference material.
5. **Recover the other material's stress** by multiplying by **m**: σ_steel = m × σ_timber at that level.
6. Check **both** materials against their own permissible stresses.

**Step 6 matters**: either material may govern, and which one does depends on the geometry and on the ratio of permissible stresses — not on which is stronger in absolute terms.

**The same method covers a family of problems:**

| Application | Transformation |
|---|---|
| **Flitched beam** (timber + steel plates) | Steel → equivalent timber |
| **Reinforced concrete** (working stress method) | Steel → equivalent concrete, area **× m** |
| **Composite steel–concrete** beams | Concrete → equivalent steel |
| Any bonded two-material section | Either way |

**For reinforced concrete there is an extra step**: concrete is assumed to carry **no tension**, so the transformed section includes **only the concrete above the neutral axis** plus **mA_st** below it. The neutral axis is then found from the condition that the two first moments of area balance.

**And a caution for concrete specifically**: **concrete CREEPS and steel does not**. Since the two must strain together, creep progressively **transfers load to the steel**. IS 456 accounts for this by specifying a **long-term modular ratio m = 280/(3σ_cbc)**, deliberately larger than the elastic E_s/E_c — which looks like an error until the creep reason is understood.

examTip.trap: "Equal stress in both materials" is exactly backwards. The **STRAINS** are equal; with m ≈ 20 the steel carries about **twenty times** the stress — which is the whole point of adding it.
examTip.trick: Multiply the **WIDTH** by m, never the depth. Scaling the depth would move material to a different distance from the neutral axis and change I entirely, which breaks the equal-strain condition the method rests on.
examTip.mnemonic: **Equal strain → σ_s = m σ_t → transform the WIDTH.** Then check **BOTH** materials against their own permissible stresses — either can govern.

questions.stem: For a short column of rectangular section b × d carrying an eccentric axial load, no tension develops anywhere on the section provided the eccentricity does not exceed:
questions.solution:
**d/6** — the **middle third rule**.

**Derivation.** The stress under combined axial load and bending is:

> **σ = P/A ± Mc/I = P/A ± (Pe)(d/2)/(bd³/12) = (P/A)(1 ± 6e/d)**

> For **no tension**, the minimum stress must be **≥ 0**:
> **1 − 6e/d ≥ 0**, so **e ≤ d/6** ✓

**Because the load may be eccentric either way, the resultant must lie within the middle third — a band of width d/3 centred on the axis.**

**The stress states:**

| Eccentricity | Stress distribution | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **e = 0** | **Uniform** P/A | Full |
| **0 < e < d/6** | **Trapezoidal**, all compression | Full |
| **e = d/6** | **Triangular**, zero at one edge | Full, just |
| **e > d/6** | **Part of the section in TENSION** | **Partial — the section lifts off** |

**For e > d/6 in a material that cannot take tension** (masonry, soil, an unbonded base):

> The contact width reduces to **x = 3(d/2 − e)**, and the maximum stress becomes **σ_max = 2P/(3bx)**.

**Why the limit is enforced rather than merely recommended:**

> Once part of the base lifts off, the **contact area shrinks**, so the **resultant moves further toward the edge**, which **reduces the contact further**. The process is **PROGRESSIVE** — and progressive instability is a different matter from a section merely being overstressed.

**Where the rule is applied:**

| Application | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Masonry columns and walls** | Masonry has negligible tensile strength |
| **GRAVITY DAMS** | The resultant must stay in the middle third — a crack at the heel would admit **full reservoir pressure** into it, and it would propagate |
| **Retaining wall bases** | No tension between base and soil |
| **Footings** | Soil cannot pull |
| Unreinforced concrete | — |

**The gravity dam case is the most consequential**, and it shapes the section:

> Concrete and, more importantly, the **rock joint at the base** cannot carry tension. So a gravity dam's section is proportioned so that the resultant of **all** forces — weight, water thrust, uplift, silt, seismic — falls within the middle third, for **both** the reservoir-full and reservoir-empty conditions.

**For a CIRCULAR section** the equivalent limit is the **middle quarter**:

> **e ≤ d/8** for a solid circle — the "kern" is a circle of diameter d/4.

**The general term is the KERN (or core)** of a section: the region within which the load must act for the whole section to remain in compression. Its shape depends on the section:

| Section | Kern |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | A **rhombus** with diagonals b/3 and d/3 |
| **Circle diameter D** | A **circle** of diameter D/4 |
| Hollow circular | Larger — hollow sections have a bigger kern |

**Note that a reinforced section is exempt**: reinforcement carries the tension, so an RCC column or footing may have the resultant well outside the middle third. The middle third rule belongs to materials and interfaces that **cannot pull**.

examTip.trap: **d/3** is the width of the middle-third **band**, but the eccentricity limit is **half of it, d/6** — measured from the centre. Confusing the band with the limit is the standard slip.
examTip.trick: Derive it in one line: **σ = (P/A)(1 ± 6e/d)**, and set the bracket to zero. The 6 in the formula is where the /6 comes from.
examTip.mnemonic: **Middle THIRD band, d/6 eccentricity.** For a **circle** it is the middle **quarter**, e ≤ d/8. Beyond the limit the section lifts off and the process is **progressive** — which is why it governs gravity dam design.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a UDL of 40 kN/m. If the section is 300 mm wide and 500 mm deep, the maximum bending stress is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 14.4 N/mm².**

> **M_max = wL²/8 = 40 × 6²/8 = 40 × 36/8 = 180 kN·m = 180 × 10⁶ N·mm**
> **Z = bd²/6 = 300 × 500²/6 = 300 × 250 000/6 = 12.5 × 10⁶ mm³**
> **σ = M/Z = 180 × 10⁶/(12.5 × 10⁶) = 14.4 N/mm²** ✓

**Check by the other route**, which should give the same number:

| Step | Value |
|---|---|
| **I = bd³/12** | 300 × 500³/12 = **3125 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |
| **y_max = d/2** | **250 mm** |
| **σ = My/I** | 180 × 10⁶ × 250/(3125 × 10⁶) = **14.4 N/mm²** ✓ |

**Both routes agree**, which is the fastest way to catch an arithmetic slip.

**Where each distractor comes from:**

| Option | Error that produces it |
|---|---|
| **7.2** | Halving — using **Z = bd²/3** or forgetting a factor of 2 |
| **28.8** | Doubling — using **y = d** instead of **d/2**, or **Z = bd²/12** |
| **3.6** | Quartering — both errors together |

> Notice that the wrong answers are all **simple multiples of 2**. That is characteristic of numerical distractors in this topic, and it is a useful signal: when the options are 3.6, 7.2, 14.4 and 28.8, the question is testing whether you handle the **factor of 2 in y = d/2** correctly.

**The engineering reading of the result:**

> **14.4 N/mm²** is a moderate bending stress. For **structural steel** (250 N/mm²) it is very low; for **timber** it would be near the permissible limit; for **reinforced concrete** the section would be designed by limit state methods, and this much elastic tensile stress would have cracked the concrete long before.

**Checking the deflection**, which for a span of this order is often the governing criterion:

> **δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI)**. Taking concrete with E = 25 000 N/mm²:
> **δ = 5 × 40 × 6000⁴/(384 × 25 000 × 3125 × 10⁶)**
> **= 5 × 40 × 1.296 × 10¹⁵/(3.0 × 10¹⁶) ≈ 8.6 mm**

> Against a limit of **span/250 = 24 mm** that is comfortable — although the **long-term** value, allowing for creep and cracking, would be several times larger.

**The span/depth check** reaches the same conclusion in one line:

> **6000/500 = 12**, against IS 456's basic limit of **20** for a simply supported beam. Comfortably proportioned.

examTip.trick: Compute it **two ways** and require them to agree: **σ = My/I** with I = bd³/12 and y = d/2, and **σ = M/Z** with Z = bd²/6. Two routes to the same number is the fastest way to catch a slip.
examTip.trap: The commonest error is using **y = d instead of d/2**, or writing **Z = bd²/12** — either doubles the answer. Remember Z = I/y_max, and y_max is only **half** the depth for a symmetrical section.
examTip.mnemonic: **M = wL²/8, Z = bd²/6, σ = M/Z.** Then sanity-check the span/depth ratio: 6000/500 = 12 against a limit of 20, so this beam is comfortably proportioned.

questions.stem: The elastic curve of a beam is the:
options: Diagram of bending moment along the span
Shape of the deflected neutral axis
Plot of shear force against distance
questions.solution:
**The shape taken by the deflected NEUTRAL AXIS of the beam.**

**Its governing differential equation:**

> **EI d²y/dx² = M(x)**

from which everything else follows by successive integration:

| Derivative | Quantity |
|---|---|
| **y** | **Deflection** |
| **dy/dx** | **Slope** (rotation) |
| **EI d²y/dx²** | **Bending moment** |
| **EI d³y/dx³** | **Shear force** |
| **EI d⁴y/dx⁴** | **Load intensity** |

> That single chain connects load, shear, moment, slope and deflection — five quantities, four derivatives. It is worth holding as one structure rather than five separate relations.

**Sketching the elastic curve is a genuinely useful skill**, and it can be done from the bending moment diagram alone:

| Where the moment is | The curve is |
|---|---|
| **Sagging (positive)** | **Concave upward** (holds water) |
| **Hogging (negative)** | **Concave downward** (sheds water) |
| **Zero (contraflexure)** | **Straight — the curvature reverses here** |
| Larger in magnitude | More sharply curved |

**Boundary conditions the curve must satisfy:**

| Support | Conditions |
|---|---|
| **Pin or roller** | **y = 0**, slope free |
| **Fixed** | **y = 0 AND dy/dx = 0** |
| **Free end** | Both free; M = 0 and V = 0 |
| **Internal hinge** | y continuous, **slope DISCONTINUOUS**, M = 0 |

**The internal hinge case is worth noting**: it is the only place where the elastic curve has a **kink** rather than being smooth. Everywhere else the curve and its slope are continuous, which is what makes the constants of integration solvable.

**Why sketching it matters in practice:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Checking a computer analysis** | An implausible deflected shape reveals a modelling error faster than reading numbers |
| **Locating contraflexure points** | Where the curvature reverses — which governs **reinforcement curtailment** |
| **MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S principle** | The influence line for any quantity **has the shape of the deflected form** when the corresponding restraint is released |
| Understanding frame behaviour | Sway, joint rotations, where the moments concentrate |

**Müller-Breslau's principle is the elegant application:**

> To draw the influence line for a **reaction**, remove the support and impose a unit vertical displacement. For a **moment**, insert a **hinge** and impose a unit relative rotation. For a **shear**, insert a shear release and impose a unit relative slip. In each case the **deflected shape IS the influence line**.

> Its great value is for **indeterminate** structures, where influence lines are **curved** and cannot be obtained by statics — but the deflected shape can still be sketched qualitatively, which is enough to identify the critical load positions.

**A caution on the small-deflection assumption**: the exact curvature is

> **1/R = (d²y/dx²)/[1 + (dy/dx)²]^{3/2}**

and the familiar **1/R ≈ d²y/dx²** holds only when the slope is small enough for **(dy/dx)²** to be negligible. For ordinary structural deflections (span/250 or better) that is amply satisfied. It fails for very flexible members — cables, thin strips, and large-deflection problems — which need a **non-linear** analysis.

examTip.trick: Sketch it straight from the **bending moment diagram**: **sagging → concave up, hogging → concave down**, and the curve is **straight where the moment is zero** — which locates every contraflexure point by eye.
examTip.trap: An **internal hinge** is the one place the elastic curve has a **KINK** — the deflection is continuous but the **slope is not**. Drawing it smooth through a hinge is a common error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load → shear → moment → slope → deflection**, each one integration apart. Read it backwards (**EI y'''' = w**) and the whole chain is one equation.

questions.stem: Rankine's formula for the crippling load of a column is preferred to Euler's because it:
options: Gives a higher load and is therefore more economical
Applies to both short and long columns
Requires no knowledge of the end conditions
questions.solution:
**Because it applies across the whole range — both short and long columns.**

> **P = f_c A / (1 + a(L_e/k)²)**

where **f_c** is the crushing stress and **a** is Rankine's constant, a property of the material.

**Why it bridges both limits** — check the two extremes:

| Slenderness | The formula becomes | Which is |
|---|---|---|
| **L_e/k → 0** (very short) | **P → f_c A** | The **crushing** load ✓ |
| **L_e/k → large** | **P → f_c A/(a(L_e/k)²)** | Of the **Euler form**, ∝ 1/λ² ✓ |

> With **a = f_c/(π²E)**, the second limit becomes **exactly the Euler load**. So Rankine is constructed to reduce correctly to both behaviours — which is precisely the property Euler lacks.

**Euler's limitation** is what makes Rankine necessary:

> Euler's formula is valid only while **σ_cr ≤ f_y**. Below the critical slenderness (about **89** for mild steel), it gives **absurdly high loads** — for a very short column it predicts an infinite capacity, which is obviously wrong because the column would simply crush.

| Slenderness λ | Real behaviour | Euler says |
|---|---|---|
| **< 32** | **Crushes** | Enormous, useless value |
| 32 – 120 | Both matter | Too high |
| **> 120** | **Buckles** | **Correct** |

**Rankine's constants:**

| Material | f_c (N/mm²) | a |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild steel** | 320 | **1/7500** |
| Cast iron | 550 | 1/1600 |
| Wrought iron | 250 | 1/9000 |
| Timber | 50 | 1/750 |

**Note what each distractor gets wrong:**

| Option | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| "Gives a higher load" | Rankine gives a **LOWER**, safer load than Euler in the intermediate range — that is the point |
| "No knowledge of end conditions" | It uses **L_e**, so end conditions matter just as much |
| "Exact for all materials" | It is **empirical**, fitted to test data, not exact for anything |

**Rankine's honest status** is worth stating: it is a **semi-empirical interpolation**, not a theory. Its virtue is that it is **continuous, simple, and correct at both ends of the range** — which for hand calculation is worth a great deal.

**Modern codes use neither directly.** IS 800 and its counterparts use **multiple buckling curves** derived from testing, which account for effects that both Euler and Rankine ignore:

| Effect | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Residual stresses** from rolling and welding | Cause early partial yielding, reducing capacity |
| **Initial crookedness** | Real columns are not straight; the imperfection amplifies |
| **Section shape** | Different curves for I-sections, tubes, angles |
| Load eccentricity | Unavoidable in practice |

> IS 456 handles concrete columns differently again, with a **minimum eccentricity** requirement and reduction factors for slenderness — recognising that a perfectly axially loaded column does not exist.

**The practical hierarchy**: use **Euler** to understand the physics and to check very slender members, **Rankine** for a quick hand estimate across the range, and the **code curves** for anything being built.

examTip.trap: "Gives a higher load" is exactly backwards. Rankine gives a **LOWER and safer** value than Euler in the intermediate range — Euler's error there is dangerously **unconservative**.
examTip.trick: Test any such formula at the **two limits**: at λ → 0 it must give the **crushing** load, and at large λ it must approach **Euler**. Rankine does both, which is the whole reason it exists.
examTip.mnemonic: **Euler has no strength term, so it cannot know about crushing.** Below a slenderness of about 80 it is useless. Rankine interpolates; modern codes use tested **buckling curves** that also allow for residual stress and initial crookedness.

questions.stem: In a cantilever of length L carrying a uniformly distributed load w, the slope at the free end is:
questions.solution:
**θ = wL³/(6EI)** at the free end.

**The standard cantilever results**, slope and deflection together:

| Loading | Slope at free end | Deflection at free end |
|---|---|---|
| **End point load W** | **WL²/(2EI)** | **WL³/(3EI)** |
| **UDL w** | **wL³/(6EI)** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** |
| **End couple M** | **ML/(EI)** | **ML²/(2EI)** |
| Triangular, max at fixed end | wL³/(24EI) | 11wL⁴/(120EI) |

**Option (c), wL⁴/(8EI), is the DEFLECTION for this same case** — offered as a slope distractor. Check by **units**:

> A **slope is dimensionless** (radians). **wL³/(EI)** has units (N/m)(m³)/((N/m²)(m⁴)) = **dimensionless** ✓
> **wL⁴/(EI)** has units of **metres** — that is a deflection, not a slope ✗

> **The dimensional check settles it immediately**: slope formulas have **one less power of L** than the corresponding deflection formulas.

**Derivation by the moment-area method**, which is quick for a cantilever:

> The **first theorem** says the change in slope equals the **area of the M/EI diagram**. For a cantilever under UDL, **M = −wx²/2**, so the M diagram is a **parabola** with peak **wL²/2** at the fixed end.

> Area of a parabola (with vertex at the free end) = **(1/3) × base × height = (1/3)(L)(wL²/2) = wL³/6**

> Dividing by EI: **θ = wL³/(6EI)** ✓

> Since the tangent at the **fixed end is horizontal**, the change in slope IS the slope at the free end — which is exactly why the moment-area method suits cantilevers so well.

**The pattern across the standard cases** is worth noticing:

| Loading | Slope | Deflection | Ratio δ/θ |
|---|---|---|---|
| End couple | ML/EI | ML²/2EI | **L/2** |
| End load | WL²/2EI | WL³/3EI | **2L/3** |
| UDL | wL³/6EI | wL⁴/8EI | **3L/4** |

> The ratio **δ/θ** moves from L/2 to 3L/4 as the load moves from concentrated-at-the-end toward distributed — which makes sense, since a distributed load does more of its work near the support where the lever arm is short.

**Why the slope matters in its own right**, not merely as a step toward deflection:

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Continuous beam analysis** | Slope-deflection and moment distribution both work with **end rotations** |
| **Frame joints** | Compatibility requires equal rotations of all members at a rigid joint |
| **Cantilever balconies and canopies** | The **visible tilt** at the free edge is what people notice, often before deflection |
| Bridge bearings | The rotation must be accommodated by the bearing |
| Crane girders | End rotation affects the rail alignment |

**The bearing case is a real design requirement**: a bridge bearing must permit the **end rotation** of the deck as well as its longitudinal movement, and an elastomeric bearing is sized for both. A bearing that restrains rotation it was not designed for attracts a moment the structure never allowed for.

examTip.trap: **wL⁴/(8EI) is the DEFLECTION** of this same cantilever, offered as a slope distractor. Read whether the question asks for slope or deflection before looking at the options.
examTip.trick: **Slope is dimensionless; deflection is a length.** So a slope formula always has **one less power of L** than the matching deflection formula. That check alone eliminates the wrong family instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cantilever UDL: slope wL³/6EI, deflection wL⁴/8EI. End load: WL²/2EI and WL³/3EI.** Note the denominators go **2, 3** for an end load and **6, 8** for a UDL.

questions.stem: A column is classified as short when its slenderness ratio (effective length to least lateral dimension) is:
questions.solution:
**Less than 12** — using the **effective length to least lateral dimension** ratio, which is the convention IS 456 uses for concrete columns.

**Note that TWO different slenderness measures are in circulation**, and the question specifies which:

| Measure | Used for | Short column limit |
|---|---|---|
| **L_e/D** (least lateral **dimension**) | **Concrete columns**, IS 456 | **< 12** |
| **L_e/k** (least **radius of gyration**) | **Steel columns**, IS 800 | **< 32** |

> The two are related: for a rectangle **k = D/√12 = 0.289D**, so **L_e/k = 3.46 × L_e/D**. And **12 × 3.46 ≈ 41**, which is the same order as the steel convention — the two limits describe the same physical transition in different units.

**IS 456's classification:**

| Condition | Type | Design |
|---|---|---|
| **L_ex/D < 12 AND L_ey/b < 12** | **SHORT** | No slenderness effect |
| Either ratio ≥ 12 | **SLENDER** | **Additional moments** must be added |
| L_e/D > 60 | Not permitted | — |

> **Both directions must satisfy the limit.** A column short about one axis and slender about the other is a **slender** column.

**What changes for a slender column:**

> Additional moments from the lateral deflection must be added:
> **M_ax = P D (L_ex/D)²/2000** and similarly for the other axis.

> These are **second-order (P–Δ) effects**: the column deflects sideways, the axial load then acts at that eccentricity, which increases the deflection further. The formula is a code approximation to that amplification.

**Minimum eccentricity** applies to **every** column, short or slender:

> **e_min = greater of (L/500 + D/30) and 20 mm**

> The reason is that a **perfectly axially loaded column does not exist** — construction tolerances, out-of-plumb, and unequal beam loads all introduce eccentricity. Designing for pure axial load would be designing for a condition that never occurs.

**Effective length for concrete columns** depends on the restraint at each end and on whether the frame can sway:

| Frame | Typical L_e |
|---|---|
| **Braced** (no sway) | **0.65L to 1.0L** |
| **Unbraced** (sway permitted) | **1.2L to 2.0L or more** |

> **A sway frame's columns have effective lengths GREATER than their actual length** — which is why bracing or shear walls are so valuable, and why an unbraced frame's columns are so much larger.

**The failure modes:**

| Column | Fails by |
|---|---|
| **Short** | **Material crushing** — the concrete and steel reach their strengths |
| **Slender** | **Buckling / instability** — often at a load well below the material capacity |

> **A slender column can fail while the material is nowhere near its strength**, which is the whole reason slenderness is treated separately. It is a **stability** problem, not a strength problem — and stability failures are **sudden**, without the warning that a crushing failure gives.

**Reducing slenderness** in practice: **bracing** the frame (the most effective), increasing the column dimension, or reducing the storey height. Bracing is usually cheapest, and it also reduces the effective length by converting an unbraced frame into a braced one — a change of category, not merely of degree.

examTip.trap: **Two different slenderness conventions exist** and the numbers differ: **L_e/D < 12** for concrete (least **dimension**), **L_e/k < 32** for steel (radius of **gyration**). Read which the question means — they describe the same transition in different units.
examTip.trick: Convert between them with **k = D/√12**, so **L_e/k = 3.46 L_e/D**. That is why 12 in one convention corresponds to about 40 in the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOTH directions must be under 12** to be short. And every column, however short, needs **minimum eccentricity** — because a perfectly axial load does not exist in a real building.

questions.stem: A plane truss with m members, j joints and r reaction components is statically determinate when:
questions.solution:
**m + r = 2j.**

**Where the numbers come from:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **m** | One unknown per member — its **axial force** (a pin carries no moment) |
| **r** | Unknown reaction components |
| **2j** | Each **pin joint** gives **TWO** equations: ΣH = 0 and ΣV = 0 |

> **A pin joint gives only two equations because it cannot carry moment.** That is the whole reason the truss formula has a 2 where the frame formula has a 3.

**The formulae for each structure type**, which must be kept apart:

| Structure | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Plane TRUSS** (pin-jointed) | **D_s = m + r − 2j** |
| **Plane FRAME** (rigid-jointed) | **D_s = 3m + r − 3j** |
| Space truss | D_s = m + r − 3j |
| Space frame | D_s = 6m + r − 6j |
| Beam | D_s = r − 3 − (number of hinges) |

**Interpreting the result:**

| D_s | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **< 0** | **UNSTABLE** — a mechanism, it collapses |
| **= 0** | **Determinate** — solvable by statics alone |
| **> 0** | **Indeterminate** to that degree |

**Option (c), m = 2j − 3**, is a real relation but a **special case**: it is the same formula with **r = 3** substituted, that is, for a truss with the **minimum** external restraint. It is correct for a simply supported truss and wrong for any other support arrangement — a well-made distractor.

**The critical caveat, which the arithmetic cannot detect:**

> **The count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.** A truss can satisfy m + r = 2j exactly and still be a **mechanism**.

**The geometric instabilities to look for:**

| Arrangement | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **Three PARALLEL reactions** | Cannot resist a force perpendicular to them |
| **Three CONCURRENT reactions** | Cannot resist a moment about their common point |
| **A rectangular panel with no diagonal** | The panel **racks** — a four-bar mechanism |
| Members all meeting at a point | — |

> **A rectangular panel without a diagonal is the classic case**: the joint count can be perfectly correct while one panel of the truss folds like a parallelogram. Always look at the **geometry** as well as the count.

**Internal versus external indeterminacy** is a useful breakdown:

> **External D_s = r − 3** (redundant **reactions**)
> **Internal D_s = total − external** (redundant **members**)

A truss can be **externally determinate but internally indeterminate** (a simply supported truss with an extra diagonal), or the reverse (a determinate arrangement of members on three too many supports).

**Why determinate trusses are so common** in practice: they can be analysed by statics alone, they are **insensitive to support settlement and temperature** (developing no self-stress), and their member forces do not depend on the members' areas — so the design does not need iteration.

examTip.trap: **m = 2j − 3** is offered and is correct **only when r = 3** — the minimum external restraint. For any other support arrangement it is wrong. The general form is **m + r = 2j**.
examTip.trick: Remember why the 2 is there: a **pin joint gives two equations** (ΣH, ΣV) because it carries no moment. A **rigid joint gives three**, which is why the frame formula uses 3 throughout.
examTip.mnemonic: **Truss 2, frame 3.** And the count checks **degree, not stability** — an unbraced rectangular panel gives a perfect count and a mechanism. Always look at the geometry too.

questions.stem: In the method of joints for a plane truss, the analysis must start at a joint where the number of unknown member forces does not exceed:
questions.solution:
**Two** — because each joint provides only **two** equations of equilibrium.

**At any pin joint** the members are **concurrent**, so their forces have no lever arm about the joint and **ΣM = 0 is automatically satisfied**. That leaves only:

> **ΣH = 0** and **ΣV = 0** — **two equations, hence at most two unknowns.**

**The procedure:**

1. Find the **reactions** first, by overall equilibrium.
2. Start at a joint with **no more than two unknown members** — usually a support.
3. Resolve horizontally and vertically; solve the two unknowns.
4. Move to an adjacent joint that now has only two unknowns left.
5. Continue through the truss.

**Method of joints versus method of sections:**

| | **Method of JOINTS** | **Method of SECTIONS** |
|---|---|---|
| Equations available | **2** (ΣH, ΣV) | **3** (ΣH, ΣV, ΣM) |
| Unknowns at a time | **Max 2** | **Max 3** |
| Best for | **ALL** member forces | **A FEW specific** members |
| Works by | Isolating one **joint** | Cutting through the **whole truss** |

> **Use sections when you want one member's force without solving the whole truss** — for example the force in a particular chord member of a long-span truss. Taking moments about the point where the other two cut members intersect isolates it in a single equation.

**ZERO-FORCE MEMBERS** should be identified before any calculation, because they simplify the work enormously:

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| **Two non-collinear members** at an unloaded joint | **BOTH are zero-force** |
| **Three members** at an unloaded joint, two of them collinear | The **third (odd) member is zero-force** |
| Two members at a joint with a load **along one of them** | The other is zero-force |

> Spotting these first can eliminate a third of the members in some trusses before you write a single equation.

**Why zero-force members exist at all**, since they carry nothing:

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| They carry force under a **different load case** | Truss loading patterns vary |
| They **reduce the buckling length** of long compression chords | A real structural function |
| They **stabilise the truss** out of plane | — |
| They stiffen the geometry against handling and erection loads | — |

> So a zero-force member under one load case is not a redundant member to be removed — it is usually earning its place in another way.

**Sign convention**: assume **every unknown member force is TENSILE** (pulling away from the joint). A **negative answer then means compression**, automatically and without ambiguity. Assuming compression for some members and tension for others is a reliable way to lose track of signs.

**A practical check**: at any joint, the forces must **close** into a force polygon. If they do not, the arithmetic is wrong — which is the basis of the older **graphical (Maxwell diagram)** method of truss analysis.

examTip.trick: **Identify ZERO-FORCE members before writing any equation.** Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint are both zero; three members with two collinear leave the **odd one** zero. This can eliminate a third of the truss instantly.
examTip.trap: Do not confuse the two methods' limits: **joints gives 2 equations, sections gives 3** (because a section is a rigid body and ΣM is available). Cutting more than three unknown members leaves the section unsolvable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Assume every unknown is TENSION.** A negative answer then means compression automatically — mixing assumed senses is the surest way to lose the signs.

questions.stem: In the method of sections, the cutting plane should not pass through more than:
questions.solution:
**Three unknown members**, because a free body in a plane has exactly **three** equations of equilibrium.

> **ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, ΣM = 0** — three equations, so at most three unknowns.

**Why sections gives three where joints gives two:**

| | Joint | Section |
|---|---|---|
| The free body is | A **point** (concurrent forces) | A **rigid portion** of the truss |
| Is ΣM useful? | **No** — automatically satisfied | **YES** — forces have lever arms |
| Equations | **2** | **3** |

**The power of the method** is in the choice of the moment centre:

> Take moments about the point where **two of the three cut members INTERSECT**. Those two then have **zero lever arm**, and the third member's force falls out of a **single equation** — with no simultaneous solving at all.

**A worked strategy for a parallel-chord truss:**

| To find | Take moments about |
|---|---|
| A **top chord** force | The joint where the **bottom chord and the diagonal** meet |
| A **bottom chord** force | The joint where the **top chord and the diagonal** meet |
| A **diagonal** force | Use **ΣV = 0** instead — the chords are horizontal and contribute nothing vertically |

> That last row is the neat one: for a **parallel-chord** truss the diagonal is the only cut member with a vertical component, so **ΣV = 0 gives it immediately**.

**When to use sections rather than joints:**

| Situation | Method |
|---|---|
| **All** member forces needed | **Joints** — work through the whole truss |
| **One or two specific** members | **Sections** — go straight to them |
| A member deep inside a long truss | **Sections** — joints would need dozens of steps first |
| Checking a computer output at one member | **Sections** |

**The rule can be relaxed in one case**: if **more than three** members are cut but **all but three are concurrent** (they meet at a common point), taking moments about that point still isolates the remaining one. The three-member limit is a practical guide, not an absolute law — what matters is that the equations available exceed the unknowns you need.

**The reactions must be found first**, by overall equilibrium of the whole truss, before either method can start. That is one step that never changes.

**Sign convention**, as with joints: assume every cut member is in **TENSION**, pulling away from the section. A negative result then means compression, unambiguously.

**A useful physical check** on the answers: in a simply supported truss under gravity load, the **top chord is in compression** and the **bottom chord in tension** — the truss is acting as a deep beam, with the chords doing what the flanges of an I-beam would do. If your analysis reverses that, look for a sign error.

examTip.trick: **Take moments about the point where two of the three cut members INTERSECT.** Those two lose their lever arm, and the third falls out of one equation — no simultaneous solving. For a **parallel-chord** truss, get the **diagonal** from ΣV = 0 instead, since the chords have no vertical component.
examTip.trap: Sections allows **three** unknowns because ΣM is available; joints allows only **two** because the forces are concurrent. Applying the wrong limit is the standard confusion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Joints for ALL members, sections for a FEW.** Physical check: in a simply supported truss under gravity, **top chord compression, bottom chord tension** — the truss is a deep beam.

questions.stem: At an unloaded joint of a truss where exactly two non-collinear members meet, the forces in those members are:
questions.solution:
**Both zero.**

**Why.** Resolve along a direction **perpendicular to one member**. Only the **other** member has a component in that direction, and there is no load — so that member's force must be zero. Repeat perpendicular to the second member, and it too must be zero.

> Two non-collinear directions and no external force means **neither member can carry anything**.

**The three zero-force rules:**

| Situation | Zero-force members |
|---|---|
| **Two non-collinear** members, unloaded joint | **BOTH** |
| **Three** members, two **collinear**, unloaded joint | The **odd (third)** member |
| Two members with an external load **along one** of them | The **other** member |

> **The second rule is the most useful in practice**, because it appears repeatedly along the chords of a real truss — a vertical or diagonal meeting a continuous chord at an unloaded panel point carries nothing.

**Why identify them first?** Because it **collapses the problem**:

> Once a member is known to be zero, it can be struck out and the joints beyond it become simpler — often cascading, so that a third of the truss is resolved before any equation is written.

**Why zero-force members are nevertheless built**, since they carry nothing under this load case:

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| They carry force under a **different load case** | Wind from the other side, unbalanced live load, erection |
| They **reduce the buckling length** of a long compression chord | A real and important structural function |
| They provide **out-of-plane stability** | A truss is a plane structure in a three-dimensional world |
| They stiffen the geometry for handling and transport | — |

> **The buckling-length function is the one that matters most.** A long top chord in compression would buckle at a low load if unrestrained; a vertical that carries no axial force under gravity load may nonetheless be halving that chord's effective length — and since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, halving it quadruples the capacity.

> So a zero-force member is **not a redundant member to be deleted**. Removing one because "it carries nothing" is a genuine and dangerous error.

**Note what the distractors describe:**

| Option | When it would be true |
|---|---|
| "Equal and opposite" | Two **collinear** members at an unloaded joint — the force passes straight through |
| "Equal in magnitude" | Same case |
| "Both maximum" | Never a consequence of the joint geometry |

> The **collinear** case is worth holding alongside: if the two members are **in line**, the joint simply transmits the force and the two are **equal and in the same sense**. It is the **non-collinear** condition that forces both to zero.

**A worked example of the cascade**: in a common Pratt or Howe roof truss under panel-point loading, the verticals at the unloaded panel points are zero-force, which immediately reveals the chord forces at those joints without simultaneous equations.

examTip.trick: Three rules, worth spotting before any calculation: **two non-collinear members unloaded → both zero; three members with two collinear → the odd one is zero; load along one member → the other is zero.** They cascade, often resolving a third of the truss free.
examTip.trap: **Never delete a zero-force member from the design.** It usually carries force in another load case, and — more importantly — it often **halves the buckling length of a compression chord**, which quadruples that chord's capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Non-collinear and unloaded → both ZERO. COLLINEAR → equal and passing straight through.** The distinction is the whole question.

questions.stem: The strain energy stored in a bar of length L and area A carrying an axial load P is:
questions.solution:
**U = P²L/(2AE).**

**Derivation.** The work done by a **gradually applied** load is the area under the load–extension line, which is a triangle:

> **U = ½ P δ**, and **δ = PL/(AE)**
> **U = ½ P × PL/(AE) = P²L/(2AE)** ✓

**The ½ is because the load builds up from zero** — the average force during the extension is half the final force. That single factor is the source of most errors in this topic.

**Check the units:**

> **P²L/(AE) = N² · m/(m² · N/m²) = N² · m/N = N·m = joules** ✓

> Option (a) **PL/(AE)** is the **extension δ**, a length — not an energy. Option (c) is twice the correct value. Option (d) has the wrong power of L.

**Strain energy for the three actions:**

| Action | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **Axial** | **U = P²L/(2AE)** or **∫P²dx/(2AE)** |
| **Bending** | **U = ∫M²dx/(2EI)** |
| **Torsion** | **U = T²L/(2GJ)** |
| Shear | U = ∫(V²/2GA)·k dx |

> Every one has the same shape: **(force)² × length ÷ (2 × rigidity)**. Recognising that pattern is worth more than memorising four formulas.

**Per unit volume** (the **modulus of resilience**):

> **u = σ²/(2E)** — the same relation divided through by the volume AL.

**Why strain energy matters — the ENERGY METHODS built on it:**

| Method | Statement | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **CASTIGLIANO'S first theorem** | **δ = ∂U/∂P** | Deflection at a load point |
| **Unit load (virtual work)** | **δ = Σ(PkL/AE)** for a truss | Deflection anywhere, any direction |
| **Principle of LEAST WORK** | **∂U/∂R = 0** | Solves **indeterminate** structures |
| Maxwell's reciprocal theorem | δ_AB = δ_BA | Halves influence-line work |

**Castigliano's limitation** is worth knowing: **δ = ∂U/∂P** gives the deflection only **where a real load P acts**, and only in that load's direction. For any other point you must first apply a **dummy load Q**, differentiate, then set Q = 0.

> The **unit load method** avoids that step entirely, which is why it is the more general tool — and why it handles trusses, beams and frames with the same expression.

**The principle of least work** is the elegant application to indeterminate structures:

> The redundant forces take whatever values **minimise the total strain energy**. So write U in terms of the redundant R, set **∂U/∂R = 0**, and solve.

> For a **propped cantilever** under UDL it yields **R = 3wL/8** directly, with no compatibility diagram needed.

**And the impact consequence**, which follows from the same ½:

> A **suddenly applied** load does work **Pδ**, not ½Pδ — so it stores **twice** the energy and produces **twice the stress and deflection**. The bar overshoots to twice the static deflection and oscillates back.

examTip.trap: **PL/(AE) is the EXTENSION**, not the energy — it is a length, not a joule. The dimensional check kills it instantly, and it is the most tempting distractor because it is the formula everyone knows.
examTip.trick: Every strain energy has the same shape: **(force)² × length ÷ (2 × rigidity)** — P²L/2AE axial, T²L/2GJ torsion, ∫M²dx/2EI bending. Learn the pattern, not four formulas.
examTip.mnemonic: **U = ½Pδ, because the load builds up GRADUALLY.** A **sudden** load does work Pδ instead — hence **double** the stress and deflection, which is the impact result.

questions.stem: Castigliano's first theorem states that the deflection at a point in the direction of an applied load P is given by:
options: ∂U/∂P, the partial derivative of the strain energy with respect to that load
The total strain energy divided by the span
questions.solution:
**δ = ∂U/∂P** — the partial derivative of the total strain energy with respect to that load.

**A simple confirmation.** For an axial bar, **U = P²L/(2AE)**:

> **∂U/∂P = 2PL/(2AE) = PL/(AE) = δ** ✓

And for a cantilever with an end load, **U = ∫M²dx/(2EI)** with M = −Px:

> **U = ∫₀ᴸ P²x²dx/(2EI) = P²L³/(6EI)**
> **∂U/∂P = 2PL³/(6EI) = PL³/(3EI)** ✓ — the standard cantilever deflection

**The two theorems:**

| Theorem | Statement | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| **First** | **δ = ∂U/∂P** | **Deflection** at a load point |
| **Second (least work)** | **∂U/∂R = 0** | The **redundant force** in an indeterminate structure |

**The important limitation:**

> Castigliano gives the deflection **only where a real load acts**, and **only in that load's direction**.

**The dummy load device** works around it:

1. Apply a fictitious load **Q** at the point and in the direction you want.
2. Write U including Q.
3. Differentiate: **∂U/∂Q**.
4. **Set Q = 0** in the result.

> It works, but it is bookkeeping — which is exactly why the **unit load (virtual work) method** is preferred in practice. That method builds the fictitious unit load in from the start:

> **δ = Σ(PkL)/(AE)** for a truss, or **δ = ∫(Mm/EI)dx** for a beam or frame

where **k** and **m** are the member forces and moments under a **unit load** applied at the point and direction of interest.

**Practical comparison:**

| Method | Best when |
|---|---|
| **Castigliano** | Strain energy is **easy to write in one expression** |
| **Unit load** | **Trusses** (a simple summation) and **frames** — the general workhorse |
| Moment-area / conjugate beam | Cantilevers, varying EI, one point only |
| Macaulay | Several point loads on a beam |

**The rotation version** is worth knowing: differentiating with respect to an applied **couple M** gives the **rotation** at that point:

> **θ = ∂U/∂M**

and if no real couple acts there, a **dummy couple** is used and then set to zero — exactly as for a dummy load.

**THE PRINCIPLE OF LEAST WORK** (Castigliano's second theorem) is the more powerful of the two:

> In an indeterminate structure the redundant forces take the values that **MINIMISE the total strain energy**, subject to equilibrium. So **∂U/∂R = 0**.

> Applied to a **propped cantilever** under UDL, it gives **R = 3wL/8** in a few lines, with no released-structure diagram. Applied to a **two-hinged arch**, it gives the horizontal thrust **H = ∫My ds/EI ÷ ∫y² ds/EI**.

**A necessary condition for all of this**: the structure must be **linearly elastic**, and the **principle of superposition** must hold. Energy methods in this form do not apply once any part of the structure yields.

examTip.trap: The theorem gives the deflection **only where a real load acts, and only in that load's direction.** For any other point you must add a **dummy load Q**, differentiate, then set **Q = 0** — a step that is easy to forget entirely.
examTip.trick: Test any energy formula on the cantilever: U = P²L³/6EI, so ∂U/∂P = **PL³/3EI** ✓ — the known answer. If a method does not reproduce a standard case, you have it wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **∂U/∂P gives DEFLECTION; ∂U/∂M gives ROTATION; ∂U/∂R = 0 solves the REDUNDANT.** Three uses of one derivative. The **unit load method** avoids the dummy-load bookkeeping entirely, which is why it is the workhorse.

questions.stem: In the unit load method, the deflection of a joint in a pin-jointed truss is computed as:
questions.solution:
**δ = Σ(P k L)/(A E)**, summed over all members.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P** | Member force under the **REAL** loading |
| **k** | Member force under a **UNIT load** applied at the joint, in the direction of the required deflection |
| **L, A, E** | The member's length, area and modulus |

**The method in outline:**

1. Analyse the truss under the **real loads** → gives **P** in every member.
2. Remove the real loads. Apply a **single unit load** at the joint and in the direction whose deflection you want.
3. Analyse again → gives **k** in every member.
4. **Sum PkL/(AE)** over all members.

> A **positive** result means the joint moves **in the direction of the unit load**; a negative result means the opposite direction. The sign takes care of itself.

**Why it works** — the principle of **virtual work**: the external work done by the unit load moving through the real deflection equals the internal work done by the k-forces moving through the real member extensions (PL/AE).

> **1 × δ = Σ k × (PL/AE)** ✓

**Note the distractors are each a real expression in the wrong place:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Σ(PL)/(AE)** | The sum of the **extensions** — a length, but not a joint deflection |
| **Σ(kL)/(AE)** | The deflection under the unit load alone, not the real load |
| **∫(Mm/EI)dx** | The **BEAM AND FRAME** version of the same method ✓ (correct for those, wrong for a pin-jointed truss) |

> That last one is the instructive distractor: it is the **same method** expressed for **flexural** members. A truss's members carry **axial** force only, so the summation form applies; a beam or frame carries bending, so the integral form does.

**The two forms side by side:**

| Structure | Deflection |
|---|---|
| **Truss** (axial) | **δ = Σ(PkL)/(AE)** |
| **Beam / frame** (bending) | **δ = ∫(Mm/EI) dx** |
| Combined | Add both terms |

**Why the unit load method is the workhorse:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| Gives the deflection at **ANY point, in ANY direction** | Unlike Castigliano, which needs a real load there |
| Gives **ROTATION** too | Apply a **unit COUPLE** instead of a unit load |
| Handles **trusses, beams and frames** with one idea | — |
| Handles **temperature and lack of fit** | Replace PL/AE with the actual member extension, whatever caused it |
| Extends to **indeterminate** structures | Combined with compatibility, it becomes the flexibility method |

> **The temperature and lack-of-fit extension is genuinely useful**: for a member heated by ΔT, the extension is **αΔT·L** instead of PL/AE, and the same summation gives the resulting joint movement. Nothing else in the method changes.

**For a rotation**, apply a **unit couple** at the joint and the same summation gives θ.

**Practical tip**: tabulate the calculation with one row per member and columns for **L, A, P, k, PkL/AE**. The arithmetic is repetitive and the table makes errors visible — and it is exactly how the method is set out in practice.

examTip.trap: **∫(Mm/EI)dx is the SAME method for BEAMS and FRAMES** — correct there, wrong for a pin-jointed truss whose members carry only axial force. Read what kind of structure the question is about.
examTip.trick: **P is from the real load; k is from a unit load at the joint you care about.** Tabulate one row per member with columns L, A, P, k, PkL/AE — the arithmetic is repetitive and the table makes slips visible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Truss: Σ PkL/AE. Beam or frame: ∫ Mm/EI dx.** Apply a unit **COUPLE** instead of a unit load and the same expression gives the **rotation**. For temperature effects, replace PL/AE with **αΔT·L**.

questions.stem: The principle of superposition is valid only when the structure:
options: Behaves linearly elastically and undergoes small deformations
questions.solution:
**Only when the structure behaves LINEARLY ELASTICALLY and undergoes SMALL deformations.**

**Both conditions are needed:**

| Condition | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Linear elastic material** | Stress must be proportional to strain, so doubling the load doubles the response |
| **Small deformations** | The geometry used to write equilibrium must not change appreciably as the structure deflects |

> **Note that determinacy is irrelevant.** Superposition works perfectly well for **indeterminate** structures — indeed, almost every method for analysing them (flexibility, moment distribution, influence lines) depends on it.

**What superposition permits:**

> The effect of several loads acting together equals the **sum of their individual effects**.

| Application | How it uses superposition |
|---|---|
| **Load combinations** | Dead + live + wind computed separately and added |
| **Influence lines** | Each load's effect read off and summed |
| **Flexibility (force) method** | Released structure + redundant effects, added |
| **Moment distribution** | Fixed-end moments + successive corrections |
| Pattern loading envelopes | Individual cases superimposed |

> **Almost every structural analysis method assumes it**, which is why the conditions matter.

**Where superposition FAILS:**

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **P–Δ (second-order) effects** in slender columns | The axial load acts on the deflected shape — the effect is **not proportional** to the load |
| **Cables and membranes** | Geometry changes substantially under load |
| **Plastic analysis** | The material is no longer linear |
| **Buckling** | An instability, inherently non-linear |
| Soil, cracked concrete, gap-opening joints | Non-linear material or contact |
| **Uplift / lift-off** of a foundation | The contact area changes with load |

**The P–Δ case is the practically important one:**

> In a slender column or an unbraced frame, the lateral deflection Δ creates an additional moment **P × Δ**, which increases the deflection, which increases the moment. The response **amplifies** rather than adding linearly.

> That is why codes require a **second-order analysis** or an approximate **moment magnifier** for slender members — and why IS 456 adds explicit **additional moments** for slender columns rather than simply superimposing the axial and bending cases.

**A revealing consequence for stability**: because buckling is non-linear, **you cannot superimpose two buckling analyses**. A column's capacity under combined axial load and moment is found from an **interaction** relation, not by adding the two separate capacities.

**And a consequence for plastic design**: the **collapse load of a structure is not the sum of the collapse loads under separate loadings**. Plastic analysis works instead by identifying **mechanisms** and equating internal to external work — a completely different logic, precisely because superposition is unavailable.

**In practice**, ordinary building structures at working loads satisfy both conditions comfortably: steel and concrete are near enough linear below yield, and deflections limited to span/250 are small enough that the undeformed geometry is an excellent approximation. Superposition fails at the margins — slender members, cable structures, and anything approaching collapse — which is exactly where the codes impose special methods.

examTip.trap: **Determinacy has nothing to do with it.** Superposition works fine for indeterminate structures — in fact the flexibility method, moment distribution and influence lines all depend on it.
examTip.trick: Ask whether **doubling the load doubles the response**. If the geometry changes enough to alter the equilibrium equations (P–Δ, cables) or the material yields, the answer is no and superposition fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **Linear material AND small deflections — both required.** The practical failure is **P–Δ in slender columns and unbraced frames**, which is why codes demand second-order analysis or an explicit additional moment.

questions.stem: Maxwell's reciprocal theorem states that for a linear elastic structure:
options: The deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals the deflection at B due to a unit load at A
The strain energy equals the external work in all cases
The sum of the reactions equals the sum of the loads
The deflection is proportional to the load
questions.solution:
**δ_AB = δ_BA** — the deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals the deflection at B due to a unit load at A.

**Why it holds.** It is a direct consequence of the **symmetry of the flexibility matrix** (and equivalently of the stiffness matrix) for any **linear elastic** structure — which itself follows from the fact that the strain energy is a **single-valued function of the final state**, independent of the order in which the loads were applied.

**Betti's theorem** is the general form, of which Maxwell's is the special case for unit loads:

> The work done by a **first** set of forces moving through the displacements caused by a **second** set equals the work done by the **second** set moving through the displacements caused by the **first**.

**What it is good for:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Halves the work** in flexibility calculations | Compute one coefficient and its mirror is free |
| Makes the **flexibility matrix symmetric** | A useful arithmetic check on a hand calculation |
| **Underpins MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S principle** | The theoretical foundation of influence lines |
| Model testing | A measurement at one point substitutes for one at another |

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S PRINCIPLE** is the important consequence:

> The influence line for any response quantity has the **same shape as the DEFLECTED FORM** the structure takes when the corresponding **restraint is released** and a **unit displacement** imposed.

| Influence line for | Release | Impose |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction** | The **support** | Unit **vertical displacement** |
| **Moment** at a section | Insert a **HINGE** | Unit **relative rotation** |
| **Shear** at a section | Insert a **shear release** | Unit **relative slip** |

> Its great value is for **INDETERMINATE** structures, whose influence lines are **curved** and cannot be obtained by statics. The deflected shape can still be **sketched qualitatively**, and that alone identifies the critical load positions and patterns — which is usually all the designer needs.

**The pattern-loading rules for continuous beams come directly from it:**

| To maximise | Load |
|---|---|
| **Sagging** moment in a span | That span **plus alternate** spans |
| **Hogging** moment at a support | The **two adjacent** spans, plus alternate ones beyond |

> Because the influence line for a sagging moment is **positive in that span and alternate spans** and **negative in the adjacent ones**, loading only the positive regions maximises the response. **Loading every span is NOT the worst case** — which is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and a code requirement (IS 456 cl. 22.4.1).

**The conditions**, which are the same as for superposition:

> **Linear elastic material** and **small deformations**. The theorem fails for plastic behaviour, for cables, and wherever P–Δ effects matter.

**A caution on interpretation**: the theorem relates a **deflection** at A to a **deflection** at B, both caused by **unit loads**. The generalised form pairs any **force quantity** with its corresponding **displacement quantity** — so a unit **couple** at A relates to a **rotation** at B, and mixing a load with a rotation requires Betti's more general statement rather than Maxwell's.

examTip.trick: Use it as an **arithmetic check**: any flexibility matrix you compute by hand must come out **symmetric**. If δ_AB ≠ δ_BA, there is an error — no exceptions for a linear elastic structure.
examTip.trap: It requires **linear elastic behaviour and small deflections**, exactly like superposition. It does not hold once anything yields, nor for cables, nor where P–Δ matters.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maxwell → MÜLLER-BRESLAU → pattern loading.** That chain is why **loading every span is NOT the worst case** for a continuous beam: the influence line is negative in the adjacent spans, so loading them partly cancels.

questions.stem: The strain energy stored in a beam due to bending is:
questions.solution:
**U = ∫(M²/2EI) dx**, integrated over the length of the beam.

**Why an integral rather than a simple product**: the bending moment **M varies along the span**, so the energy must be accumulated element by element. Option (c) assumes M is constant, which is true only for **pure bending** — a beam loaded by end couples only.

**Check the pattern against the other actions:**

| Action | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **Axial** | **∫P²dx/(2AE)**, or P²L/(2AE) if P is constant |
| **Bending** | **∫M²dx/(2EI)** |
| **Torsion** | **∫T²dx/(2GJ)**, or T²L/(2GJ) if T is constant |
| Shear | ∫kV²dx/(2GA) |

> Every one is **(force quantity)² × length ÷ (2 × rigidity)**. Recognising that shape is worth more than memorising four formulas — and it makes the **2 in the denominator** obviously the same ½ that comes from a gradually applied load.

**A worked example** — cantilever with an end load W:

> **M = −Wx** at distance x from the free end
> **U = ∫₀ᴸ (Wx)²dx/(2EI) = W²/(2EI) × [x³/3]₀ᴸ = W²L³/(6EI)**

**Then Castigliano gives the deflection immediately:**

> **δ = ∂U/∂W = 2WL³/(6EI) = WL³/(3EI)** ✓ — the standard cantilever result

> That agreement is the check worth doing on any energy calculation: **if the method does not reproduce a standard case, the setup is wrong.**

**Shear strain energy is usually neglected**, and it is worth knowing when that is safe:

| Beam | Shear energy as a fraction of bending energy |
|---|---|
| **Slender** (span/depth > 10) | **Negligible** — under a few percent |
| Span/depth ≈ 5 | Around 10% |
| **Deep beam** (span/depth < 3) | **Substantial** |
| **Shear wall** | **Dominant** |

> The ratio scales as **(d/L)²**, which is why it vanishes for slender members and matters for stubby ones. Ignoring shear deformation in a **shear wall** analysis is a real error.

**Where the bending strain energy expression is used:**

| Method | Application |
|---|---|
| **Castigliano** | δ = ∂U/∂P for beam and frame deflections |
| **Least work** | ∂U/∂R = 0 for indeterminate structures |
| **Two-hinged arch** | **H = ∫My ds/EI ÷ ∫y² ds/EI** — derived by minimising U |
| Flexibility coefficients | The δ terms in the compatibility equations |

**The two-hinged arch is the classic application**, and it is worth seeing why an integral is unavoidable there: the moment varies along a curved axis, and the rise y varies with it, so the thrust can only be found by integrating over the whole arch.

**For a frame**, the integration is done **member by member** and summed — the same expression, applied to each straight segment with its own M(x) expression and its own EI.

examTip.trap: **M²L/(2EI) is right only for PURE BENDING**, where M is constant along the span. For any real loading M varies, so the integral is unavoidable.
examTip.trick: Verify any energy method on a standard case: for a cantilever, **U = W²L³/6EI**, and **∂U/∂W = WL³/3EI** ✓ — the known deflection. If it does not reproduce that, the setup is wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **(force)² × length ÷ (2 × rigidity)** — one pattern for all four actions. Shear energy scales as **(d/L)²**, so it is negligible for slender beams and **dominant in a shear wall**.

questions.stem: The kinematic indeterminacy of a structure is the number of unknown:
questions.solution:
**The number of unknown JOINT DISPLACEMENTS — the degrees of freedom.**

**The two indeterminacies, side by side:**

| | **STATIC D_s** | **KINEMATIC D_k** |
|---|---|---|
| Counts | Redundant **FORCES** | Unknown **DISPLACEMENTS** |
| Extra unknowns beyond | Equilibrium equations | Compatibility |
| Used by | **FORCE (flexibility)** methods | **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness)** methods |
| Methods | Consistent deformation, least work, three-moment, column analogy | **Slope-deflection, moment distribution, MATRIX STIFFNESS** |

**Counting D_k for a plane frame:**

> Each **free joint** has **three** degrees of freedom: **two translations and one rotation**. Subtract the ones the supports restrain.

> **D_k = 3j − (restraints)**

**The usual simplification** — axial deformations are almost always neglected in frame analysis, because members are far stiffer axially than in bending:

> Neglecting axial change means the members act as **rigid links** for translation purposes, which greatly reduces the count. A single-bay single-storey portal frame with fixed bases then has just **three** degrees of freedom: **two joint rotations and one sway**.

**Choosing a method** used to depend on which number was smaller:

> **If D_s < D_k**, a **force** method has fewer unknowns. **If D_k < D_s**, a **displacement** method does.

**But modern practice uses stiffness methods almost universally**, and the reason is decisive:

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **SYSTEMATIC** | The structure is assembled from standard member stiffness matrices |
| **No judgement required** | A force method needs you to **choose** the redundants, and a poor choice makes the arithmetic far worse |
| **Easily PROGRAMMED** | Every commercial analysis package is a stiffness solver |
| Handles any structure uniformly | Trusses, frames, grids, shells |

**Worked examples:**

| Structure | D_s | D_k (neglecting axial) |
|---|---|---|
| **Propped cantilever** | 1 | 1 (the prop rotation) |
| **Fixed beam** | 3 | 0 |
| **Portal frame, fixed bases** | 3 | 3 (two rotations + sway) |
| **Portal frame, hinged bases** | 1 | 3 |

> Note the **fixed beam**: it is statically indeterminate to degree 3 but **kinematically determinate** — no joint can move or rotate at all. A displacement method solves it in one step, while a force method needs three compatibility equations. That contrast shows why the choice used to matter.
