**A useful mental check**: **D_k counts what can MOVE; D_s counts what is EXTRA holding it.** A structure with many supports has a high D_s and a low D_k; a lightly supported one is the reverse.

**In the matrix stiffness method** the degrees of freedom become the size of the global stiffness matrix — so D_k is literally the number of simultaneous equations the computer solves. For a real building that is thousands, which is why the method waited for computers even though its theory is a century old.

examTip.trap: "Redundant forces" is the **STATIC** indeterminacy D_s, and the two are constantly swapped. **D_s counts forces; D_k counts displacements.**
examTip.trick: For a plane frame, each free joint has **three** degrees of freedom (two translations, one rotation) — but **neglecting axial deformation** (standard practice) collapses most of the translations, so a fixed-base portal frame has only **three**: two rotations and one sway.
examTip.mnemonic: **D_s → FORCE methods (flexibility, moment distribution). D_k → DISPLACEMENT methods (slope-deflection, matrix stiffness).** Modern software is always a stiffness solver, because it needs no choice of redundants.

questions.stem: In a portal frame with fixed bases subjected to a horizontal load, the frame deforms mainly by:
options: Sway, with double curvature bending in the columns
questions.solution:
**By SWAY, with the columns bending in DOUBLE CURVATURE.**

**What happens.** A horizontal load pushes the frame sideways. Because the joints are **rigid**, the beam stays essentially horizontal and forces the column tops to remain vertical in slope — so each column bends into an **S-shape**, hogging at one end and sagging at the other.

> **Double curvature means a POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE near the mid-height** of each column.

**The moment distribution under lateral load:**

| Location | Moment |
|---|---|
| **Column base** | Maximum (hogging) |
| **Column mid-height** | **ZERO — contraflexure** |
| **Column top** | Maximum, opposite sign |
| Beam ends | Balance the column moments at the joint |

**The portal method** of approximate analysis is built on exactly this:

| Assumption | Statement |
|---|---|
| **1** | A **point of contraflexure at the MID-HEIGHT of every column** |
| **2** | A **point of contraflexure at the MID-SPAN of every beam** |
| **3** | The shear is distributed among columns in proportion to their bay widths (interior columns take **twice** an exterior one) |

> Those three assumptions make the frame **determinate**, so a multi-storey frame under wind can be analysed by hand in minutes. The **cantilever method** is its companion, distributing axial forces in proportion to distance from the centroid instead — better for **tall, slender** frames where overall bending dominates.

**Sway versus non-sway** is the fundamental distinction:

| Frame | Behaviour | Effective length of columns |
|---|---|---|
| **BRACED (non-sway)** | Joints translate negligibly | **0.65L to 1.0L** |
| **UNBRACED (sway)** | Joints translate freely | **1.2L to 2.0L or more** |

> **An unbraced frame's columns have effective lengths GREATER than their actual length.** Since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, that can quarter their buckling capacity — which is why bracing or shear walls are so structurally valuable, and why an unbraced frame's columns are so much larger.

**P–Δ effects** are the other consequence of sway:

> The frame deflects sideways by Δ, and the **gravity load P then acts at that eccentricity**, adding a moment **PΔ**, which increases Δ further. The response **amplifies** rather than adding linearly — so **superposition fails** and a **second-order analysis** or a moment magnifier is required.

**How the frame's stiffness is provided:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Moment-resisting frame** | The joints themselves resist sway — flexible, ductile, but large members |
| **BRACING** (diagonal, X, K) | Very stiff and efficient — carries load **axially** rather than in bending |
| **SHEAR WALLS** | Very stiff; the usual solution in RC buildings |
| Core walls (stair and lift shafts) | Structurally free, since they exist anyway |

**In seismic design** the choice matters greatly: a **moment-resisting frame** is **ductile** and can absorb energy through plastic hinging at the beam ends, while a **braced frame** is **stiffer but less ductile**. That is why the response reduction factor R differs between them — and why ductile detailing (IS 13920, NBC 105) concentrates on the beam-end and column plastic hinge zones.

**The design principle that follows** is **STRONG COLUMN – WEAK BEAM**: hinges should form in the **beams**, not the columns, so that the failure is local and the building does not lose its vertical load path.

examTip.trick: **Double curvature means a contraflexure point near column mid-height** — which is exactly assumption 1 of the **portal method**, together with contraflexure at beam mid-span. Those two assumptions make a sway frame determinate and solvable by hand.
examTip.trap: An **unbraced** frame's columns have **effective lengths GREATER than L** (1.2–2.0L), not less. Since P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², that can quarter the buckling capacity — which is the whole structural value of bracing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sway → P–Δ → superposition FAILS → second-order analysis needed.** And in seismic design, **STRONG COLUMN, WEAK BEAM** — hinge the beams, never the columns, or the building loses its vertical load path.

questions.stem: A pin-jointed truss has 13 members, 8 joints and 3 reaction components. It is:
questions.solution:
**Statically determinate.**

> **D_s = m + r − 2j = 13 + 3 − 2(8) = 16 − 16 = 0** ✓

**A degree of zero means the truss can be solved by statics alone** — the equations of equilibrium exactly match the unknowns.

**Interpreting the count:**

| D_s | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negative** | **UNSTABLE** — a mechanism |
| **Zero** | **Determinate** |
| **Positive** | **Indeterminate** to that degree |

**The essential caveat**, which no arithmetic can supply:

> **The count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.** A truss can give D_s = 0 exactly and still be a **mechanism**, if the members or reactions are badly arranged.

**The geometric instabilities:**

| Arrangement | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **Three PARALLEL reactions** | Cannot resist a force perpendicular to them |
| **Three CONCURRENT reactions** | Cannot resist a moment about their common point |
| **A rectangular panel with no diagonal** | Racks as a four-bar mechanism |
| Two members collinear at a joint where a third meets | Locally unstable |

> **Always look at the geometry after doing the count.** A perfectly correct arithmetic result on a truss with an unbraced panel is worthless.

**Why determinate trusses are the norm in practice:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| Solvable by **statics alone** | No compatibility equations, no material properties needed |
| Member forces **do not depend on member areas** | So the design needs **no iteration** |
| **Insensitive to support settlement** | Develops **no self-stress** — settlement causes movement, not force |
| Unaffected by **temperature and lack of fit** | Same reason |
| Easy to check by hand | — |

> **The insensitivity to settlement is the practically important one**, and it is why determinate arrangements are chosen on poor or variable ground: a determinate structure simply accommodates the movement, while an indeterminate one resists it and stresses itself doing so.

**The price is REDUNDANCY**, and it is a real price:

> A determinate truss has **exactly enough** members. **Lose one and it becomes a mechanism** — it collapses. An indeterminate truss can **redistribute** load around a failed member, which is the structural basis of **robustness** and the defence against **progressive collapse**.

**A quick sanity check on the numbers**: a simple triangulated truss grows by **two members per added joint** (each new joint is fixed by two members), starting from a base triangle of 3 members and 3 joints. So **m = 2j − 3** for a simply supported truss — and with j = 8, that gives m = 13 ✓, confirming the arrangement is a properly triangulated simple truss.

> That check is worth doing: if m falls short of 2j − 3, the truss has too few members somewhere and there is a panel that will rack.

examTip.trick: **m + r − 2j = 13 + 3 − 16 = 0.** Then cross-check with the simple-truss rule **m = 2j − 3 = 13** ✓ — a properly triangulated truss grows by exactly two members per added joint.
examTip.trap: **A count of zero does NOT prove stability.** Three parallel or three concurrent reactions, or an unbraced rectangular panel, all give a valid count and a mechanism. Look at the geometry after the arithmetic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Determinate: no self-stress from settlement or temperature, but NO redundancy — lose one member and it collapses.** That trade-off is why bridges over settling ground are often determinate and buildings usually are not.

questions.stem: The principle of least work states that in an indeterminate structure, the redundant forces take values that:
options: Make the strain energy a maximum
Make the total strain energy a minimum
questions.solution:
**They take the values that make the total strain energy a MINIMUM.**

> **∂U/∂R = 0** for each redundant R — Castigliano's second theorem.

**Why minimum rather than maximum**: the strain energy is a **positive definite quadratic** function of the redundants, so its stationary point is necessarily a minimum. Physically, the structure settles into the state that stores the **least** energy consistent with equilibrium and compatibility.

**The method in outline:**

1. Identify the **redundant** force R and release it.
2. Write the internal forces (**M, P, T**) in terms of the applied loads **and R**.
3. Write the **strain energy U** in terms of R.
4. Set **∂U/∂R = 0** and solve.

**A worked application — the propped cantilever under UDL:**

> With R the prop reaction, **M(x) = Rx − wx²/2**
> **U = ∫₀ᴸ M²dx/(2EI)**
> **∂U/∂R = ∫₀ᴸ M(∂M/∂R)dx/(EI) = ∫₀ᴸ (Rx − wx²/2)(x)dx/(EI) = 0**
> **RL³/3 − wL⁴/8 = 0**, so **R = 3wL/8** ✓

> That is the standard result, obtained in four lines and with **no released-structure deflection diagram**.

**Its most elegant application is the TWO-HINGED ARCH:**

> Releasing the horizontal thrust H and minimising U gives
> **H = ∫(M y ds/EI) ÷ ∫(y² ds/EI)**

> There is no simpler route to that result — which is why the two-hinged arch is the standard textbook illustration of the method.

**Why ∂U/∂R = 0 is the right condition** has a physical reading worth having:

> Castigliano's first theorem says **∂U/∂R = the displacement in the direction of R**. For a **redundant** force at an **unyielding** support, that displacement is **zero** — so **∂U/∂R = 0** is simply the **compatibility condition** written in energy form.

> That is the connection between the energy method and the ordinary flexibility method: they are the same equation in different clothing.

**And it generalises to a yielding support:**

> If the support **settles by δ**, the condition becomes **∂U/∂R = δ** rather than zero — which handles settlement problems directly, with no extra machinery.

**Where the method fits among the alternatives:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Least work** | Elegant for **one or two** redundants; good for **arches** |
| **Consistent deformation** | The same idea with explicit deflection diagrams |
| **Slope-deflection** | Displacement method; systematic |
| **Moment distribution** | Iterative; excellent by hand for continuous beams and frames |
| **Matrix stiffness** | The general and programmable method |

> Least work becomes cumbersome beyond about two redundants, because U must be written and differentiated in every one of them — which is why moment distribution and stiffness methods took over for real structures.

**The conditions**: the structure must be **linearly elastic** with **small deflections**, and the redundant supports must be **unyielding** (or their movement known). Once anything yields, the strain energy is no longer a quadratic and the principle does not apply.

examTip.trick: The condition **∂U/∂R = 0 IS the compatibility condition** in energy form — because Castigliano's first theorem makes ∂U/∂R the displacement at R, and at an unyielding support that displacement is zero.
examTip.trap: For a **yielding** support the condition is **∂U/∂R = δ**, not zero. That extension handles settlement problems directly, and forgetting it gives the wrong redundant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Propped cantilever: ∂U/∂R = 0 gives R = 3wL/8 in four lines.** Two-hinged arch: **H = ∫My ds/EI ÷ ∫y² ds/EI**. Beyond two redundants it gets cumbersome — use moment distribution or stiffness instead.

questions.stem: In a simply supported truss carrying gravity loads at its panel points, the top chord members are generally in:
questions.solution:
**Compression.**

**Why.** A simply supported truss under gravity load behaves as a **deep beam**: it sags, so the **top fibres shorten and the bottom fibres lengthen**. The chords do exactly what an I-beam's flanges do.

| Chord | Force | Beam analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **TOP** | **COMPRESSION** | Compression flange |
| **BOTTOM** | **TENSION** | Tension flange |
| **Web members (diagonals, verticals)** | Either | Carry the **SHEAR** |

> That mapping is the quickest way to check any truss analysis for a sign error: if your calculation puts the top chord in tension under gravity load, something is wrong.

**For a CANTILEVER truss the pattern reverses:**

| Chord | Force |
|---|---|
| **TOP** | **TENSION** (hogging — tension at the top) |
| **BOTTOM** | **COMPRESSION** |

> Same reasoning: a cantilever hogs, so the top fibres stretch.

**The design consequence is substantial**, because tension and compression members are not equally difficult:

| Member | Governed by | Section required |
|---|---|---|
| **Tension chord** | **Strength** (net area × f_y) | **Small** — slenderness only limits sag and vibration |
| **Compression chord** | **BUCKLING** (slenderness) | **Much larger**, and it grows with the unbraced length |

> **The compression chord is almost always the critical member** and usually the heaviest. Its capacity depends on **L_e/k**, so **reducing its unbraced length is the most effective economy** available in truss design.

**Which is why the top chord is braced:**

| Bracing | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Purlins** at panel points | Restrain the top chord in the plane of the roof |
| **Lateral bracing** between trusses | Restrain it out of plane |
| **Sag rods, tie rods** | — |

> A member that is **zero-force under one load case** may exist purely to halve the compression chord's buckling length — and since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, halving it **quadruples** the capacity. That is exactly why zero-force members must never be deleted as "redundant".

**In the two common roof trusses**, the web members differ in a way worth knowing:

| Truss | Diagonals under gravity load |
|---|---|
| **PRATT** | Diagonals in **TENSION**, verticals in compression |
| **HOWE** | Diagonals in **COMPRESSION**, verticals in tension |

> **The Pratt is generally preferred** because its **long diagonals are in tension** and its **short verticals take the compression** — putting the buckling problem in the shortest members. The Howe does the opposite, which is why it suited timber (strong in compression along the grain) but suits steel less well.

**A Warren truss** has no verticals, and its diagonals alternate between tension and compression — which makes it efficient in material but means every second diagonal must be sized for buckling.

**The reversal caution**: under **wind uplift**, a roof truss's chord forces can **reverse entirely** — the bottom chord going into compression and the top into tension. A bottom chord sized only for tension, with no lateral restraint, can then buckle. Checking the **uplift** case is a real design requirement, not a formality.

examTip.trick: **Treat the truss as a deep beam.** Simply supported and sagging → **top compression, bottom tension**, exactly like an I-beam's flanges. A **cantilever** truss hogs, so the pattern reverses.
examTip.trap: **Check the WIND UPLIFT case.** Chord forces can reverse completely — a bottom chord sized only for tension, with no lateral restraint, will buckle when uplift puts it into compression.
examTip.mnemonic: **PRATT: long diagonals in TENSION, short verticals in compression** — the buckling problem lands in the shortest members, which is why Pratt is preferred for steel. Howe is the reverse and suited timber.

questions.stem: A determinate structure subjected to a support settlement develops:
options: Stresses only in the members near the support
questions.solution:
**No stresses at all.**

**Why.** A determinate structure has **exactly enough** restraints. When a support moves, the structure simply **moves with it as a rigid body or changes shape freely** — there is no redundant restraint to resist the movement, so nothing is stressed.

> **A determinate structure accommodates imposed movement; an indeterminate one RESISTS it, and stresses itself doing so.**

**The general principle, which covers a family of effects:**

| Imposed effect | Determinate structure | Indeterminate structure |
|---|---|---|
| **Support settlement** | **No stress** | **Large secondary stresses** |
| **Temperature change** | **No stress** — free expansion | **Restraint stresses** |
| **Shrinkage and creep** | No stress | Induced stresses |
| **Lack of fit** (a member made too short) | Movement only | Self-stress throughout |
| Foundation heave | No stress | Stress |

> All five are the same phenomenon: an **imposed deformation** rather than an imposed load. A structure with **no redundant restraint** cannot be stressed by one.

**How large are the indeterminate stresses?** For a fixed-ended beam with one support settling by δ:

> **M = 6EIδ/L²** at each end

> That can be **comparable with the design moments** for a settlement of only a few millimetres — which is why indeterminate structures are avoided on compressible or variable ground.

**The trade-off, stated plainly:**

| | **DETERMINATE** | **INDETERMINATE** |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis | **Statics alone** | Needs compatibility too |
| **Settlement, temperature, lack of fit** | **No stress** | **Induces stress** |
| **REDUNDANCY** | **NONE** — one failure is collapse | **Alternative load paths** |
| Material efficiency | Lower | **Higher** — moments shared, peaks reduced |
| Deflections | Larger | Smaller |

**Where determinate arrangements are deliberately chosen:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Poor or variable founding conditions** | Differential settlement is expected |
| **Long bridges** with large thermal movement | Avoids restraint forces |
| Structures on **mining or subsidence** ground | Movement is certain |
| **Three-hinged arches** | Determinate, so settlement and temperature are free |
| **GERBER (hinged) beams** | Continuity's efficiency without its settlement sensitivity |

> The **Gerber beam** is the classic compromise: hinges are placed at the natural **points of contraflexure** of the equivalent continuous beam, so the moment distribution is essentially unchanged while the structure becomes determinate.

**But redundancy is why most buildings ARE indeterminate:**

> An indeterminate structure can **redistribute** load around a failed element. That is the structural basis of **robustness** and the defence against **progressive collapse** — a determinate structure that loses one member becomes a mechanism.

**A practical consequence for construction**: because a determinate structure develops no lack-of-fit stress, its members can be fabricated and erected to ordinary tolerances. An indeterminate structure that is **forced together** during erection carries those forcing stresses permanently — which is why fit-up and the **order of making connections** matter on an indeterminate frame.

examTip.trick: The rule covers a whole family: **settlement, temperature, shrinkage, creep and lack of fit** all stress an **indeterminate** structure and none of them stress a **determinate** one. They are imposed *deformations*, not loads.
examTip.trap: Do not read "no stress" as "no movement". A determinate structure **moves freely** — it simply does not resist the movement, so nothing is stressed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixed beam with δ settlement: M = 6EIδ/L² at each end** — comparable with the design moment for only a few millimetres. That number is why indeterminate structures are avoided on compressible ground.

questions.stem: The vertical deflection at the free end of a cantilever carrying a couple M at that end is:
questions.solution:
**δ = ML²/(2EI)**, with the slope at the free end being **θ = ML/(EI)**.

**Derivation by the moment-area method**, which is quick because the moment is constant:

> The bending moment is **M everywhere** along the cantilever, so the **M/EI diagram is a RECTANGLE** of height M/EI and length L.

> **First theorem** (area) gives the slope: **θ = (M/EI) × L = ML/(EI)** ✓
> **Second theorem** (moment of area about the free end): **δ = (M/EI)(L)(L/2) = ML²/(2EI)** ✓

> The tangent at the fixed end is **horizontal**, so the deviation from it **is** the deflection — which is exactly why the moment-area method suits cantilevers.

**Option (a), ML/(EI), is the SLOPE** at the free end, offered as a deflection distractor. Settle it by **units**:

> A **slope is dimensionless**; a **deflection is a length**. **ML/(EI)** = (N·m)(m)/((N/m²)(m⁴)) = dimensionless ✓ — a slope, not a deflection.

> **Deflection formulas always carry one more power of L than the matching slope formula.**

**The three cantilever standard cases, slope and deflection together:**

| Loading | Slope at free end | Deflection at free end |
|---|---|---|
| **End couple M** | **ML/(EI)** | **ML²/(2EI)** |
| **End point load W** | **WL²/(2EI)** | **WL³/(3EI)** |
| **UDL w** | **wL³/(6EI)** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** |

> Notice the **denominators**: **1 and 2** for a couple, **2 and 3** for an end load, **6 and 8** for a UDL. The more distributed the load, the larger the denominators — because more of the load acts near the support where its lever arm is short.

**Where the end-couple case arises in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| A **bracket** on a column | The eccentric load resolves into a force **plus a couple** |
| **Slope-deflection** and moment distribution | Member-end rotations under applied end moments |
| A beam framing into a cantilever tip | Transfers a moment |
| **Balanced cantilever** bridge construction | End moments during erection |

**The bracket case is the everyday one and is worth stating explicitly:**

> A load **P at eccentricity e** is statically equivalent to **P on the axis PLUS a couple Pe**. The force and the couple must **both** be applied. Analysing only the transferred force understates the moment, and it is a genuine and common error in the design of brackets, corbels and eccentric connections.

**A cross-check using stiffness**: the slope result **θ = ML/(EI)** inverts to **M = (EI/L)θ**, so the **rotational stiffness of a cantilever tip is EI/L**. Compare that with the standard member stiffnesses used in moment distribution — **4EI/L** for a far end fixed and **3EI/L** for a far end hinged. The cantilever is the most flexible of the three, as it must be, having no restraint at all at the far end.

examTip.trap: **ML/(EI) is the SLOPE**, not the deflection — and it is the first option offered. A **slope is dimensionless** and a **deflection is a length**, so deflection formulas always carry **one more power of L**.
examTip.trick: For a constant moment the M/EI diagram is a **rectangle**, so moment-area gives both answers in one line: **area = ML/EI (slope)** and **moment of area = ML²/2EI (deflection)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cantilever denominators: couple 1 and 2; end load 2 and 3; UDL 6 and 8.** And remember where the couple comes from in practice: a **bracket** load P at eccentricity e is **P plus a couple Pe** — apply both.

questions.stem: An influence line differs from a bending moment diagram in that the influence line shows:
options: The moment at every section for a fixed load
The deflected shape of the beam
The stress distribution across the depth
One response quantity at one fixed section as a unit load moves
questions.solution:
**One response quantity, at ONE fixed section, as a unit load MOVES across the structure.**

**The distinction, stated plainly:**

| | **Bending moment diagram** | **INFLUENCE LINE** |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | The moment at **EVERY section** | **ONE quantity at ONE section** |
| For | A **FIXED** set of loads | A **MOVING unit load** |
| Horizontal axis is | Position along the **BEAM** | Position of the **LOAD** |
| Answers | "How is this loading resisted?" | "Where should the load go to make this worst?" |

> They can have the **same shape** for simple cases — both are triangular for a simply supported span — which is exactly why the confusion persists. But they answer entirely different questions.

**Standard influence lines for a simply supported span L**, section at distance a from the left (b = L − a):

| Quantity | Shape | Peak value |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | **Linear**, 1 at A falling to 0 at B | **1** at A |
| **Moment at the section** | **TRIANGULAR** | **ab/L** at the section |
| **Shear at the section** | Two **parallel lines with a UNIT STEP** at the section | **+b/L** and **−a/L** |

**Using an influence line** — two rules cover everything:

| Load | Response |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × (ordinate at the load's position)** |
| **UDL w over a length** | **w × (AREA under the influence line over that length)** |
| Several point loads | **Σ W_i y_i** |

**And the placement rules follow immediately:**

| To maximise | Place the load |
|---|---|
| With a **point load** | At the **maximum ORDINATE** |
| With a **UDL** | Over the **whole length of the same SIGN** |
| **Shear** with a UDL | Over **ONE SIDE ONLY** |

> **The shear case is the instructive one.** Because the shear influence line has **positive area on one side and negative on the other**, loading the whole span **partly cancels**. The maximum shear at a section comes from loading only one side — which is exactly the **pattern loading** principle.

**Where influence lines matter:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **BRIDGE design** | The essential tool — the vehicle must be positioned for the worst effect |
| **Crane runway girders** | Moving wheel loads |
| **Continuous beams** with pattern live load | Alternate-span loading |
| Industrial floors with moving plant | — |

**For a bridge**, the design vehicle (IRC Class A, Class AA, 70R) is moved along the influence line until the response is maximised. The process is now automated, but its entire logic is contained in the two placement rules above.

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S PRINCIPLE** is the general method for drawing them, and it becomes essential for indeterminate structures whose influence lines are **curved** and cannot be obtained by statics.

examTip.trap: The two are confused constantly because a moment influence line and a bending moment diagram are **both triangular** for a simply supported span. The discriminator: the horizontal axis is the position of the **LOAD** for an influence line, and a position on the **BEAM** for a BMD.
examTip.trick: **Point load → maximum ORDINATE. UDL → whole region of ONE SIGN.** Because a shear influence line changes sign at the section, maximum shear comes from loading **one side only** — loading both partly cancels.
examTip.mnemonic: **"One quantity, one section, moving load."** Peak moment ordinate is **ab/L**; the shear line has a **unit step** of +b/L and −a/L.

questions.stem: The influence line for the reaction at support A of a simply supported beam AB of span L is:
options: A straight line varying from 1 at A to 0 at B
A triangle with peak L/4 at midspan
questions.solution:
**A straight line, with ordinate 1 at A falling linearly to 0 at B.**

**Derive it directly.** With a unit load at distance x from A:

> **R_A = (L − x)/L**

| Load position x | R_A |
|---|---|
| **0** (at A) | **1** |
| L/4 | 0.75 |
| **L/2** | **0.5** |
| 3L/4 | 0.25 |
| **L** (at B) | **0** |

> Linear in x, from 1 to 0 ✓

**The physical reading is obvious once seen**: a load standing directly on A is carried entirely by A; a load at B is carried entirely by B; and it shares in proportion as it moves between them.

**The three basic influence lines for a simply supported span:**

| Quantity | Shape | Key ordinate |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction R_A** | **Linear**, 1 → 0 | **1** at A |
| **Reaction R_B** | Linear, 0 → 1 | 1 at B |
| **Moment at section a from A** | **Triangular** | **ab/L** at the section |
| **Shear at that section** | Two parallel lines, **unit step** | **+b/L**, **−a/L** |

**Using it:**

> For a **UDL w over the whole span**: **R_A = w × (area) = w × ½ × L × 1 = wL/2** ✓ — the familiar result, confirming the method.

> For a **point load W at midspan**: **R_A = W × 0.5 = W/2** ✓

**Note that both checks reproduce answers you already know**, which is the right way to gain confidence in an influence line before using it on something unfamiliar.

**To maximise the reaction at A**: place the loads **as close to A as possible**, since that is where the ordinate is greatest. For a train of wheel loads, that means running the leading wheel right up to the support.

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU confirms the shape without any algebra:**

> Remove the support at A and impose a **unit vertical displacement** there. The beam, being rigid between its remaining support and A, tilts as a **straight line** — 1 at A, 0 at B. That deflected shape **is** the influence line ✓

> For a **determinate** structure the released shape is always made of **straight segments**, which is why all its influence lines are straight-line figures. For an **indeterminate** structure the released shape is a **curve**, and so is the influence line — which is precisely why they cannot be obtained by statics there.

**A caution about the vertical scale**: an influence line for a **reaction or a shear** is **dimensionless** (it is a force per unit force), while an influence line for a **moment** has units of **length** (force × length per unit force). That is why the moment ordinate ab/L is a length and the reaction ordinate is a pure number.

examTip.trick: Check any influence line by reproducing a **known** result. UDL over the whole span: R_A = w × area = w × ½L × 1 = **wL/2** ✓. If it does not give back what you already know, the line is wrong.
examTip.trap: The **triangle with peak L/4** is the influence line for the **MOMENT at midspan** (ab/L with a = b = L/2), not for a reaction. Read which quantity is asked for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reaction and shear influence lines are DIMENSIONLESS; a moment influence line has units of LENGTH.** That is why the moment ordinate ab/L is a length and the reaction ordinate is a pure number.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam of span L, the maximum ordinate of the influence line for bending moment at a section distant a from the left support (b = L − a) is:
questions.solution:
**ab/L**, occurring when the unit load stands **at the section itself**.

**Derivation.** With the unit load at the section:

> **R_A = b/L**, and the moment at the section is **M = R_A × a = ab/L** ✓

**The shape is a triangle** with:

| Position | Ordinate |
|---|---|
| At A | **0** |
| **At the section** | **ab/L — the peak** |
| At B | **0** |

**Check it at midspan**, where a = b = L/2:

> **ab/L = (L/2)(L/2)/L = L/4** ✓

> So for a **unit load at midspan** the moment there is **L/4**, and for a load **W** it is **WL/4** — the familiar result. Option (a), L/4, is therefore the **special case** offered as a distractor: correct only at midspan, wrong everywhere else.

**And it recovers the general point-load formula:**

> For a load W at the section: **M = W × ab/L = Wab/L** ✓ — the standard result for a point load on a simply supported span.

**Where the maximum occurs along the span:**

> **ab/L is greatest when a = b = L/2**, since the product ab is maximised for a fixed sum. So of all sections, **midspan has the largest possible moment influence ordinate** — which is why a **single moving load produces its absolute maximum moment at midspan**.

**Using the line:**

| Loading | Moment at the section |
|---|---|
| Point load W at the section | **W ab/L** |
| **UDL w over the whole span** | **w × area of triangle = w × ½ L × ab/L = wab/2** |
| UDL over part of the span | w × area under that part |

> Check the UDL result at midspan: **w(L/2)(L/2)/2 = wL²/8** ✓ — the familiar simply supported value, which confirms the method.

**For a MOVING UDL shorter than the span** (a train, a lane load), the rule is to position it over the **greatest area** of the influence line — which for a triangular line means **straddling the peak**, with the load divided by the apex in the same ratio as the triangle's base segments.

**Note the units again**: this ordinate **ab/L has the dimensions of LENGTH**, because a moment influence line gives moment per unit force. Multiplying by a force gives a moment ✓ — a useful check that you have the right kind of influence line.

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU gives the same shape instantly**: insert a **hinge** at the section, impose a **unit relative rotation**, and the beam breaks into two straight segments forming a triangle. The peak ordinate works out to ab/L, and for a determinate beam the segments are straight — which is why the figure is a triangle and not a curve.

examTip.trap: **L/4 is the SPECIAL CASE at midspan** (a = b = L/2), offered as though it were general. It is correct only there — the general ordinate is **ab/L**.
examTip.trick: Verify with a UDL over the whole span: **w × ½L × ab/L = wab/2**, which at midspan gives **wL²/8** ✓. Reproducing a known result is the fastest check on any influence line.
examTip.mnemonic: **ab/L, peaking when the load sits AT the section.** And since ab is largest when a = b, **midspan gives the biggest ordinate of all** — which is why a single moving load does its worst at midspan.

questions.stem: The influence line for shear force at a section of a simply supported beam consists of:
options: Two parallel straight lines with a unit step at the section
questions.solution:
**Two parallel straight lines with a UNIT STEP at the section.**

**Derive it.** For a section at distance a from A (b = L − a), consider the shear just to the right of the section:

| Unit load position | Shear at the section |
|---|---|
| **To the LEFT** of the section | **−x/L**, running from 0 at A to **−a/L** just left of the section |
| **To the RIGHT** of the section | **+(L−x)/L**, running from **+b/L** just right of the section to 0 at B |

> The two lines are **parallel** (both of slope 1/L) and there is a **jump of exactly 1** across the section: from **−a/L** to **+b/L**, and **b/L − (−a/L) = (a + b)/L = 1** ✓

**The unit step is the signature of a shear influence line**, and it comes directly from the unit load crossing the section.

**The crucial consequence for loading:**

> The line has **NEGATIVE area on one side and POSITIVE area on the other**. So loading the **whole span partly CANCELS**.

> **Maximum shear at a section is produced by loading ONE SIDE ONLY** — the side whose ordinates have the sign you want.

**That is exactly the pattern-loading principle**, and it is why loading everything is not the worst case:

| To maximise | Load |
|---|---|
| **Positive** shear at the section | The **right-hand** portion only |
| **Negative** shear at the section | The **left-hand** portion only |
| Sagging moment in a span (continuous beam) | That span **plus alternate** spans |
| Hogging moment at a support | The **two adjacent** spans |

**Maximum shear for various loadings:**

| Loading | Maximum shear at the section |
|---|---|
| **Single point load W** | **W × b/L** (load placed just right of the section) |
| **UDL w over one side** | **w × ½ × b × (b/L) = wb²/(2L)** |
| UDL over the whole span | The two areas partly cancel — **less** than loading one side |

**Where the absolute maximum shear occurs:**

> **At the SUPPORT**, where a = 0 and the ordinate reaches its full value of 1. For a single moving load W, the maximum shear anywhere in the beam is **W**, with the load standing at the support.

> For a **UDL over the whole span**, the maximum shear is **wL/2** at the supports ✓ — again the familiar result.

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU reproduces the shape at once**: insert a **shear release** at the section (allowing the two sides to slide vertically past each other while keeping their slopes parallel) and impose a **unit relative slip**. The result is two parallel segments with a unit step ✓ — which is exactly why the release is described as it is.

**A practical note for bridges**: because shear is worst near the supports and moment worst near midspan, a girder's **web thickness and shear connectors are governed near the ends** while its **flange size is governed at midspan**. The two influence lines together explain why a plate girder is detailed the way it is.

examTip.trick: The **unit step** is the signature: the ordinates are **−a/L** just left and **+b/L** just right, and their difference is exactly **1** — the unit load crossing the section.
examTip.trap: Because the line changes **sign** at the section, **loading the whole span partly cancels**. Maximum shear needs **one side loaded only** — which is the pattern-loading principle in its simplest form.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment ILD: triangle. Shear ILD: unit step.** Maximum shear is at a **support** (ordinate 1); maximum moment is at **midspan** (ordinate L/4). That is why a plate girder's web is sized at the ends and its flanges at midspan.

questions.stem: When a uniformly distributed load of intensity w covers part of a span, the value of a response quantity is obtained from its influence line as:
options: w times the area under the influence line over the covered length
questions.solution:
**w × the AREA under the influence line over the covered length.**

**Why.** An element of the UDL, **w dx**, is a point load, contributing **w dx × y** where y is the ordinate at that position. Integrating over the loaded length:

> **Response = ∫ w y dx = w ∫y dx = w × (area under the influence line)** ✓

**The two rules for using any influence line:**

| Load | Response |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × ORDINATE** at the load's position |
| **UDL w** | **w × AREA** under the line over the loaded length |
| Several point loads | **Σ W_i y_i** |

> **Point load reads the ordinate; UDL reads the area.** That single distinction is the whole of influence line application.

**Checking it against known results:**

| Case | Influence line area | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **R_A, UDL over the whole span** | ½ × L × 1 = L/2 | **wL/2** ✓ |
| **Moment at midspan, UDL over whole span** | ½ × L × L/4 = L²/8 | **wL²/8** ✓ |
| **Shear at support, UDL over whole span** | ½ × L × 1 = L/2 | **wL/2** ✓ |

> All three reproduce the familiar formulas, which is the right way to gain confidence in the method.

**How to place a partial UDL for the worst effect:**

| Influence line | Place the UDL |
|---|---|
| **All one sign** (e.g. a moment ILD on a simple span) | Over the **whole span** |
| **Changes sign** (e.g. a shear ILD, or a continuous beam) | Over the region of **ONE sign only** |
| A **moving UDL shorter than the span** | Straddling the **peak**, positioned for greatest area |

**The straddling rule** for a moving UDL of length shorter than the span is worth stating:

> Position the load so that the **apex divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span**. That places the greatest possible area under the load.

**Pattern loading for continuous beams** is the same principle applied to live load:

| To maximise | Load |
|---|---|
| **Sagging** moment in a span | That span **plus ALTERNATE** spans |
| **Hogging** moment at a support | The **two ADJACENT** spans, plus alternate ones beyond |

> **Loading every span is NOT the worst case** — because the influence line for a sagging moment is **negative in the adjacent spans**, so loading them partly cancels. IS 456 cl. 22.4.1 requires the pattern cases, and analysing only the full-load case is unconservative.

**Dead load is the exception**: it is permanent and cannot be patterned, so it always goes on **every** span. Only the **live** load is varied.

**The result is a design ENVELOPE**: each pattern gives one diagram, and the design must satisfy the **worst value at every section across all cases**. Two consequences follow — a section may need **both top and bottom steel**, and the **points of contraflexure move** between cases, so reinforcement curtailment must be based on the envelope rather than on any single analysis.

examTip.trick: **Point load reads the ORDINATE; UDL reads the AREA.** Check it against a known case: moment at midspan under a full UDL gives w × ½L × L/4 = **wL²/8** ✓.
examTip.trap: For an influence line that **changes sign**, load only the region of **one sign** — loading everything partly cancels. That is why **alternate-span loading** governs a continuous beam, not full loading.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead load on EVERY span (it cannot be patterned); LIVE load patterned.** The result is an **envelope** — so some sections need both top and bottom steel, and contraflexure points move between cases.

questions.stem: Müller-Breslau's principle states that the influence line for a response quantity has the same shape as the:
options: Bending moment diagram for a unit load at midspan
Deflected form when the corresponding restraint is released and a unit displacement imposed
Shear force diagram under the design load
Elastic curve under the full design load
questions.solution:
**The deflected form the structure takes when the corresponding restraint is RELEASED and a UNIT DISPLACEMENT imposed** in the direction of that quantity.

**The recipe:**

| Influence line for | Release | Impose |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction** at a support | The **support** | A **unit VERTICAL displacement** |
| **Moment** at a section | The moment restraint — insert a **HINGE** | A **unit relative ROTATION** |
| **Shear** at a section | The shear restraint — insert a **shear release** | A **unit relative SLIP** |
| Axial force in a member | Cut the member | A unit relative axial displacement |

**Check it against the standard results:**

| Case | Released shape | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Reaction at A | Remove the support, lift A by 1 — the beam **tilts as a straight line** | Linear, 1 → 0 ✓ |
| Moment at a section | Insert a hinge, rotate — two straight segments forming a **triangle** | Triangular, peak ab/L ✓ |
| Shear at a section | Insert a shear release, slide — **two parallel lines with a unit step** | ✓ |

> **All three standard influence lines fall out of the principle immediately**, which is a good reason to learn the principle rather than the three shapes.

**Why it is true** — it follows from **Betti's (and hence Maxwell's) reciprocal theorem**. The work done by the unit load moving through the released displacement field equals the work done by the released force moving through the load's displacement, and rearranging gives the result.

**Its real value is for INDETERMINATE structures:**

> For a **determinate** structure the released shape is made of **straight segments**, so the influence line is a straight-line figure that statics could have given anyway.

> For an **INDETERMINATE** structure the released shape is a **CURVE**, and the influence line is curved — and it **cannot be obtained by statics at all**.

> But the shape can still be **sketched qualitatively**, and that alone identifies the **critical load positions and patterns** — which is usually all the designer needs before handing the numbers to software.

**The pattern-loading rules come straight from it.** Sketch the released shape for a sagging moment in one span of a continuous beam: it is **positive in that span, negative in the adjacent ones, positive again beyond**. Hence:

| To maximise | Load |
|---|---|
| **Sagging** moment in a span | That span **plus ALTERNATE** spans |
| **Hogging** moment at a support | The **two ADJACENT** spans |

> **That is why loading every span is not the worst case** — a genuinely counter-intuitive result that falls out of one sketch.

**The conditions**, which are the same as for superposition and for Maxwell's theorem:

> **Linear elastic** material and **small deflections**. It does not hold once anything yields.

**A practical caution on scale**: the principle gives the **SHAPE** of the influence line directly, but the **ordinates** require the actual released deflections to be computed (or the shape to be normalised so the imposed displacement is exactly unity). For qualitative work — deciding where to put the load — the shape alone is enough, which is how the principle is most often used.

examTip.trick: **Release the restraint that corresponds to the quantity.** For a **moment**, insert a **hinge** and rotate; for a **shear**, insert a shear release and slide; for a **reaction**, remove the support and lift. The deflected shape is the influence line.
examTip.trap: It gives the **SHAPE** directly; the **ordinates** still require the released deflections to be computed, or the shape normalised to a unit displacement. For deciding where to put the load, the shape alone suffices.
examTip.mnemonic: **Determinate → straight segments. INDETERMINATE → curves that statics cannot give.** That is where the principle earns its keep — and it is where the alternate-span pattern-loading rules come from.

questions.stem: For a single concentrated load rolling across a simply supported beam, the absolute maximum bending moment occurs:
options: Under the load when it is at midspan
questions.solution:
**Under the load, when the load stands at MIDSPAN**, with value **WL/4**.

**Why.** For a load W at distance a from the left support (b = L − a):

> **M = Wab/L**

> Since a + b = L is fixed, the product **ab is maximised when a = b = L/2**. So:

> **M_max = W(L/2)(L/2)/L = WL/4** ✓

**The two questions that are easily confused:**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Maximum moment at a **GIVEN section**? | When the **load is AT that section**: **Wab/L** |
| **ABSOLUTE** maximum moment anywhere? | When the load is at **MIDSPAN**: **WL/4** |

> Both answers are "under the load" — the difference is whether the section is fixed or free to be chosen.

**Companion results for a single moving load:**

| Quantity | Maximum | Load position |
|---|---|---|
| **Moment** | **WL/4** | Midspan |
| **Shear** | **W** | At a **support** |
| Reaction | **W** | At that support |

**FOR A TRAIN OF LOADS the rule is different and less obvious:**

> The absolute maximum moment occurs **under the load nearest the resultant**, when the **midspan BISECTS the distance between that load and the RESULTANT of all the loads on the span**.

> Equivalently: position the train so that the **centre of the span lies midway between the resultant and the load under consideration**.

**Why it is under a load rather than between loads**: for a set of point loads the bending moment diagram is made of **straight segments**, so its peak must sit at a **vertex** — that is, under one of the loads. The moment can never peak between two point loads.

**The procedure for a train:**

1. Find the **resultant** of all the loads on the span and its position.
2. Try each load in turn as the "critical" one.
3. For each, position the train so midspan bisects the distance between that load and the resultant.
4. Compute the moment under that load.
5. Take the **largest** result.

> In practice the critical load is usually the **heaviest one near the centre of the group**, so only two or three trials are needed.

**A caution**: a load may **run off the span** during this positioning, in which case the resultant changes and the calculation must be redone for the loads actually on the beam. Checking whether every load in the assumed group is still on the span is a standard oversight.

**For bridge design** this is now automated, but the logic matters for checking output: an influence line approach reaches the same answer, positioning the train for the **greatest Σ W_i y_i**.

examTip.trick: **M = Wab/L, and ab is greatest when a = b.** So a single moving load does its worst at midspan, giving **WL/4** — no differentiation needed, just the observation that a product with a fixed sum peaks when the factors are equal.
examTip.trap: Distinguish **maximum at a GIVEN section** (load at that section, Wab/L) from the **ABSOLUTE maximum** (load at midspan, WL/4). Both are "under the load"; only the second is free to choose the section.
examTip.mnemonic: **Single load: moment worst at MIDSPAN, shear worst at a SUPPORT.** For a **train**, the peak is **under the load nearest the resultant**, with midspan bisecting the gap between them — and always under a load, never between, because the BMD is made of straight segments.

questions.stem: A three-hinged arch is statically determinate because:
options: The third hinge provides an additional equation
questions.solution:
**Because the third hinge provides an additional equation — the bending moment there must be ZERO.**

**The count.** A three-hinged arch has **two pinned supports**, giving **four** reaction components (H and V at each). Against that:

> **3 equilibrium equations + 1 condition equation (M = 0 at the crown hinge) = 4** ✓

> **D_s = 4 − 4 = 0** — determinate.

**Comparison across the arch family:**

| Arch | Reactions | Conditions | D_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Three-hinged** | 4 | **1** (crown hinge) | **0 — determinate** |
| **Two-hinged** | 4 | 0 | **1** |
| **Fixed (hingeless)** | 6 | 0 | **3** |

**Solving a three-hinged arch:**

1. **ΣM about one support** gives the other's vertical reaction.
2. **ΣV = 0** gives the first vertical reaction.
3. **ΣM about the CROWN HINGE**, taking one half of the arch as a free body, gives the horizontal thrust:

> **H = M_crown(computed as a simple beam) / rise**

> That last relation is the workhorse: the horizontal thrust is the **simple-beam moment at the crown divided by the rise**.

**The consequence is the arch's whole structural virtue:**

> **M_arch = M_beam − H y**

> The horizontal thrust **subtracts** from what the bending moment would otherwise be. A greater rise means a smaller H but a larger lever arm y — and for the right shape the two cancel the beam moment **entirely**.

**The ideal arch shape** for a given loading is the one that makes **M_arch = 0 everywhere**:

| Loading | Ideal shape |
|---|---|
| **UDL on the horizontal projection** | **PARABOLA** |
| **Self-weight along the arch** | **CATENARY** |
| Point loads | A funicular polygon |

> An arch of the ideal shape carries its load by **pure axial compression** — which is why masonry, which cannot take tension, can span so far as an arch and not at all as a beam.

**Real arches carry some bending**, because the loading varies while the shape is fixed. A parabolic arch designed for a UDL develops moments under partial or point loading — which is why a real arch has a finite depth of section rather than being a line.

**Why choose a three-hinged arch despite the extra hinge?**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Determinate** — solvable by statics | No compatibility equations |
| **NO stress from support settlement** | The hinges accommodate the movement |
| **No stress from temperature change** | Same reason |
| No stress from shrinkage, creep or rib shortening | Same |

> **That insensitivity is the real reason for the third hinge**, not the easier arithmetic. A **two-hinged** or **fixed** arch develops substantial thrust changes from temperature and abutment movement — and an arch's whole action depends on its abutments not spreading.

**The price** is the usual one: **no redundancy**, a hinge to detail and maintain, and slightly larger deflections. For **long-span concrete and steel arches on sound rock** the fixed arch is preferred for its stiffness and material efficiency; the three-hinged form is chosen where **movement is expected**.

The moment there being zero.

examTip.trick: **H = M_crown(as a simple beam) / rise.** Take moments about the crown hinge with half the arch as a free body — one equation, and the thrust falls out.
examTip.trap: "Arches carry no bending moment" is true only for the **ideal shape under the design loading** (parabola for a UDL, catenary for self-weight). Under any other loading a real arch bends, which is why it has a finite section depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **M_arch = M_beam − Hy** — the thrust subtracts the beam moment away. And the third hinge is there for **settlement and temperature freedom**, not for the easier arithmetic.

questions.stem: A three-hinged parabolic arch of span L and rise h carries a uniformly distributed load w over its whole span. The horizontal thrust is:
questions.solution:
**H = wL²/(8h).**

**Derivation.** Using **H = M_crown(as a simple beam)/rise**:

> The simple-beam moment at midspan under a full UDL is **wL²/8**.
> **H = (wL²/8)/h = wL²/(8h)** ✓

**Check the dimensions**: (N/m)(m²)/m = N ✓ — a force, as a thrust must be. Option (c), wL/(2h), gives N/m, which is wrong.

**The remarkable property of this case:**

> A **PARABOLIC** arch under a **UDL on the horizontal projection** carries the load with **ZERO bending moment everywhere**.

**Proof.** For a parabola, **y = 4hx(L − x)/L²**. At any section:

> **M_arch = M_beam − H y**
> **M_beam = wx(L − x)/2**
> **H y = (wL²/8h) × 4hx(L−x)/L² = wx(L−x)/2**

> **M_arch = wx(L−x)/2 − wx(L−x)/2 = 0** ✓ **everywhere along the span.**

> **The parabola is the funicular shape for a UDL** — the thrust line coincides exactly with the arch axis, so there is no eccentricity and therefore no bending.

**The consequence is why arches exist:**

> The arch carries the load by **PURE AXIAL COMPRESSION**. That is what allows **masonry**, which cannot take tension, to span distances impossible for a masonry beam.

**The rise–thrust trade-off:**

> **H ∝ 1/h** — a **flatter arch** (small h) develops a **much larger thrust**.

| Rise/span | Relative thrust | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **h/L = 1/2** (semicircular) | Low | Large headroom needed |
| **h/L = 1/5** | Moderate | Common for bridges |
| **h/L = 1/10** | **Double** the 1/5 value | Flat arch, heavy abutments |

> A flat arch looks elegant and needs little headroom, but its **abutments must resist an enormous horizontal thrust**. That is the arch's fundamental practical constraint.

**The abutment is the arch's weak point:**

> An arch **must** have abutments capable of resisting H without spreading. If the abutments **spread even slightly**, the arch's geometry changes, the thrust line no longer follows the axis, and bending moments appear where none were designed for.

> That is why arches are built on **sound rock**, or with a **TIE** connecting the two springings to take the thrust internally — a **tied arch (bowstring)**, which converts the horizontal thrust into tension in the tie and leaves the supports carrying only vertical load.

**The ideal shapes, by loading:**

| Loading | Funicular shape |
|---|---|
| **UDL on the horizontal projection** (a deck) | **PARABOLA** |
| **Self-weight along the arch length** | **CATENARY** |
| Point loads | Funicular polygon |

> The **catenary** and the parabola are close but not identical; for a shallow arch (h/L below about 1/5) the difference is negligible, which is why parabolas are used in practice for both cases.

**Note that the same H applies to a two-hinged parabolic arch under a full UDL** — which is a useful check when comparing the two forms. The difference between them appears under **partial** or **point** loading, and in their response to **temperature and support movement**.

examTip.trick: **H = M_crown/rise**, and the crown moment for a full UDL is the familiar **wL²/8** — so **H = wL²/8h** in one step. Check the units: it must come out as a **force**.
examTip.trap: **H ∝ 1/h**, so a **flatter arch develops a MUCH larger thrust**. Halving the rise doubles the thrust and the abutments must take it — which is the arch's real practical constraint.
examTip.mnemonic: **Parabola + UDL = ZERO bending everywhere** — pure axial compression, which is why masonry can span as an arch and not as a beam. If the abutments **spread**, that property is lost and bending appears.

questions.stem: The horizontal thrust in a two-hinged arch is determined by:
options: Statics alone, as for a three-hinged arch
Assuming it equals the vertical reaction
A strain energy (compatibility) condition, since the arch is indeterminate
questions.solution:
**By a strain energy (compatibility) condition** — because a two-hinged arch is **statically indeterminate to the first degree**.

**The determinacy count:**

> Four reaction components (H and V at each pinned support), three equilibrium equations, **no** condition equation — so **D_s = 4 − 3 = 1**.

> Statics gives the two vertical reactions but **cannot** give H. A fourth equation is needed, and it must come from **compatibility**.

**The condition** is that the two supports do not move apart:

> Release the horizontal restraint and require the resulting horizontal displacement to be **zero**. By Castigliano's second theorem (**least work**):

> **∂U/∂H = 0**

**Carrying it through** with the bending strain energy gives the standard result:

> **H = ∫(M y ds/EI) ÷ ∫(y² ds/EI)**

where **M** is the simple-beam bending moment and **y** the rise of the arch axis at that section.

**Contrast with the three-hinged arch**, which is why option (a) is wrong:

| | **Three-hinged** | **Two-hinged** |
|---|---|---|
| D_s | **0 — determinate** | **1 — indeterminate** |
| H from | **Statics: M_crown/rise** | **Strain energy** |
| Settlement, temperature | **No stress** | **Induces thrust changes** |
| Stiffness | Lower | Higher |

> Taking moments about the crown works for a **three**-hinged arch precisely because the moment there is **known to be zero**. A two-hinged arch has **no crown hinge**, so that equation is unavailable.

**Refinements that a full analysis includes:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **RIB SHORTENING** | The axial compression shortens the arch, **reducing H** |
| **TEMPERATURE change** | A rise in temperature makes the arch try to expand, **increasing H**: **H_t = αΔT L ÷ ∫(y²ds/EI)** |
| **Abutment yielding** | Spread **reduces H** substantially |
| Shrinkage and creep (concrete) | Reduce H over time |

> **These are not small corrections.** For a shallow arch the temperature thrust can be a large fraction of the load thrust, and **abutment yielding** can change the whole force distribution.

**Which is exactly why the three-hinged form exists:**

> A **three-hinged** arch is **determinate**, so **none** of these effects induces any stress — temperature, settlement, shrinkage and rib shortening all produce movement rather than force. That immunity, not the simpler arithmetic, is the reason it is chosen where movement is expected.

**The general arch equation** applies to all three forms:

> **M_arch = M_beam − H y**

> The thrust **subtracts** from the beam moment. For the **funicular** shape and its matching loading, the subtraction is exact and **M_arch = 0** everywhere — a parabola under UDL, or a catenary under self-weight.

**A practical note on abutments**: whichever arch form is used, the abutments must resist H without spreading. Where the ground cannot provide that, a **TIE** between the springings converts the thrust into internal tension — the **tied arch or bowstring**, which then delivers only vertical load to its supports and can be used on ordinary foundations.

examTip.trap: **"Moments about the crown" works only for a THREE-hinged arch**, because the moment there is known to be zero. A two-hinged arch has no crown hinge, so that equation does not exist.
examTip.trick: Count first: two pinned supports give **four** reaction components against **three** equilibrium equations, so **D_s = 1** and a compatibility equation is unavoidable. **H = ∫My ds/EI ÷ ∫y² ds/EI.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Two-hinged: temperature, rib shortening and abutment yielding all change H.** A **three-hinged** arch is immune to all of them because it is determinate — which is the real reason for the third hinge.

questions.stem: In an arch, the relationship between the bending moment at a section, the equivalent simple beam moment and the horizontal thrust is:
questions.solution:
**M_arch = M_beam − H y.**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **M_beam** | The bending moment at that section if the arch were a **simply supported beam** of the same span carrying the same loads |
| **H** | The **horizontal thrust** |
| **y** | The **rise of the arch axis** above the springing line at that section |

**The minus sign is the whole point:**

> The horizontal thrust **acts against** the beam moment and **reduces** it. That reduction is precisely what makes an arch a more efficient structure than a beam of the same span.

**The ideal case** is when the subtraction is exact:

> If **H y = M_beam at every section**, then **M_arch = 0 everywhere** and the arch carries its load by **PURE AXIAL COMPRESSION**.

**The shape that achieves this is the FUNICULAR shape** for that loading:

| Loading | Funicular shape |
|---|---|
| **UDL on the horizontal projection** | **PARABOLA** |
| **Self-weight along the arch** | **CATENARY** |
| Point loads | Funicular polygon |

**Verify for the parabolic arch under UDL:**

> Parabola: **y = 4hx(L − x)/L²**, and **H = wL²/(8h)**
> **H y = (wL²/8h) × 4hx(L−x)/L² = wx(L−x)/2**
> **M_beam = wx(L−x)/2**
> **M_arch = 0** ✓ at every section

**Why this matters historically and practically:**

> **Masonry cannot carry tension.** As a beam it is useless; as an arch, carrying only compression, it spans hundreds of metres — which is why every long-span structure before iron was an arch or a dome.

**The THRUST LINE is the geometric way to see it:**

> The **thrust line** (line of pressure) is the locus of the resultant force through the arch. Then:

> **M_arch = H × e**, where **e is the eccentricity of the thrust line from the arch AXIS.**

| Thrust line position | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Coincides with the axis** | **No bending** — the ideal |
| Within the **middle third** of the section | All compression — safe for masonry |
| **Outside the middle third** | **TENSION develops** — a masonry arch cracks |
| Outside the section | Collapse mechanism forms |

> **For a masonry arch the design criterion is that the thrust line stays within the middle third**, for every credible loading. A crack does not immediately mean collapse — the arch simply hinges and finds a new thrust line — but **four hinges** turn it into a mechanism, and that is the classic masonry arch failure.

**Real arches always carry some bending**, because the loading varies while the shape is fixed. An arch shaped for a full UDL develops moments under **partial** loading — which is why partial and asymmetric load cases are checked, and why a real arch has a finite section depth rather than being a line.

**The abutment condition** underlies everything: if the abutments **spread**, H falls, the subtraction is incomplete, and bending moments appear throughout. That is why arches demand sound abutments — or a **tie** between the springings to carry the thrust internally.

examTip.trick: **The thrust SUBTRACTS.** If it added, an arch would be worse than a beam — which is obviously wrong, so the sign settles itself on physical grounds without any derivation.
examTip.trap: "Arches carry no bending" holds only for the **funicular shape under its design loading**. Under **partial or asymmetric** loading a real arch bends, which is why those cases must be checked.
examTip.mnemonic: **M_arch = H × e**, the eccentricity of the **thrust line** from the axis. For **masonry**, keep the thrust line within the **middle third**; four hinges make a mechanism, and that is how masonry arches actually fail.

questions.stem: The influence line for a member force in a determinate truss is:
questions.solution:
**Made of straight line segments, with breaks (changes of slope) at the PANEL POINTS.**

**Why straight segments.** In a determinate structure the member forces are found by **statics alone**, and they depend **linearly** on the position of the unit load. Between panel points the relationship is linear, so the influence line is a straight line.

**Why breaks at the panel points.** Load reaches a truss **only at its joints** — through the deck, stringers and floor beams. As the unit load moves between two panel points, it is **distributed to the two adjacent joints in inverse proportion to its distance** from them. That distribution changes the member forces linearly, and the **slope changes** each time the load passes a panel point.

> **The influence line for a determinate truss member is therefore a polygon**, with vertices at the panel points.

**Contrast with an indeterminate truss:**

| Truss | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **Determinate** | **Straight segments** — obtainable by statics |
| **Indeterminate** | **CURVED** — statics cannot give it; needs Müller-Breslau or a full analysis |

**How to construct one** for a chord member:

1. Take a **section** cutting the member.
2. Place the unit load at each **panel point** in turn.
3. For each position, find the member force by **moments about the point where the other two cut members intersect**.
4. Plot those values and **join them with straight lines**.

> Because only the panel-point values are needed, the whole influence line follows from a handful of calculations.

**The characteristic shapes for a parallel-chord truss:**

| Member | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **Chord** (top or bottom) | **Triangular**, peaking under the panel where the member acts |
| **Diagonal** | Two straight portions of **opposite sign**, crossing within the panel it spans |
| Vertical | Similar to a diagonal |

**The diagonal's sign change is the practically important feature:**

> Because the influence line for a **diagonal** changes sign, the member goes into **tension for some load positions and compression for others**.

> **That is a load REVERSAL**, and it has two design consequences: the member must be designed for **both** senses, and a **tension-only** member (a rod or a slender flat) cannot be used there.

**For a chord member**, the influence line is all of one sign, so the force never reverses under gravity load — the top chord stays in compression and the bottom in tension, as the deep-beam analogy predicts.

**But wind uplift can reverse everything:**

> Under **uplift** the whole truss hogs instead of sagging, and the chord forces reverse — the bottom chord going into **compression**. A bottom chord sized only for tension, with no lateral restraint, will **buckle**. Checking the uplift case is a real design requirement for light roof trusses, not a formality.

**Using the influence lines**, the two rules are the same as for beams: **point load × ordinate**, **UDL × area**. For a **moving train** on a bridge truss, position the loads for the greatest **Σ W_i y_i** — and because the influence line is a polygon, the maximum always occurs with a load **at a vertex**, that is, at a panel point.

examTip.trick: **Compute the value at each PANEL POINT and join with straight lines.** Load reaches a truss only at its joints, so nothing interesting happens between them — which is why a handful of calculations gives the whole line.
examTip.trap: A **DIAGONAL's** influence line **changes sign**, so the member reverses between tension and compression as the load moves. It must be designed for **both**, and a tension-only rod cannot be used there.
examTip.mnemonic: **Determinate → straight segments (a polygon). Indeterminate → curves.** And check the **wind uplift** case: it reverses the chord forces entirely, and a bottom chord sized only for tension will buckle.

questions.stem: To produce the maximum shear force at a section of a simply supported beam under a moving uniformly distributed load longer than the span, the load should cover:
options: Only the portion of the span on one side of the section
The two ends, leaving the middle clear
questions.solution:
**Only the portion of the span on ONE side of the section.**

**Why.** The influence line for shear at a section has **positive area on one side and negative area on the other**, separated by a **unit step** at the section.

> Since a UDL's effect is **w × the AREA under the influence line**, loading **both** sides means the two areas **partly cancel**. Loading only the side whose ordinates carry the sign you want gives the maximum.

**The numbers.** For a section at distance a from the left support (b = L − a):

| Loading | Shear at the section |
|---|---|
| **Right side only** (length b) | **+w b²/(2L)** — the maximum positive |
| **Left side only** (length a) | **−w a²/(2L)** — the maximum negative |
| **Whole span** | **w(b² − a²)/(2L)** — **less** in magnitude |

> At **midspan** (a = b = L/2) the whole-span case gives **exactly zero**, while loading one side gives **wL/8**. That is the starkest illustration: covering the whole span produces no shear at all at midspan, and covering half of it produces the maximum.

**This is the pattern-loading principle in its clearest form**, and it generalises:

| To maximise | Load |
|---|---|
| **Shear** at a section | **One side only** |
| **Moment** at a section (simple span) | The **whole span** — the influence line is all one sign |
| **Sagging** moment in a span of a continuous beam | That span **plus ALTERNATE** spans |
| **Hogging** moment at a support | The **two ADJACENT** spans |

> **The rule is always the same: load the region where the influence line has the sign you want, and leave the rest clear.** Whether that means the whole span, half of it, or alternate spans depends only on the shape of the influence line.

**Why "loading everything" is a persistent misconception**: for a simply supported beam's **moment**, loading the whole span **is** correct, because the moment influence line is entirely positive. Candidates generalise from that case to shear and to continuous beams, where it is wrong.

**Where the absolute maximum shear occurs:**

> **At the SUPPORT**, with the load covering the **whole span** — because there a = 0 and the entire influence line is of one sign. **V_max = wL/2** ✓

> So the section-by-section answer and the whole-beam answer differ: **at a general section load one side; at the support load everything.**

**In codified design** this appears as **pattern loading** requirements (IS 456 cl. 22.4.1 for continuous beams) and as **lane loading** rules for bridges, where the design lane load is applied over whatever length produces the worst effect rather than over the full span automatically.

**Dead load is exempt** from all of this: it is permanent and cannot be patterned, so it always acts over the whole structure. Only the **live load** is positioned adversely — and the design result is an **envelope** over all the patterns considered.

examTip.trick: **Load only where the influence line has the sign you want.** For shear that means **one side**; for a simple-span moment it means the **whole span** (all one sign); for a continuous beam it means **alternate spans**.
examTip.trap: At **midspan**, loading the **whole span gives ZERO shear** while loading half gives **wL/8** — the maximum. That contrast is the clearest demonstration that "load everything" is not a general rule.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum shear at a general section: one side (wb²/2L). At the SUPPORT: whole span (wL/2).** Dead load always covers everything; only **live** load is patterned.

questions.stem: A tied arch (bowstring girder) differs from an ordinary arch in that:
options: It has no bending moment anywhere
The horizontal thrust is taken by a tie
It must be built of masonry
questions.solution:
**The horizontal thrust is taken internally by a TIE**, so the supports carry only **vertical** reactions.

**The problem it solves.** An ordinary arch develops a large **horizontal thrust H** which the abutments must resist without spreading. Where the ground cannot provide that — soft soil, a pier on piles, or a bridge that must sit on ordinary bearings — the arch is unbuildable in that form.

> A **tie** connecting the two springings takes H as **internal TENSION**, so the thrust never reaches the supports at all.

**The result:**

| | **Ordinary arch** | **TIED arch** |
|---|---|---|
| Support reactions | **Vertical AND horizontal** | **VERTICAL only** |
| Foundation requirement | **Sound rock or massive abutments** | **Ordinary** — like a simply supported beam |
| Behaves externally as | An arch | A **simply supported beam** |
| Tie force | — | **T = H** (tension) |

> **Externally the tied arch behaves as a simply supported girder**, which is why it can be placed on the same bearings as any other span, and why it can be **fabricated on the ground and lifted into place** — a decisive construction advantage.

**How the load is carried internally:**

| Component | Force |
|---|---|
| **Arch rib** | **COMPRESSION** |
| **Tie** | **TENSION**, equal to the thrust H |
| **Hangers** | Tension, suspending the deck from the rib |

> The rib and the tie form a **self-contained equilibrium system** — the same arrangement as a bow and its string, which is where "bowstring" comes from.

**The critical detail is the TIE:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| It carries the **full thrust in tension** | A large force, often the largest in the structure |
| Its **failure is CATASTROPHIC** | The arch spreads and the whole span collapses |
| It is often **inaccessible** for inspection | Buried in the deck |
| **Corrosion protection** is critical | — |

> **The tie is a non-redundant, high-consequence element.** Modern practice provides **multiple tie elements** so that one can fail without collapse, and makes them **inspectable and replaceable**. Several bowstring bridges have been lost or condemned because a single buried tie corroded unseen.

**Where it is used:**

| Application | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Bridges on poor foundations** | No horizontal thrust to resist |
| **Long-span roofs** | Supports need only carry vertical load |
| Spans that must be **lifted into place** | The structure is self-contained |
| Crossings where abutments cannot be enlarged | — |

**Note what the distractors get wrong:**

| Option | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "Carries no vertical load" | It carries the full vertical load — that is its purpose |
| "No bending moment anywhere" | True only for the **funicular shape under its design loading**; partial and asymmetric loads cause bending in any arch |
| "Must be masonry" | **Masonry cannot take the tie's TENSION.** A tied arch is necessarily steel or reinforced concrete — masonry arches are the ones that specifically **require** thrust-resisting abutments |

> That last point is worth holding: the tied arch is exactly the form that **masonry cannot use**, because the tie must pull.

The supports carry only vertical reactions.

examTip.trick: Ask **where the thrust goes**. In an ordinary arch it goes into the **abutments**; in a tied arch it goes into the **tie as tension**, so the supports see only vertical load — and the span behaves externally like a simply supported girder.
examTip.trap: "Must be masonry" is exactly backwards. **Masonry cannot carry the tie's TENSION**, so a tied arch is necessarily steel or RC. Masonry is the material that specifically *needs* thrust-resisting abutments.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rib in compression, tie in tension, hangers carrying the deck — a bow and its string.** The tie is **non-redundant and often buried**: provide multiple elements and make them inspectable, or a hidden corrosion failure takes the whole span.

questions.stem: A rise in temperature in a two-hinged arch with unyielding abutments causes:
options: No change, since the arch is free to expand
An increase in the horizontal thrust
questions.solution:
**An increase in the horizontal thrust.**

**Why.** A rise in temperature makes the arch want to **expand and push its springings apart**. The **unyielding abutments prevent that**, so the restraint generates an **additional horizontal thrust**.

> **H_temperature = αΔT L ÷ ∫(y² ds/EI)**

**The general principle at work:**

> An **imposed deformation** stresses an **indeterminate** structure and leaves a **determinate** one unstressed. A two-hinged arch is indeterminate to degree 1, so it resists the expansion and stresses itself doing so.

**Which is exactly why the THREE-hinged arch exists:**

| Arch | D_s | Temperature effect | Settlement effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Three-hinged** | **0** | **NONE** — the crown hinge lets it flex freely | **NONE** |
| **Two-hinged** | 1 | **Thrust changes** | Thrust changes |
| **Fixed** | 3 | **Largest effects** | Largest |

> The three-hinged arch simply **rotates about its hinges** to accommodate the expansion, developing no force. That immunity — not the simpler arithmetic — is the real reason for the third hinge.

**How large is the effect?** For a shallow arch it can be substantial:

> Because **H_t ∝ 1/∫(y²ds/EI)**, a **flatter arch** (small y throughout) has a **small denominator** and therefore a **large temperature thrust**. A flat arch is doubly penalised: it already has a large load thrust (H ∝ 1/h) and it is more sensitive to temperature as well.

**The other imposed-deformation effects on a two-hinged arch:**

| Effect | Direction |
|---|---|
| **Temperature RISE** | **Increases** H |
| Temperature fall | Decreases H |
| **RIB SHORTENING** (axial compression under load) | **Decreases** H |
| **ABUTMENT YIELDING (spread)** | **Decreases** H substantially |
| Shrinkage and creep (concrete) | Decrease H |

> **Rib shortening and abutment yielding both RELIEVE the thrust**, while a temperature rise increases it. A full analysis includes all of them, and for concrete arches the **creep and shrinkage** reductions are large enough that the long-term thrust differs materially from the short-term value.

**Abutment yielding deserves emphasis:**

> Even a **small spread** of the abutments relieves the thrust considerably — which sounds helpful but is not. As H falls, the subtraction in **M_arch = M_beam − Hy** becomes incomplete, and **bending moments appear throughout the arch** where none was designed for.

> That is why an arch demands **sound, non-yielding abutments**, and why the **tied arch** exists for sites that cannot provide them.

**The design responses to temperature thrust:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| Use a **three-hinged** form | Complete immunity, at the cost of redundancy and stiffness |
| Design the section for the **combined** thrust | The straightforward option |
| Provide **temporary hinges** during construction, closed later | Common in concrete arches — the arch is completed at a chosen temperature |
| Choose a **deeper rise** | Reduces both the load thrust and the temperature sensitivity |

**The construction-hinge technique is worth knowing**: a concrete arch is often built with a temporary crown hinge and **closed at a specified temperature**, so that the locked-in thrust corresponds to a chosen mean condition rather than to whatever the weather happened to be on the day.
