examTip.trap: "No change, free to expand" would be right for a **THREE-hinged** arch, which is determinate. A two-hinged arch is indeterminate, so the restraint generates force.
examTip.trick: Apply the general rule: **an imposed deformation stresses an INDETERMINATE structure and leaves a DETERMINATE one unstressed.** Temperature, settlement, shrinkage and rib shortening are all imposed deformations.
examTip.mnemonic: **Temperature rise INCREASES H; rib shortening and abutment spread DECREASE it.** A **flatter** arch suffers doubly — larger load thrust (H ∝ 1/h) and greater temperature sensitivity. Concrete arches are often closed at a chosen temperature for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: For a bridge girder, the equivalent uniformly distributed load (EUDL) for a given train of loads is defined as the UDL which produces:
options: The same total load on the span
The same maximum bending moment (or shear) as the actual train
questions.solution:
**The UDL that produces the SAME maximum bending moment (or shear) as the actual train of loads.**

**Why it exists.** Positioning a train of wheel loads for the worst effect is laborious — every span length and every response quantity needs its own positioning calculation. The EUDL packages that work into a **single equivalent load** that can be applied directly.

> Codes tabulate EUDL against **span**, separately for **bending moment** and for **shear**, so the designer reads off one number instead of positioning a train.

**The critical point, and the reason for the bracket in the question:**

> **The EUDL for BENDING MOMENT and the EUDL for SHEAR are DIFFERENT**, because the two influence lines have different shapes and are maximised by different load positions.

> Using the moment EUDL to compute shear (or the reverse) is a real error, and the tables are printed in separate columns for precisely that reason.

**How it varies with span:**

| Span | EUDL behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Short** | **High** — a single heavy axle dominates, and it sits over the peak of the influence line |
| **Long** | **Falls toward the train's average intensity** — many axles spread across the span, averaging out |

> The physical reason is that a short span "sees" only one or two axles at the influence line's peak, while a long span sees the whole train and therefore something close to its mean load per metre.

**Related devices in bridge loading:**

| Concept | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **EUDL** | Replaces a train with an equivalent UDL |
| **IMPACT FACTOR** | Allows for the **dynamic** effect of a moving load — larger for **short** spans, where a single axle's arrival is abrupt |
| **Lane load** | A notional UDL plus a knife-edge load, positioned adversely |
| Reduction for multiple lanes | Recognises that all lanes are unlikely to be fully loaded at once |

**The impact factor follows the same span logic:**

> **Impact is greatest on SHORT spans**, because a single axle arriving on a short span is a sudden event relative to the structure's response time. IRC gives factors reducing with span, and they can add 25% or more to the static effect on a short span.

**In Nepali and Indian practice** the standard loadings are **IRC Class A, Class B, Class AA (tracked and wheeled) and 70R**, and each has its own EUDL and impact provisions. The design must consider **whichever produces the worst effect**, which is not always the heaviest vehicle — a tracked load spread over a long contact length can govern a short span while a wheeled load governs a longer one.

**The check that matters** when using tabulated values: confirm that the table is for the **right loading class, the right span, and the right response quantity**. Those three together are what makes the number meaningful, and taking a value from the wrong column is the commonest misuse.

**For hand verification**, the underlying method is always available: place the train on the influence line, compute **Σ W_i y_i**, and try the few positions that could govern. The EUDL is a convenience, not a different theory.

examTip.trap: **The EUDL for MOMENT and for SHEAR are different numbers**, because the two influence lines are maximised by different load positions. Codes print them in separate columns — taking a value from the wrong one is the commonest misuse.
examTip.trick: Remember the span trend: **EUDL and IMPACT are both HIGHEST on SHORT spans**, where a single axle dominates and its arrival is abrupt. On long spans both fall toward the train's average intensity.
examTip.mnemonic: **EUDL replaces the positioning calculation, not the theory.** The underlying method is always available: place the train on the influence line and maximise **Σ W_i y_i**.

questions.stem: A three-hinged parabolic arch has a span of 24 m and a rise of 4 m. It carries a UDL of 10 kN/m over the whole span. The horizontal thrust is:
questions.solution:
**180 kN.**

> **H = wL²/(8h) = 10 × 24²/(8 × 4) = 10 × 576/32 = 5760/32 = 180 kN** ✓

**Or by the general route**, which works for any loading:

> **H = M_crown(as a simple beam)/rise**
> **M_crown = wL²/8 = 10 × 576/8 = 720 kN·m**
> **H = 720/4 = 180 kN** ✓

**Both routes agree**, and the second is worth using because it generalises — the first is a shortcut valid only for a full UDL.

**The vertical reactions**, by symmetry:

> **V_A = V_B = wL/2 = 10 × 24/2 = 120 kN**

> Note that **120 kN is offered as a distractor** — it is the **vertical** reaction, not the thrust.

**The support reaction resultant:**

> **R = √(120² + 180²) = √(14 400 + 32 400) = √46 800 = 216 kN**, inclined at **tan⁻¹(120/180) = 33.7°** to the horizontal.

> The abutment must resist that **inclined** force — which is why arch abutments are massive and are shaped to deliver the resultant into the foundation without sliding.

**Check the rise-to-span ratio:**

> **h/L = 4/24 = 1/6** — a fairly shallow arch, which is why the thrust (180 kN) exceeds the vertical reaction (120 kN).

**How the thrust would change with the rise:**

| Rise h | h/L | H = wL²/8h |
|---|---|---|
| 2 m | 1/12 | **360 kN** |
| **4 m** | **1/6** | **180 kN** |
| 6 m | 1/4 | 120 kN |
| 12 m | 1/2 | 60 kN |

> **H ∝ 1/h** — halving the rise **doubles** the thrust. A flat arch is elegant and needs little headroom, but its abutments must be correspondingly heavier.

**And the bending moment in this arch:**

> Because it is a **parabola under a full UDL**, the shape is **funicular** for that loading, so **M_arch = 0 at every section** — the arch carries the load by **pure axial compression**.

> The axial thrust at the crown is simply **H = 180 kN** (horizontal there), rising toward the springings where it also carries the vertical component.

**The caution that goes with that result**: the zero-moment property holds **only for this loading**. Under **partial** loading — say the UDL over half the span — the arch is no longer funicular for the applied load, and bending moments appear. Those partial and asymmetric cases must be checked, and they are what determine the arch section's depth.

examTip.trap: **120 kN is the VERTICAL reaction (wL/2)**, offered as a thrust distractor. Read which force is asked for — the arch has both, and they are different.
examTip.trick: Use **H = M_crown/rise** rather than the wL²/8h shortcut: it works for **any** loading, and here M_crown = wL²/8 = 720, so H = 720/4 = **180 kN**.
examTip.mnemonic: **H ∝ 1/h — halve the rise, double the thrust.** Here h/L = 1/6, so H (180) exceeds V (120) and the abutment resultant is **216 kN at 33.7°**. And the parabola under full UDL carries **zero bending** — but only under that loading.

questions.stem: In the flexibility (force) method of analysis, the equations solved are:
options: Compatibility equations, with redundant forces as the unknowns
Equilibrium equations, with joint displacements as the unknowns
Yield criteria at the plastic hinges
questions.solution:
**Compatibility equations, with the redundant FORCES as the unknowns.**

**The procedure:**

1. Determine the degree of static indeterminacy **D_s**.
2. **Choose D_s redundants** and release them, leaving a stable **determinate primary structure**.
3. Analyse that primary structure under the **applied loads** → gives the displacements at the released points.
4. Analyse it under **unit values of each redundant** → gives the flexibility coefficients.
5. Write **compatibility**: the total displacement at each released point must equal its true value (usually **zero**).
6. Solve for the redundants.

> **The compatibility equation** for one redundant: **δ_load + R × δ_unit = 0**, giving **R = −δ_load/δ_unit**.

**The two families of method, side by side:**

| | **FLEXIBILITY (force)** | **STIFFNESS (displacement)** |
|---|---|---|
| Unknowns | **Redundant FORCES** | **Joint DISPLACEMENTS** |
| Equations | **COMPATIBILITY** | **EQUILIBRIUM** |
| Number of unknowns | **D_s** | **D_k** |
| Methods | Consistent deformation, **least work**, three-moment, column analogy | **Slope-deflection, moment distribution, MATRIX STIFFNESS** |
| Matrix | Flexibility **[f]**, symmetric | Stiffness **[k]**, symmetric |

> The two matrices are **inverses** of each other: **[k] = [f]⁻¹**. And both are **symmetric**, by Maxwell's reciprocal theorem — which is a useful arithmetic check on any hand calculation.

**Choosing the redundants** is the method's characteristic difficulty:

| Choice | Consequence |
|---|---|
| A **good** choice | The primary structure is easy to analyse; the coefficients are simple |
| A **poor** choice | The arithmetic becomes far worse, though the answer is the same |
| An **invalid** choice | The primary structure is **unstable** — a mechanism |

> **That the answer does not depend on the choice, but the labour does, is the flexibility method's signature.** Any valid set of releases gives the same final forces.

> **The releases must leave a STABLE structure.** Removing the wrong support can turn the primary structure into a mechanism, and the method then fails — which is a real trap when several supports could each be treated as redundant.

**Why modern practice uses stiffness methods instead:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **No choice required** | The stiffness method has no equivalent of "choosing the redundants" |
| **Systematic** | The structure is assembled from standard member stiffness matrices |
| **Easily PROGRAMMED** | Every commercial analysis package is a stiffness solver |
| Handles all structure types uniformly | Trusses, frames, grids, shells |

> The flexibility method's requirement for **judgement** is precisely what makes it hard to automate — and that, rather than any theoretical defect, is why it lost.

**Where the flexibility method still earns its place:**

> For a structure with **few redundants** (one or two), it is often the quickest route by hand — and it is conceptually transparent, which is why **propped cantilevers, two-hinged arches and single-redundant frames** are still taught this way.

**A worked illustration** — the propped cantilever under UDL:

> Release the prop. The cantilever's free-end deflection is **wL⁴/(8EI)** downward. A unit upward force there gives **L³/(3EI)**. Compatibility (net deflection zero):

> **wL⁴/(8EI) = R L³/(3EI)** → **R = 3wL/8** ✓

**Both conditions must always be satisfied** in any method: **equilibrium AND compatibility**. The two families differ only in which is used to generate the equations and which is satisfied automatically.

examTip.trick: Remember the pairing: **FORCE method → unknowns are FORCES → equations are COMPATIBILITY.** The stiffness method is the exact mirror: unknowns are displacements, equations are equilibrium.
examTip.trap: **The releases must leave a STABLE primary structure.** Removing the wrong support turns it into a mechanism and the method collapses — a real trap when several supports could each be called redundant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Any valid choice of redundants gives the same answer — only the LABOUR differs.** That need for judgement is exactly why the stiffness method, which requires none, won for computer analysis.

questions.stem: The slope-deflection equation for the end A of a member AB of length L and flexural rigidity EI is:
questions.solution:
**M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM_AB.**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **θ_A, θ_B** | Rotations of the two ends |
| **Δ** | **Relative TRANSVERSE displacement** of the ends (sway or settlement) |
| **FEM_AB** | **Fixed-end moment** at A due to the loads on the span |
| 2EI/L | The member's stiffness coefficient |

**The equation expresses one idea:** the end moment is the sum of what the **loads** would produce with both ends fixed (the FEM), plus the corrections for the ends actually **rotating** and **displacing**.

> **M = (what the loads do with fixed ends) + (what the joint movements do)**

**Why option (b) is the trap:** it is the **same equation with the Δ term omitted**, which is correct **only for a non-sway frame with unyielding supports**. Omitting Δ when the frame **sways** or a **support settles** is a genuine and serious error, and it is the commonest mistake in applying the method.

> **The 3Δ/L term is what carries sway and settlement into the analysis.** Without it, a sway frame cannot be solved at all.

**Note the coefficients:**

> **2θ_A + θ_B** — the **near end counts double**. That is why the member's own end stiffness is **4EI/L** while the **carry-over** to the far end is **2EI/L**, a ratio of **½**.

**The procedure:**

1. Compute the **fixed-end moments** for every member.
2. Write a slope-deflection equation for **each member end**.
3. Write **equilibrium** at each joint: **ΣM = 0** (the moments at a rigid joint must balance).
4. For a **sway** frame, add a **shear (sway) equation** for each independent sway degree of freedom.
5. Solve the simultaneous equations for the unknown θ and Δ.
6. Back-substitute to get the end moments.

**It is a DISPLACEMENT method**, so its unknowns are the **joint rotations and sways** — that is, **D_k** of them, not D_s.

**Standard fixed-end moments**, needed at step 1:

| Loading | FEM at each end |
|---|---|
| **UDL w** | **wL²/12** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8** |
| **Point load W at a from left** | **Wab²/L²** (left), **Wa²b/L²** (right) |
| Couple M at midspan | M/4 |
| Triangular, zero to w | wL²/30 and wL²/20 |

> For an **off-centre** point load the two FEMs are **unequal**, and the **larger one is at the NEARER support** — intuitive once seen, easy to reverse under pressure.

**Relation to moment distribution:**

> **Moment distribution is an ITERATIVE solution of the same slope-deflection equations.** Instead of solving the simultaneous equations directly, it releases and re-fixes each joint in turn until the moments balance. Hardy Cross's insight was that the iteration converges quickly and needs no simultaneous equations at all — which made frame analysis possible by hand.

**For a settling support**, Δ is the settlement itself, and the induced moments follow directly — which is how the standard result **M = 6EIδ/L²** for a fixed beam is obtained: set θ_A = θ_B = 0 and Δ = δ in the equation.

examTip.trap: Option (b) is the **same equation with the Δ term dropped** — valid only for a **non-sway** frame with **unyielding** supports. Omitting 3Δ/L when the frame sways or a support settles makes the analysis impossible, and it is the classic error.
examTip.trick: Read the coefficients: **2θ_A + θ_B** means the **near end counts double** — which is exactly why end stiffness is **4EI/L** and the carry-over is **2EI/L**, a ratio of **½**.
examTip.mnemonic: **M = (fixed-end moment from the LOADS) + (correction for the JOINTS moving).** Set θ = 0 and Δ = δ and it gives the standard settlement moment **6EIδ/L²** directly.

questions.stem: In the moment distribution method, the distribution factor for a member at a joint is the ratio of:
options: Its stiffness to the sum of the stiffnesses of all members meeting at that joint
Its length to the total length of members at the joint
Its fixed-end moment to the total fixed-end moment
Its second moment of area to the sum of all second moments
questions.solution:
**Its stiffness divided by the SUM of the stiffnesses of all members meeting at that joint.**

> **DF = k / Σk**, and therefore **the distribution factors at any joint SUM TO 1** — a useful arithmetic check at every step.

**Why stiffness and not length or I alone:** the unbalanced moment at a joint is shared among the members in proportion to how **stiff** each is against rotation. Stiffness depends on **both** I and L, so neither alone will do.

> **k = 4EI/L** when the **far end is FIXED**
> **k = 3EI/L** when the **far end is HINGED**

**The four numbers that constitute the whole method:**

| Quantity | Far end fixed | Far end hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **Stiffness k** | **4EI/L** | **3EI/L** |
| **Carry-over factor** | **½** | **ZERO** |

> **Using 3EI/L for a hinged far end, with zero carry-over, saves an entire round of iteration** — because nothing is carried over to a pin, which cannot hold a moment anyway. It is the standard simplification for a simply supported end span.

**The procedure:**

1. Compute **fixed-end moments** for every member, assuming all joints locked.
2. Compute **distribution factors** at each free joint.
3. **Release** one joint: distribute the unbalanced moment among its members in proportion to DF, with **opposite sign** to the imbalance.
4. **Carry over half** of each distributed moment to the far end.
5. Re-lock, move to the next joint, repeat.
6. Continue until the carried-over moments are negligible; **sum each column**.

**Why it converges quickly:** each cycle reduces the imbalance by roughly a factor determined by the carry-over, so **three or four cycles** usually give engineering accuracy. That rapid convergence is what made hand analysis of multi-storey frames practical before computers.

**What the method is doing conceptually:**

> It is an **iterative solution of the slope-deflection equations** — releasing and re-fixing each joint in turn instead of solving all the simultaneous equations at once. Hardy Cross's contribution was noticing that the iteration converges fast enough to be done by hand.

**Arithmetic checks worth applying:**

| Check | Statement |
|---|---|
| **DFs at each joint sum to 1** | Catches a stiffness error immediately |
| **Final moments at each joint sum to zero** | Equilibrium is satisfied |
| A **fixed support** has **DF = 0** | It absorbs moment without rotating |
| A **pinned end** has **DF = 1** | It cannot hold any moment |

**For a SWAY frame** the method needs an extra stage:

> Analyse first with sway **prevented** (an artificial prop), find the **prop force**, then analyse for an arbitrary sway with no loads, and **scale and superpose** so the artificial prop force is cancelled.

> That two-stage process is where moment distribution becomes laborious, and it is the point at which matrix methods take over.

**Sign convention** must be fixed at the outset and held: the usual choice is **clockwise moments on the member ends positive**. Mixing conventions mid-calculation is the reliable way to produce a wrong answer that looks plausible.

examTip.trick: **The distribution factors at every joint must sum to 1.** Check it before distributing anything — it catches a stiffness error in one glance.
examTip.trap: Stiffness depends on **both I and L** (k = 4EI/L), so neither "length ratio" nor "I ratio" alone is right. And use **3EI/L with ZERO carry-over** for a hinged far end — it saves a whole cycle.
examTip.mnemonic: **Four numbers run the method: 4EI/L and 3EI/L for stiffness, ½ and 0 for carry-over.** Distribute in proportion to stiffness, carry over half, repeat — three or four cycles is usually enough.

questions.stem: The carry-over factor for a prismatic member whose far end is fixed is:
questions.solution:
**0.5** — half of the moment applied at the near end is carried over to the far end.

**Where it comes from.** Apply a moment M at end A of a member with end B **fixed**, and solve the slope-deflection equations with **θ_B = 0**:

> **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A) = 4EIθ_A/L**
> **M_BA = (2EI/L)(θ_A) = 2EIθ_A/L**

> **M_BA/M_AB = 2/4 = ½** ✓

**The two cases:**

| Far end | Stiffness | Carry-over factor |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** | **½** |
| **HINGED** | **3EI/L** | **ZERO** |

**Why a hinged far end carries over nothing** is worth understanding rather than memorising:

> A **pin cannot hold a moment**. So there is nothing to carry over — and the near end is correspondingly less stiff (3EI/L rather than 4EI/L), because the far end rotates freely instead of resisting.

> **Using 3EI/L with zero carry-over for a simply supported end span saves an entire cycle of the distribution**, and it is the standard simplification.

**The two numbers work together in every cycle:**

1. **Distribute** the unbalanced moment in proportion to **stiffness**.
2. **Carry over** half of each distributed moment to the far end.
3. That carried-over moment becomes a new imbalance at the far joint, which is then distributed in turn.

> **The carry-over factor of ½ is what makes the method converge.** Each cycle passes on only half of what it distributed, so the residuals fall geometrically and **three or four cycles** normally give engineering accuracy.

**Sign**: the carried-over moment has the **SAME sign** as the distributed moment that produced it, under the usual clockwise-positive convention. That is easy to get wrong and produces a plausible but incorrect answer.

**A useful special case** — the **symmetrical structure symmetrically loaded**:

> Members on the axis of symmetry can be given modified stiffnesses (**2EI/L** for symmetry, **6EI/L** for antisymmetry) and analysed on **half the structure**, halving the work.

**A non-prismatic member** has a different carry-over factor, and it is generally **not ½** and **not the same in both directions** — a haunched beam carries over more toward its stiffer end. Tabulated coefficients exist for standard haunch shapes, and this is one of the situations where matrix methods are markedly simpler.

**The relation to the stiffness matrix**: the member stiffness matrix for a beam element contains exactly these terms — **4EI/L** and **2EI/L** on the rotational diagonal and off-diagonal. The carry-over factor is simply the ratio of the off-diagonal to the diagonal term, so moment distribution and matrix analysis are the same physics in different bookkeeping.

examTip.trick: Derive it rather than recall it: with θ_B = 0, **M_AB = 4EIθ/L** and **M_BA = 2EIθ/L**, so the ratio is **½**. The same two numbers are the diagonal and off-diagonal of the beam stiffness matrix.
examTip.trap: A **HINGED** far end carries over **ZERO** — a pin cannot hold a moment. Its stiffness drops to **3EI/L** to match. Using 4EI/L and ½ for a simply supported end span wastes a whole cycle and gives wrong intermediate values.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ½ is what makes it converge** — each cycle passes on only half of what it distributed, so residuals fall geometrically and three or four cycles suffice.

questions.stem: In a fixed beam of span L, if one support settles by an amount δ relative to the other, the moment induced at each end is:
questions.solution:
**M = 6EIδ/L²** at each end.

**Derive it from the slope-deflection equation** with both ends fixed (θ_A = θ_B = 0) and a relative displacement Δ = δ:

> **M = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) = (2EI/L)(−3δ/L) = −6EIδ/L²** ✓

**Compare with a PROPPED cantilever**, where one end is pinned:

> **M = 3EIδ/L²** — exactly **half**, because the pinned end offers no rotational restraint.

> Option (a), 3EIδ/L², is therefore the propped-cantilever value offered as a distractor. And **12EIδ/L³** is the **FORCE** (shear) required to produce the settlement, not the moment — check the units to reject it.

**The magnitude is the point of the question.** Take a realistic case: a 6 m beam of 300 × 500 mm concrete (I = 3125 × 10⁶ mm⁴, E = 25 000 N/mm²) with a **10 mm** settlement:

> **M = 6 × 25 000 × 3125 × 10⁶ × 10/(6000)² = 4.69 × 10¹⁴/3.6 × 10⁷ = 13 kN·m**

> Against a design moment of perhaps 90 kN·m, that is **14% of the design moment from 10 mm of settlement** — and settlements of that order are entirely ordinary.

**The general principle:**

> **An imposed deformation stresses an INDETERMINATE structure and leaves a DETERMINATE one unstressed.**

| Structure | Effect of settlement |
|---|---|
| **Determinate** (simply supported, three-hinged arch, Gerber beam) | **NO stress** — it simply moves |
| **Indeterminate** (fixed, continuous, two-hinged arch) | **Stresses induced** |

**Note the L² in the denominator**, which has a practical consequence:

> **M ∝ 1/L²** — so a **SHORT span is far more sensitive** to differential settlement than a long one. A 3 m beam suffers **four times** the moment of a 6 m beam for the same settlement.

> That is why short, stiff members between separately founded elements are particularly vulnerable, and why a **movement joint** is often better than trying to design for the moment.

**What relieves the effect in practice:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **CREEP** in concrete | Relaxes settlement-induced moments substantially over time — the effective E falls |
| Cracking | Reduces I, and hence the induced moment |
| Gradual settlement | Allows creep to keep pace |
| A **movement joint** | Removes the restraint entirely |

> **Creep is the reason concrete structures tolerate settlement better than the elastic calculation suggests** — a slowly developing settlement induces perhaps half the elastic moment. A **sudden** settlement gets no such relief.

**The design responses**, in order of preference:

1. **Prevent the differential settlement** — proportion footings for **equal settlement**, not equal pressure.
2. **Tie the structure together** with a raft, so it settles as one body.
3. **Separate** the parts with a movement joint.
4. **Design for the induced moments** — the last resort, since the settlement is rarely known accurately.

> **Never mix foundation types under one structure** — piles under part and pads under the rest will settle differentially however carefully each is designed, because their mechanisms and timescales differ entirely.

examTip.trap: **3EIδ/L² is the PROPPED CANTILEVER value** — exactly half, because a pinned end gives no rotational restraint. And **12EIδ/L³ is a FORCE**, not a moment; the units reject it instantly.
examTip.trick: Get it from slope-deflection by setting **θ = 0 and Δ = δ**: M = (2EI/L)(−3δ/L) = **6EIδ/L²**. No separate formula to remember.
examTip.mnemonic: **M ∝ 1/L², so SHORT spans are far more settlement-sensitive** — a 3 m beam suffers four times a 6 m beam's moment. In concrete, **creep relaxes about half** of a slowly developing settlement moment; a sudden settlement gets no relief.

questions.stem: Clapeyron's theorem of three moments relates the bending moments at:
options: Three consecutive supports of a continuous beam
The three hinges of an arch
Three points on a single simply supported span
The three members meeting at a rigid joint
questions.solution:
**Three consecutive supports of a continuous beam.**

> **M_A L₁ + 2M_B(L₁ + L₂) + M_C L₂ + 6A₁x̄₁/L₁ + 6A₂x̄₂/L₂ = 0**

where **A₁, A₂** are the areas of the simply supported bending moment diagrams for the two spans and **x̄₁, x̄₂** the distances of their centroids from the respective outer supports.

**What the equation expresses:** the **continuity of slope** over the intermediate support B. The beam is continuous there, so the slope computed from the left span must equal the slope computed from the right span — and imposing that gives the relation.

> It is therefore a **FORCE (flexibility) method**: the unknowns are the **support moments**, and the equations are **compatibility**.

**Using it:**

> For a beam with **n** intermediate supports, write the equation at **each** of them, giving **n** simultaneous equations in the **n** unknown support moments.

| Beam | Equations needed |
|---|---|
| Two spans (one interior support) | **1** — solved directly |
| Three spans | 2 |
| Four spans | 3 |

**Handling the end conditions:**

| End | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **M = 0** at that support |
| **Overhanging** | M at the support = the moment from the overhang, computed by statics |
| **FIXED** | Add an **imaginary span of zero length** beyond it, which supplies the extra equation |

> **The zero-length imaginary span is the standard device** for a fixed end, and it is the part most often forgotten.

**For settlement**, the theorem extends by adding displacement terms:

> **… + 6E I (δ₁/L₁ + δ₂/L₂)** — which is how settlement effects enter a continuous beam analysis by this route.

**Where it sits among the methods:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Three-moment theorem** | **Force** method; neat for **continuous BEAMS**; poor for frames |
| **Moment distribution** | Displacement method; iterative; **excellent by hand** for beams **and frames** |
| **Slope-deflection** | Displacement method; simultaneous equations; handles sway |
| **Matrix stiffness** | The general, programmable method |

> The three-moment theorem's limitation is that it applies naturally only to **beams**, not to frames — because it is built on the continuity of a single line of members. Moment distribution superseded it for general work precisely because it handles frames and sway.

**Its enduring advantage** is that for a **two-span** or **three-span** continuous beam it gives the answer in one or two equations with no iteration — quicker than setting up a distribution table.

**A worked check** worth carrying: for **two equal spans L** carrying a **UDL w**, with simply supported ends, the theorem gives the interior support moment as **wL²/8** — and the resulting span moment is **9wL²/128**. Those are the standard two-span results, and reproducing them is the fastest verification that the equation has been set up correctly.

examTip.trick: It enforces **continuity of SLOPE** over the intermediate support — which is why it is a compatibility (force) method with the **support moments** as unknowns.
examTip.trap: For a **FIXED end**, add an **imaginary span of ZERO length** beyond it to supply the extra equation. Forgetting that device is the standard failure, and the beam then appears to have too few equations.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check with two equal spans under UDL: interior support moment wL²/8, span moment 9wL²/128.** Reproducing those confirms the setup. The theorem suits **beams only** — moment distribution took over because it handles frames and sway.

questions.stem: The influence line for a response quantity in a continuous beam is:
questions.solution:
**A CURVE**, because the structure is statically indeterminate.

**Why the shape differs from a determinate beam's:**

| Structure | Influence line | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **DETERMINATE** | **Straight segments** | Statics alone gives the response, and it varies **linearly** with load position |
| **INDETERMINATE** | **CURVED** | The response depends on the **relative stiffnesses**, and the released structure deflects as a curve |

> **Müller-Breslau makes this immediate**: the influence line has the shape of the **deflected form** when the corresponding restraint is released. For a determinate structure that released shape is made of **straight segments**; for an indeterminate one it is a **flexural curve**.

**The practical consequence:**

> An indeterminate influence line **cannot be obtained by statics**. Its ordinates require a full analysis at each load position, or a stiffness-based computation.

> **But the SHAPE can still be sketched qualitatively** — and that alone identifies the **critical load positions and patterns**, which is usually all the designer needs before handing the numbers to software.

**The pattern-loading rules come directly from those sketched shapes:**

> Sketch the released shape for a **sagging moment in one span** of a continuous beam. It is **positive in that span**, **negative in the adjacent spans**, and **positive again beyond** — an alternating pattern that dies away with distance.

| To maximise | Load pattern |
|---|---|
| **Sagging** moment in a span | That span **plus ALTERNATE** spans |
| **Hogging** moment at a support | The **TWO ADJACENT** spans, plus alternate ones beyond |
| **Reaction** at a support | The adjacent spans |
| **Shear** at a section | One side of it |

> **Loading every span is NOT the worst case.** Because the influence line is **negative in the adjacent spans**, loading them **partly cancels** the response — which is the whole reason pattern loading exists as a code requirement (IS 456 cl. 22.4.1).

**Why alternate-span loading increases the sagging moment**, in physical terms:

> An **unloaded adjacent span** provides **less rotational restraint** at the shared support. The loaded span's end therefore rotates more freely, it behaves more like a simply supported beam, and its **midspan sagging moment increases**.

**Dead load cannot be patterned** — it is permanent and acts on every span. Only the **live (imposed)** load is varied.

**The result is a design ENVELOPE:**

> Each pattern gives one bending moment diagram. The design must satisfy the **worst value at every section across ALL cases**, so the diagrams are superimposed and the outer envelope taken.

**Two consequences of the envelope, both practical:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| A section may need **BOTH top and bottom steel** | Because its moment is hogging in one case and sagging in another |
| The **points of contraflexure MOVE** between cases | So reinforcement curtailment must follow the **envelope**, never a single analysis |

> That second point is why IS 456's curtailment rules carry generous margins — bars must extend a **development length beyond** the theoretical cut-off, and at least **d or 12φ** past it.

**A code simplification**: for beams of approximately equal span carrying substantially uniform load, IS 456 cl. 22.5.1 permits **tabulated coefficients** (wL²/12 at the first interior support, wL²/16 in the end span, and so on) which already embody the pattern-loading envelope — avoiding the analysis entirely for standard cases.

examTip.trick: **Müller-Breslau settles it in one sketch**: release the restraint and draw the deflected shape. A **determinate** structure releases into **straight segments**; an **indeterminate** one into a **flexural curve**.
examTip.trap: The influence line is **NOT always positive** — it alternates in sign across successive spans, which is exactly why **loading every span is not the worst case** and why alternate-span patterns govern.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sagging in a span: that span + ALTERNATE spans. Hogging at a support: the TWO ADJACENT spans.** Dead load on everything; only live load is patterned. The result is an **envelope**, so some sections need both top and bottom steel.

questions.stem: In the matrix stiffness method, the global stiffness matrix of a structure is:
options: Symmetric, and assembled from the individual member stiffness matrices
Rectangular, with one row per member
questions.solution:
**Symmetric, and assembled from the individual member stiffness matrices.**

**The method in outline:**

1. Form each **member stiffness matrix** in its own local coordinates.
2. **Transform** each to global coordinates.
3. **Assemble** them into the global matrix by adding each member's contribution into the rows and columns corresponding to its degrees of freedom.
4. Apply the **boundary conditions** (delete or restrain the fixed degrees of freedom).
5. Solve **[K]{d} = {F}** for the displacements.
6. Back-substitute to get the member forces.

**Why it is SYMMETRIC:**

> By **Maxwell's reciprocal theorem**, **k_ij = k_ji** for any linear elastic structure. That symmetry is not a coincidence of the arithmetic but a theorem — and it is a **useful check** on any matrix assembled by hand.

**Why it is SINGULAR before boundary conditions are applied**, and not after:

> An unrestrained structure can undergo **rigid body motion** — translation and rotation with no force. That means [K] has no unique solution, so it is singular.

> **Applying the supports removes those rigid body modes** and makes the matrix invertible. Option (c) is therefore half right and, as stated, wrong: the **restrained** matrix is not singular.

**The beam element stiffness matrix** contains the terms already met in moment distribution:

> **4EI/L** and **2EI/L** on the rotational diagonal and off-diagonal — which is exactly why the **carry-over factor is their ratio, ½**.

> **Moment distribution and matrix stiffness are the same physics in different bookkeeping.**

**Properties of the assembled matrix:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Symmetric** | k_ij = k_ji (Maxwell) |
| **Banded / sparse** | Only members sharing a joint interact, so most entries are zero |
| **Positive definite** (after restraints) | Because strain energy is positive |
| **Singular** (before restraints) | Rigid body modes |
| **Size = D_k** | One equation per degree of freedom |

> The **banded structure** is what makes large models tractable: a building with 10 000 degrees of freedom has a matrix of 10⁸ entries, of which only a small fraction are non-zero, and solvers exploit that ruthlessly.

**Why the stiffness method dominates modern practice:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **SYSTEMATIC** — no judgement required | Unlike the flexibility method, which needs the redundants to be **chosen** |
| **Easily PROGRAMMED** | Every commercial package is a stiffness solver |
| Handles **all structure types** uniformly | Trusses, frames, grids, plates, shells |
| Extends naturally to **dynamics and non-linearity** | [M]{ü} + [C]{u̇} + [K]{u} = {F} |

> **The absence of judgement is the decisive advantage.** A flexibility method requires someone to choose a valid, convenient set of redundants — which is exactly what a computer cannot do.

**The relationship to flexibility:**

> **[K] = [F]⁻¹** — the stiffness and flexibility matrices are **inverses**, and both are symmetric. They are two descriptions of the same structure.

**A caution about output**: because the method is systematic, it is easy to run and hard to sanity-check. The disciplines that matter are **checking the deflected shape looks plausible**, **verifying overall equilibrium** (do the reactions sum to the applied load?), and **spot-checking one member by hand**. A model with a wrong restraint or a disconnected node produces confident nonsense.

examTip.trick: **Symmetry follows from Maxwell's reciprocal theorem** (k_ij = k_ji) — so checking that a hand-assembled matrix is symmetric catches errors immediately.
examTip.trap: It is **singular BEFORE the boundary conditions are applied** (rigid body modes exist) and **non-singular after**. Option (c) states half the truth and is wrong as written.
examTip.mnemonic: **The beam element's 4EI/L and 2EI/L are exactly moment distribution's stiffness and carry-over** — same physics, different bookkeeping. And always sanity-check output: deflected shape, overall equilibrium, one member by hand.

questions.stem: The degree of static indeterminacy of a continuous beam on five simple supports, with no internal hinges, is:
questions.solution:
**3.**

> **D_s = r − 3 − (number of internal hinges)**

> Five simple supports give **five vertical reaction components**, plus one horizontal restraint at the pin — but for a beam analysed for vertical loads the standard count is:

> **D_s = (number of supports) − 2 = 5 − 2 = 3** ✓

**The general rule for a continuous beam:**

| Supports | D_s |
|---|---|
| 2 (simply supported) | **0 — determinate** |
| 3 | 1 |
| 4 | 2 |
| **5** | **3** |
| n | **n − 2** |

> Equivalently, **D_s equals the number of INTERIOR supports** — because each one beyond the first two is a redundant restraint.

**Checking against the standard cases:**

| Beam | D_s |
|---|---|
| Simply supported | **0** |
| Cantilever | **0** |
| Overhanging | **0** |
| **Propped cantilever** | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | **3** |
| Continuous, 3 spans (4 supports) | **2** |

> **A fixed end counts as three restraints** (H, V, M) rather than one, which is why a fixed beam reaches D_s = 3 with only two supports.

**Each internal HINGE reduces D_s by one**, because it supplies the condition **M = 0**:

| Beam | D_s |
|---|---|
| Fixed both ends | 3 |
| Fixed both ends, **1 hinge** | 2 |
| Fixed both ends, **2 hinges** | 1 |
| Fixed both ends, **3 hinges** | **0 — determinate** |

> That is the principle behind **GERBER (hinged) beams**: insert the right number of hinges in the right places and a continuous beam becomes **determinate**.

**Why anyone would want that:**

> A determinate structure develops **no self-stress** — settlement, temperature, shrinkage and lack of fit produce **movement but no force**. An indeterminate one **resists** the movement and stresses itself doing so.

> The hinges are placed at the **natural points of contraflexure** of the equivalent continuous beam, so the moment distribution is essentially unchanged while the settlement sensitivity disappears.

**The trade-off, once more:**

| | **Determinate** | **Indeterminate** |
|---|---|---|
| Settlement, temperature | **No stress** | **Stresses induced** |
| **Redundancy** | **NONE** — one failure is collapse | **Alternative load paths** |
| Material efficiency | Lower | **Higher** — moments shared, peaks reduced |
| Deflections | Larger | Smaller |

**Which method to use for D_s = 3:**

| Method | Suitability |
|---|---|
| **Three-moment theorem** | 3 equations — workable |
| **Moment distribution** | **Excellent** — iterative, no simultaneous equations |
| Slope-deflection | 3 unknown rotations |
| Matrix stiffness | The general answer |

> Note that **D_k** here (the joint rotations at the three interior supports, neglecting axial deformation) is also **3** — so neither family has an advantage on count, and **moment distribution wins on convenience** for hand calculation.

**A stability caution applies as always**: the count checks **degree, not stability**. A beam with all its reactions parallel and no horizontal restraint is unstable horizontally regardless of what the vertical count says.

examTip.trick: For a continuous beam, **D_s = (number of supports) − 2**, which is the same as the **number of INTERIOR supports**. Five supports, three interior, D_s = 3.
examTip.trap: A **FIXED end counts as THREE restraints** (H, V, M), not one — which is why a fixed beam with only two supports reaches D_s = 3. And each **internal hinge subtracts one**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three hinges in a fixed beam make it DETERMINATE — that is a Gerber beam.** Place them at the natural contraflexure points and you keep continuity's efficiency while losing its settlement sensitivity.

questions.stem: IS 456 permits the elastic bending moments in a continuous beam to be redistributed by a maximum of:
questions.solution:
**30%**, subject to conditions.

**What redistribution is.** A **ductile** reinforced concrete section, having reached its capacity, **continues to rotate without losing strength**. The moment it cannot take is shed to less-stressed parts of the structure, which then carry more than the elastic analysis predicted.

> **The structure does not fail when the first section reaches its elastic moment** — it redistributes, and collapse requires enough hinges to form a mechanism.

**The conditions (IS 456 cl. 37.1.1):**

| Condition | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Equilibrium must be maintained** | The redistributed diagram must still be statically valid |
| Redistribution **≤ 30%** | Limits the plastic rotation demanded |
| **x_u/d ≤ 0.6 − δM/100** | Ensures the section is **ductile enough to rotate** |
| Applies to the **ultimate limit state only** | Serviceability checks use the **elastic** moments |

**The x_u/d condition is the essential safeguard**, and it is the one most often overlooked:

> Redistribution requires **plastic rotation** at the yielding section. Only an **UNDER-REINFORCED** section — with the neutral axis high — can supply it. An **over-reinforced** section fails by **concrete crushing without rotating**, so redistribution assumed but not delivered is a genuine hazard.

> The formula makes the link explicit: the more you redistribute, the **lower the permitted x_u/d**, and the more ductile the section must be.

**Why redistribution is useful in practice** — it is a detailing tool as much as an economy:

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduces the peak HOGGING moments at supports** | Where reinforcement from two spans meets and congestion is worst |
| Allows a **more uniform** distribution of steel | Easier to fix, easier to place concrete |
| Can **equalise** span and support moments | Simplifies detailing |
| Modest material saving | Secondary |

> **Relieving support congestion is the real motive.** At an interior support the top steel from both spans must pass through the same region, and reducing that moment by 20–30% can be the difference between a buildable detail and a congested one.

**The related concept — PLASTIC ANALYSIS** in steel:

> Steel structures take this further: **plastic analysis** assumes full redistribution until a **collapse MECHANISM** forms, and the collapse load is found by equating **external work to internal work at the hinges**.

| Structure | Hinges needed for a mechanism |
|---|---|
| Simply supported beam | **1** |
| Propped cantilever | **2** |
| Fixed beam | **3** |
| General | **D_s + 1** |

> **The number of hinges to form a mechanism is D_s + 1** — the structure must first be reduced to determinacy, then one more hinge makes it a mechanism.

**Why concrete is limited to 30% while steel permits full plastic analysis:**

> **Steel has a long yield plateau and enormous rotation capacity.** **Concrete's rotation capacity is limited** by the concrete's crushing strain, and it depends on the reinforcement percentage, the confinement, and the steel grade. The 30% cap is a conservative bound on what a normally detailed RC section can reliably deliver.

**A caution**: redistribution changes the **shape** of the moment diagram, so the **points of contraflexure move**. Reinforcement curtailment must be based on the **redistributed** diagram, and the shear must be checked for the redistributed condition too — which is a step sometimes forgotten.

examTip.trick: The real motive is **detailing, not economy**: cutting the peak **hogging** moment at an interior support relieves the reinforcement congestion where top steel from two spans meets.
examTip.trap: Redistribution demands **plastic rotation**, which only an **UNDER-reinforced** section can supply — hence the **x_u/d ≤ 0.6 − δM/100** condition. Assuming redistribution in an over-reinforced section is a real hazard: it crushes without rotating.
examTip.mnemonic: **30% in concrete; steel permits full plastic analysis** because it has a long yield plateau. Number of hinges to form a mechanism is **D_s + 1**.

questions.stem: For a two-span continuous beam of equal spans L carrying a uniformly distributed load w, with simply supported ends, the bending moment at the central support is:
questions.solution:
**wL²/8** (hogging) at the central support.

**Derive it by the three-moment theorem.** With M_A = M_C = 0 (simply supported ends) and both spans equal:

> **2M_B(L + L) + 6A₁x̄₁/L + 6A₂x̄₂/L = 0**

> For a UDL the simply supported BMD is a parabola of area **A = (2/3)L(wL²/8) = wL³/12**, with its centroid at **L/2**:

> **4M_B L + 2 × 6(wL³/12)(L/2)/L = 0**
> **4M_B L + wL³/2 = 0**
> **M_B = −wL²/8** ✓ (the minus sign indicating hogging)

**The full set of results for this beam:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Moment at central support** | **wL²/8** (hogging) |
| **Maximum sagging moment in each span** | **9wL²/128** at **0.375L** from the outer support |
| **End reactions** | **3wL/8** each |
| **Central reaction** | **10wL/8 = 1.25wL** |

> **Check the reactions**: 3wL/8 + 10wL/8 + 3wL/8 = 16wL/8 = **2wL** ✓ — the total load on two spans.

**The central reaction is worth noting**: at **1.25wL** it is **more than twice** either end reaction. Load flows toward stiffness, and the central support is the stiffest point of the beam.

**Comparison with two separate simply supported spans:**

| | **Two simple spans** | **Continuous** |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum moment | **wL²/8** (sagging, at midspan) | **wL²/8** (hogging, at support) |
| Span moment | wL²/8 | **9wL²/128 = 0.0703 wL²** |
| Central reaction | wL | **1.25 wL** |

> **The peak moment magnitude is the SAME**, but continuity **moves it from midspan to the support** and **reduces the span moment by 44%**. That relocation is often the practical benefit — a deeper section is usually available over a support (where a column or wall is), and the span steel is reduced.

**Note the trap in the distractors**: **wL²/12** is the fixed-ended beam's support moment, and **wL²/16** is a coefficient from IS 456's continuous beam table for a different span and support condition. Both are real values in adjacent contexts.

**IS 456's tabulated coefficients** (cl. 22.5.1) for beams of approximately equal span under substantially uniform load already embody the pattern-loading envelope:

| Location | Dead load coefficient | Live load coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| **Near middle of END span** | **wL²/12** | wL²/10 |
| **At FIRST interior support** | **wL²/10** | wL²/9 |
| At middle of interior span | wL²/16 | wL²/12 |
| At other interior supports | wL²/12 | wL²/9 |

> Those coefficients differ from the exact two-span values because they cover **three or more spans** and include the **pattern-loading** envelope — which is why an exact analysis of a specific beam and a coefficient from the table need not agree.

**Pattern loading matters here too**: loading **only one span** of the two-span beam gives a **larger sagging moment** in that span than loading both, because the unloaded span offers less rotational restraint at the central support.

examTip.trap: **wL²/12 is the FIXED-ended beam's support moment** and **wL²/16 is an IS 456 coefficient** for a different case. All three are real values in adjacent contexts, so read which beam is described.
examTip.trick: Check the reactions: **3wL/8 + 10wL/8 + 3wL/8 = 2wL** ✓. The central reaction at **1.25wL** is more than twice an end reaction — load flows toward stiffness.
examTip.mnemonic: **Continuity does not reduce the PEAK moment here — it MOVES it from midspan to the support** and cuts the span moment by 44% (to 9wL²/128). The relocation is the benefit, since a deeper section is usually available over a support.

questions.stem: In the analysis of a sway frame by moment distribution, the additional step required compared with a non-sway frame is:
questions.solution:
**A separate SWAY analysis, scaled and superposed so that the artificial restraining force is cancelled.**

**The two-stage procedure:**

**Stage 1 — sway prevented.**
> Insert an imaginary **horizontal prop** at the beam level. Distribute the moments as for a non-sway frame. Then compute the **prop force R** required to hold the frame — from the horizontal equilibrium of the columns, using their shears.

**Stage 2 — sway only.**
> Remove the loads. Impose an **arbitrary sway Δ′**, which generates fixed-end moments **−6EIΔ′/L²** in each column. Distribute those. Compute the horizontal force **R′** that this sway corresponds to.

**Superpose.**
> Scale stage 2 by the factor **k = −R/R′** so that the artificial prop force is exactly cancelled, then **add** the two sets of moments.

> **Final moments = (stage 1) + k × (stage 2)**

**Why the artificial prop is needed at all:**

> Moment distribution balances **joint moments**, but sway is a **translation**, not a rotation. The method cannot generate it. Propping the frame removes the sway degree of freedom so the ordinary distribution can proceed — and the second stage puts it back.

**The sway fixed-end moments** come straight from slope-deflection with θ = 0:

> **M = −6EIΔ/L²** at both ends of each column, of the **same sign** (both hogging or both sagging), because the column bends in **double curvature**.

**When a frame sways:**

| Condition | Sways? |
|---|---|
| **Braced** (shear wall, cross-bracing, rigid core) | **No** |
| **Unbraced** with lateral load | **Yes** |
| **Unbraced** with **unsymmetrical loading or geometry** | **YES** — even under purely vertical load |
| Symmetrical frame, symmetrical vertical load | No |

> **That third row is the trap**: an unbraced frame with **unequal spans, unequal column stiffnesses, or asymmetric vertical loading** will sway under gravity load alone. Assuming no sway because there is no horizontal load is a real error.

**Multiple sway degrees of freedom:**

> A **multi-storey** frame has **one sway degree of freedom per storey**, so an n-storey frame needs **n** sway cases plus the non-sway case, and the superposition becomes a set of simultaneous equations in the scaling factors.

> **That is where moment distribution becomes genuinely laborious**, and it is the point at which matrix stiffness methods take over decisively — a stiffness solver treats sway as just another degree of freedom, with no special procedure at all.

**The P–Δ consequence** must be checked separately:

> Once the frame has swayed by Δ, the **gravity load P acts at that eccentricity**, adding a moment **PΔ** which increases Δ further. The response **amplifies**, so **superposition itself breaks down** and a **second-order analysis** or a moment magnifier is required.

> Note the irony: the sway analysis above **relies on superposition**, which the P–Δ effect then invalidates. For slender frames the first-order result must be amplified afterwards.

**The design lesson**: an **unbraced frame's columns have effective lengths GREATER than their actual length** (1.2L to 2.0L or more). Since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, bracing a frame can **quadruple** its column capacity — which is why shear walls and bracing are so structurally valuable, and why they are almost always cheaper than the columns they save.

examTip.trick: Moment distribution balances **rotations**, not **translations** — so sway must be propped out, analysed separately, and superposed. The scaling factor is **k = −R/R′**, chosen to cancel the artificial prop force.
examTip.trap: An unbraced frame sways under **purely vertical load** if the geometry or loading is **unsymmetrical**. Assuming no sway because there is no horizontal load is a genuine and common error.
examTip.mnemonic: **One sway degree of freedom per STOREY** — which is where moment distribution becomes laborious and matrix stiffness takes over. And check **P–Δ** afterwards: it invalidates the very superposition the method relied on.

questions.stem: The stiffness of a prismatic member at one end, when the far end is hinged, is:
questions.solution:
**3EI/L** when the far end is hinged, against **4EI/L** when it is fixed.

**Why the hinged case is less stiff:** a **pin cannot resist moment**, so the far end **rotates freely** instead of pushing back. The near end therefore meets less resistance and the member is **three quarters as stiff**.

**The four numbers that constitute moment distribution:**

| Far end | Stiffness | Carry-over factor |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** | **½** |
| **HINGED** | **3EI/L** | **ZERO** |

> The two go together: **a pin cannot hold a moment, so nothing is carried over to it** — and the reduced stiffness is the same fact seen from the other end.

**The practical value of the modified stiffness:**

> Using **3EI/L with zero carry-over** for a member framing into a **simply supported end** removes that joint from the iteration entirely, **saving a full cycle** of distribution. It is the standard simplification for the end span of a continuous beam.

**Derivation** from slope-deflection, applying a moment M at A with B hinged (so M_BA = 0):

> **M_BA = (2EI/L)(2θ_B + θ_A) = 0** → **θ_B = −θ_A/2**
> **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B) = (2EI/L)(2θ_A − θ_A/2) = (2EI/L)(3θ_A/2) = 3EIθ_A/L** ✓

**Other modified stiffnesses** for special cases, all of which halve the work when they apply:

| Case | Modified stiffness |
|---|---|
| Far end **fixed** | **4EI/L** |
| Far end **hinged** | **3EI/L** |
| **Symmetrical** structure, symmetrical loading | **2EI/L** for the member on the axis |
| **Symmetrical** structure, **anti**symmetrical loading | **6EI/L** |

> **The symmetry cases allow analysis of HALF the structure**, which is a substantial saving on a symmetric multi-bay frame. The modified stiffness accounts for what the omitted half would have done.

**Where stiffness governs behaviour** — the recurring principle:

> **LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS.** In an indeterminate structure, the member or support with the greater **EI/L** attracts the larger share of the moment.

| Consequence | Example |
|---|---|
| A stiffer member takes more moment | Deep beams attract moment from shallow ones |
| A **fixed** end attracts more than a **pinned** one | The propped cantilever's 5/8 versus 3/8 reaction split |
| A **short** column attracts more shear than a tall one | **Shear ∝ 1/L³** — the origin of the **short column failure** in earthquakes |

**The short column effect is worth knowing** because it kills people:

> In a frame where **infill masonry** leaves a short clear height of column (a partial-height wall, or a window band), that column becomes **far stiffer** than its full-height neighbours and attracts a **disproportionate share of the seismic shear** — then fails in brittle shear before any ductile mechanism can develop.

> It is one of the commonest observed failures in earthquakes, and the remedy is either to **isolate the infill** from the frame or to detail the short column for the shear it will actually attract.

**Relation to the stiffness matrix**: **4EI/L** and **2EI/L** are the diagonal and off-diagonal rotational terms of the beam element stiffness matrix — so **the carry-over factor is simply their ratio**, and moment distribution is matrix analysis done by hand.

examTip.trick: **3EI/L pairs with ZERO carry-over; 4EI/L pairs with ½.** They are the same fact from two ends: a pin cannot hold a moment, so nothing carries over to it and the member is less stiff.
examTip.trap: Using 4EI/L and ½ for a **simply supported end span** wastes a full cycle of distribution and gives wrong intermediate values. Use the modified stiffness and drop that joint from the iteration.
examTip.mnemonic: **LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS** — and shear goes as **1/L³**, which is why a **short column** created by partial-height infill attracts huge seismic shear and fails brittly. One of the commonest earthquake failures.

questions.stem: The substitute frame method for analysing a multi-storey building frame under vertical load assumes that:
options: The whole frame behaves as a single cantilever
Each floor may be analysed separately with the columns above and below fixed at their far ends
All the beams have the same span
questions.solution:
**Each floor may be analysed separately, with the columns above and below taken as FIXED at their far ends.**

**Why the simplification is valid** under vertical load:

> A load applied on one floor produces moments that **die away rapidly** with distance. By the second floor above or below, the effect is negligible — so a floor can be analysed with only its immediately adjacent columns, and those columns' far ends may be treated as fixed with very little error.

**The substitute frame comprises:**

| Component | Treatment |
|---|---|
| The **beams of one floor** | Full continuity |
| The **columns immediately above and below** | Included, **fixed at their far ends** |
| Everything else | Ignored |

> The result is a small, tractable frame — analysed by **moment distribution** in a few minutes — instead of the whole building.

**Its limitation, which is the essential caveat:**

> **It applies to VERTICAL load only.** Under **LATERAL (wind or seismic) load** the frame **sways as a whole**, and the storeys are not independent at all — a load at roof level produces shear in every column right down to the foundation.

> For lateral load the **portal** and **cantilever** methods are used instead.

**The two lateral-load approximate methods:**

| Method | Assumptions | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **PORTAL** | Contraflexure at **mid-height of columns** and **mid-span of beams**; shear shared in proportion to bay width (interior columns take **twice** an exterior one) | **Low to medium rise** — shear-dominated behaviour |
| **CANTILEVER** | Column **axial** forces proportional to distance from the centroid; contraflexure at mid-height and mid-span | **TALL, slender** frames — overall bending dominates |

> The choice reflects how the building actually resists lateral load: a **squat** frame behaves like a shear beam, a **slender** one like a cantilever. A rough guide is a height-to-width ratio of about 4.

**Pattern loading still applies** within the substitute frame:

| To maximise | Load |
|---|---|
| **Sagging** in a span | That span **plus alternate** spans |
| **Hogging** at a support | The **two adjacent** spans |
| **Column moment** | The **adjacent spans loaded unequally** |

> That last case is important and easy to forget: a column's moment comes from the **imbalance** between the beams either side, so it is maximised by loading one span and not the other — not by loading everything.

**Why approximate methods still matter** when software is universal:

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Preliminary sizing** before a model exists | Members must be estimated to build the model |
| **CHECKING** computer output | A model with a wrong restraint produces confident nonsense |
| Understanding **how the frame works** | Which member attracts what, and why |
| Rapid feasibility studies | — |

> **The checking role is the most valuable.** A designer who can estimate a frame's moments by hand to within 20% will notice when a model returns something implausible; one who cannot will not.

**IS 456's tabulated coefficients** (cl. 22.5.1) are a further simplification for beams of approximately equal span under substantially uniform load — they already embody the pattern-loading envelope, and for standard cases they replace the analysis entirely.

examTip.trap: **It is for VERTICAL load only.** Under lateral load the frame sways as a whole and the storeys are not independent — a roof-level load produces shear in every column down to the foundation. Use the **portal** or **cantilever** method instead.
examTip.trick: The justification is that vertical-load moments **die away within one floor**, so fixing the far ends of the adjacent columns introduces very little error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Portal method for low-rise (shear behaviour); CANTILEVER method for tall slender frames (bending behaviour).** And note: a **column's** moment comes from the **imbalance** between the beams either side, so it is maximised by loading one span and not the other.

questions.stem: A propped cantilever of span L carries a UDL w. The bending moment at the fixed end is:
questions.solution:
**wL²/8** (hogging) at the fixed end.

**Derive it by compatibility.** Release the prop, leaving a cantilever:

> Free-end deflection under the UDL: **wL⁴/(8EI)** downward
> Deflection from an upward prop force R: **RL³/(3EI)**
> Setting the net deflection to zero: **R = 3wL/8**

> Then taking moments about the fixed end:
> **M = wL²/2 − (3wL/8)(L) = wL²/2 − 3wL²/8 = wL²/8** ✓

**The complete results:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Moment at fixed end** | **wL²/8** (hogging) |
| **Reaction at fixed end** | **5wL/8** |
| **Reaction at prop** | **3wL/8** |
| **Maximum sagging moment** | **9wL²/128** at **0.375L** from the prop |
| **Point of contraflexure** | **0.25L** from the prop |
| Maximum deflection | wL⁴/(185EI) at 0.4215L from the prop |

**Note that 9/128 = 0.0703 is less than 1/8 = 0.125**, so **the fixed-end hogging moment governs** the design — which is characteristic of propped cantilevers and of the end spans of continuous beams.

**The unequal reactions illustrate the recurring principle:**

> **LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS.** The fixed end is stiffer than the prop, so it takes **5/8** against the prop's **3/8**.

**Comparison of the three UDL cases:**

| Beam | M_max | δ_max | D_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **wL²/8** (midspan) | 5wL⁴/384EI | 0 |
| **Propped cantilever** | **wL²/8** (fixed end) | wL⁴/185EI | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | **wL²/12** (supports) | wL⁴/384EI | **3** |

> **Interesting**: the propped cantilever's maximum moment is the **same as the simply supported beam's** — but its **deflection is 2.6 times smaller**, and the moment has moved from midspan to the support, where a deeper section is usually available.

**Note the distractors are all real values in adjacent contexts:**

| Option | Which case |
|---|---|
| **wL²/12** | **Fixed-ended** beam, support moment |
| **wL²/24** | Fixed-ended beam, **midspan** moment |
| **wL²/16** | An IS 456 continuous-beam coefficient |

**Where propped cantilevers occur in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| The **end span of a continuous beam** | Behaves very nearly as one — fixed at the interior support by continuity, simply supported at the end wall |
| **Temporary propping** during construction | Creates the condition explicitly |
| A cantilever with a support added at its tip | — |

> **The construction case is why the sequence of prop removal is specified** rather than left to site judgement: removing props in the wrong order can impose a load case the member was never designed for.

**A caution about the prop's stiffness:**

> The result **R = 3wL/8** assumes the prop is **UNYIELDING**. If it settles by δ, the reaction reduces:

> **R = 3wL/8 − 3EIδ/L³**

> And if the settlement reaches **wL⁴/(8EI)**, the prop reaction vanishes entirely and the member reverts to a pure cantilever with a fixed-end moment of **wL²/2** — **four times** the design value.

> That sensitivity to support movement is the defining characteristic of indeterminate structures, and it must be checked wherever the prop's stiffness is uncertain.

examTip.trap: **All three distractors are real values**: wL²/12 (fixed beam, support), wL²/24 (fixed beam, midspan), wL²/16 (an IS 456 coefficient). Identify the beam before looking at the options.
examTip.trick: Get R by compatibility — cantilever deflection **wL⁴/8EI** cancelled by **RL³/3EI** gives **R = 3wL/8** — then take moments. Check: **5wL/8 + 3wL/8 = wL** ✓.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixed end 5/8, prop 3/8 — LOAD FLOWS TOWARD STIFFNESS.** And the result assumes an **unyielding prop**: settlement reduces R, and enough settlement reverts the member to a cantilever with **four times** the moment.

questions.stem: Compared with a force method, a displacement method is generally preferred for computer analysis because it:
options: Requires no choice of redundants and is systematic to program
Does not require the material properties
questions.solution:
**Because it requires no choice of redundants and is systematic to program.**

**The decisive difference:**

| | **FORCE (flexibility)** | **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness)** |
|---|---|---|
| Unknowns | Redundant **forces** | Joint **displacements** |
| Requires a **choice** | **YES — which redundants to release** | **NO** |
| A bad choice | Makes the arithmetic far worse | Cannot occur |
| An invalid choice | Leaves an **unstable** primary structure | Cannot occur |
| Assembly | Case by case | **Standard member matrices, added together** |

> **The need for judgement is what a computer cannot supply.** Choosing a valid and convenient set of redundants requires understanding the structure — which is exactly the step the stiffness method does not have.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "Always has fewer unknowns" | **Not true.** D_k can exceed D_s — a **fixed beam** has D_s = 3 but D_k = 0, so the force method has *more* unknowns there. Neither dominates in general |
| "Does not require material properties" | **Both require E and I.** Indeterminate analysis of any kind depends on relative stiffnesses |
| "More accurate" | **Both are exact** for a linear elastic structure. They differ in convenience, not in accuracy |

> **That both methods give the same exact answer** is worth stating plainly: the choice is entirely one of labour and programmability.

**Why the stiffness method suits computers so well:**

| Feature | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Standard element matrices** | Beam, truss, plate — each coded once and reused |
| **Assembly by addition** | Contributions simply added into the global matrix at the right rows and columns |
| **Symmetric and BANDED** | Only members sharing a joint interact, so most entries are zero and solvers exploit it |
| **Extends to dynamics** | **[M]{ü} + [C]{u̇} + [K]{u} = {F}** — the same [K] |
| Extends to non-linearity | Tangent stiffness updated iteratively |

> **The extension to dynamics and non-linearity is decisive for modern practice.** Seismic analysis, buckling analysis and staged construction all build directly on the same stiffness formulation, while the flexibility method has no comparable path.

**Where the force method still earns its place:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **One or two redundants**, by hand | Often the quickest route |
| **Two-hinged arches** | The strain-energy formulation is natural |
| **Conceptual transparency** | It shows *why* the redundant takes the value it does |
| Teaching | The compatibility idea is easier to see |

**A practical caution about stiffness output:**

> Because the method is systematic, it is easy to run and hard to sanity-check. A model with a **wrong restraint**, a **disconnected node**, or an **incorrect member release** produces confident nonsense.

**The disciplines that catch it:**

| Check | What it reveals |
|---|---|
| Does the **deflected shape** look plausible? | Wrong restraints, missing members |
| Do the **reactions sum to the applied load**? | Load input errors |
| Does a **hand check of one member** agree within 20%? | Systematic modelling errors |
| Are the **support reactions** in sensible proportion? | Stiffness or connectivity errors |

> **A designer who can estimate a frame's moments by hand will notice when a model returns something implausible.** That is the enduring value of the approximate methods — portal, cantilever, substitute frame — in an era when nobody analyses a building by hand.

examTip.trap: "Always fewer unknowns" is **false** — a **fixed beam** has D_s = 3 but **D_k = 0**, so the force method has more unknowns there. Neither method dominates on count.
examTip.trick: **Both methods are EXACT** for a linear elastic structure. The choice is entirely about **labour and programmability**, never accuracy — which is why "more accurate" is always the wrong answer to this question.
examTip.mnemonic: **No choice of redundants = programmable.** And always sanity-check output: **deflected shape plausible? reactions sum to the load? one member checked by hand?** A model with a wrong restraint produces confident nonsense.

questions.stem: In a fixed beam of span L carrying a uniformly distributed load w, the ratio of the support moment to the midspan moment is:
questions.solution:
**2 : 1** — the support moment is **wL²/12** and the midspan moment **wL²/24**.

> **(wL²/12)/(wL²/24) = 24/12 = 2** ✓

**Check the sum**, which is the most useful relation in this topic:

> **wL²/12 + wL²/24 = 2wL²/24 + wL²/24 = 3wL²/24 = wL²/8** ✓

> **That is exactly the FREE bending moment** of a simply supported span. Fixing the ends does not reduce the total — it **REDISTRIBUTES** it between the supports and the span.

**The general principle:**

> **Support moment + midspan moment = the free moment (wL²/8).** That relation holds for any degree of end fixity, and it is the quickest way to check a continuous beam result.

**The full comparison:**

| Beam | Support moment | Span moment | Maximum | δ_max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | 0 | **wL²/8** | wL²/8 | 5wL⁴/384EI |
| **Propped cantilever** | **wL²/8** | 9wL²/128 | wL²/8 | wL⁴/185EI |
| **Fixed both ends** | **wL²/12** | **wL²/24** | **wL²/12** | **wL⁴/384EI** |

**The benefits of full fixity:**

| Quantity | Improvement |
|---|---|
| **Maximum moment** | **33% less** (wL²/12 against wL²/8) |
| **Maximum deflection** | **80% less** — one fifth |

> **The deflection reduction is the more dramatic**, and it is why continuity is so structurally valuable: a continuous beam is significantly lighter than a series of simply supported ones for the same span and load.

**The points of contraflexure** are at **0.211L from each end** — which is where the moment changes sign and where the tension face swaps from top to bottom. That locates the reinforcement curtailment.

**The costs of fixity:**

| Cost | Note |
|---|---|
| **Settlement induces moments** | **M = 6EIδ/L²** — comparable with the design moment for only a few millimetres |
| **Temperature and shrinkage** induce stress | The restraint is the source of the stress |
| **True fixity is hard to achieve** | A real support lies somewhere between pinned and fixed |
| Analysis is more involved | Compatibility as well as equilibrium |

> **The settlement sensitivity is the practical objection**, and it is why fixed ends are avoided on compressible or variable ground.

**Standard fixed-end moments**, needed for moment distribution and slope-deflection:

| Loading | FEM at each end |
|---|---|
| **UDL w** | **wL²/12** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8** |
| **Point load W at a from left** | **Wab²/L²** (left), **Wa²b/L²** (right) |
| Couple M at midspan | M/4 |
| Triangular, zero to w | wL²/30, wL²/20 |

> For an **off-centre point load** the two FEMs are **unequal**, and the **larger is at the NEARER support**. That is intuitive once seen and easy to reverse under pressure.

**A useful check for the central point load case**: FEM = WL/8 at each end, and the midspan moment is also **WL/8** — so the ratio there is **1 : 1**, not 2 : 1. The ratio depends on the loading, which is why the question specifies a UDL.

examTip.trick: **Support + midspan = the FREE moment wL²/8** — always, for any degree of end fixity. Here wL²/12 + wL²/24 = wL²/8 ✓, which confirms both values in one line.
examTip.trap: The **2 : 1 ratio is specific to a UDL**. For a **central point load** the fixed-end and midspan moments are both **WL/8**, so the ratio is **1 : 1**. Read the loading.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixing the ends cuts the peak moment by a THIRD and the deflection to a FIFTH** — that is the value of continuity. The price is **6EIδ/L²** from settlement, which is why fixed ends are avoided on compressible ground.
